### The lane root is the handshake's secret, and the transcript only salts it (2026-11-04)

The parked sealing design derived each stream's key from the lane's **handshake
hash**. That is wrong, and it is wrong in the direction that matters: the
handshake hash is a digest of the messages both ends exchanged. Anyone who
watched the handshake — or who holds either static key and can replay the
exchange — recomputes it. A key schedule built on it would move forward secrecy
from per-stream to per-lane and then hand it away, which is worse than the
per-stream handshake it exists to replace, because that handshake was at least
secret.

So [`LaneRoot`](src/transport/mhd/cipher.rs) takes two inputs and documents
why neither alone will do:

- the **raw split** — Noise's own secret output, the exact material
  `into_transport_mode` installs, reached through snow's `risky-raw-split`
  feature (`dangerously_get_raw_split`). Named "risky" by the crate because it
  exports key material; that is precisely what a derivation root needs, and it
  is the reason the feature is the right tool here rather than a re-implementation
  of the state machine;
- the **handshake hash**, as the HKDF **salt** — a public value that binds the
  root to one handshake without ever being derivable from it.

`HKDF-SHA256(salt = transcript, ikm = split[0] ‖ split[1], info = "molehill mhd
lane root v1")` gives the root; `StreamCipher::derive` then derives one
(direction, stream) key from it as before. A test pins both halves: changing
the secret while holding the transcript fixed changes every stream key, and so
does changing the transcript while holding the secret fixed — the regression
that would ship a transcript-only root while still passing every "both ends
agree" test.

Two consequences written down rather than discovered later:
- `from_handshake` answers `Option`, and `None` means **do not seal** — the
  caller falls back to the per-stream handshake instead of sealing under a root
  nobody computed;
- the nonce is the packet number, which is `u32` per connection. A wrap would
  reuse a nonce with the same key, so the sealing path must refuse near the
  wrap (or re-establish the lane) rather than wrap silently. 2³² datagrams is
  ~6 TB, which no test will reach — which is exactly why it has to be an
  explicit refusal and not an assumption.

### The sealed failure is not the harness, and its signature was not what it looked like (2026-11-05)

Two corrections, both from measuring with a detector that cannot be fooled by a
debug line:

- **`mhd transport selector timed out` is not the failure signature.** It appears in
  *passing* runs too — four streams whose selector never arrives while the group still
  gathers enough channels and carries the whole transfer. An earlier entry read it as
  the server waiting on the streams that mattered; it does not say that.
- **the test's echo is not the cause.** With a strict detector (`test result: ok`), the
  sealed striped test passes **3 of 8** with the coupled `io::copy` echo and **2 of 8**
  with the decoupled reader/queue/writer one. Reverted, for the second time and now
  with a detector worth trusting.

So the sealed path fails about five times in eight and nothing about the harness
explains it. The trace of a failing run is consistent from run to run: the client's
response direction — whose source is the local echo — reads a variable number of frames
(123 / 3 975 680 bytes in one run; 455 KiB, 440 KiB, 826 KiB in others) and then
`stripe source read has not returned for two seconds`, forever, while the visitor reads
EOF at that byte. The number is not stable across runs (the three appearances of
465 920 were one batch, not a law), so it is a stopping point rather than a boundary.

What is now excluded for this path: the two never-sent packet numbers (fixed), the
repair path itself (a sealed stream repairs a dropped packet correctly in a unit test),
the harness's echo (measured twice), and the control plane and every arrival stage
(measured in the rounds above). What is left is the stripe layer's own accounting over
sealed streams — where `MAX_SEALED_PAYLOAD` clamps the packet but the frame is 32 KiB,
and the reorder loop's `written` is the byte count the visitor's EOF is measured
against.

### A second never-sent packet number, and the deadlock gets better but not gone (2026-11-05)

The first leak was a refused packet consuming a number. There was a **second**, one
level further in and reachable only on the sealed path, which is why sealing alone
deadlocked stripes: `seal_stream_payload` can fail after `encode_stream` has already
written the header and after the number was taken, and the `?` there abandoned the
packet with its number consumed — a hole in the peer's cumulative frontier that can
never be filled, and every later acknowledgement re-declares everything above it lost.

A lane that cannot seal is now **closed**, where the pool can rebuild it, instead of
continuing with a hole: `note_no_key` counts it and `closed` is set with a reason of its
own. A silent repair loop becomes one lane restart.

Two more things were measured while looking:

- a sealed stream **does** repair a dropped packet. `a_sealed_stream_repairs_one_dropped_packet`
  drops one stream packet off the wire, fires the timer, and asserts every byte lands —
  it passes, so the loop is not in the repair path itself;
- with the fix, the sealed striped test improves from two-or-three of six to **four of
  six**. Not cured. Two of the failures stopped at **465 920 bytes**, which is the same
  number two runs reached earlier in the cycle — three times now for the same value, on
  a transfer whose frame size is 32 KiB, so it is not a frame boundary and it is not yet
  explained.

So sealing is still off. What has changed is that a lane with a hole now says so
instead of looking healthy, and the sealed path's failure rate is halved by a defect
whose mechanism is understood rather than by luck.

### Sealing is wired, tested, and OFF: a striped group deadlocks with it (2026-11-04)

The derivation is now plumbed end to end — `NoiseStream::session_roots`, a lane
root installed on `Conn`, per-stream ciphers, the frame flag, the sealed
`StreamState`, and `DERIVED_SELECTOR` — and it is **disabled by default** behind
`MOLEHILL_MHD_SEAL`, because on the one topology that shares a lane between
several streams at once it hangs. The A/B is six runs of the same test on one
host, the only difference being whether the root is installed:

| `striped_data_channels` (4 stripes, 8 MiB echo) | runs passed |
|---|---|
| sealing **off** (`io::copy` echo, per-stream KK) | **6 of 6** |
| sealing **on** | **3 of 6** |

What the sealed failures look like, from the carrier's own lines:

```
mhd stalled: bytes waiting unsent_ms=212 unacked_ms=213 credit_blocked=false
  backlog_streams=0 worst_stream=5 worst_stream_unsent=950569
  worst_stream_retransmits=0 worst_stream_next=117312 worst_stream_written=950570
mhd window lane=3 cwnd=76893 flight=0
```

`written` 950 570 against `next` 117 312 — 833 KB queued behind a send cursor
that stops moving — with the peer's credit untouched, **no retransmission ever
recorded**, and a congestion window of 63–77 KB against a flight of ~0. The
server, meanwhile, logs four `mhd transport selector timed out` half a minute
later: the streams it had accepted never received their first byte. Nothing was
refused (`unsealed_tags=0`, `no_key=0`, and the two new refusal counters this
round added — `unsealed_no_root`, `unsealed_no_tag`, `unsealed_no_key` — all
read zero on the next capture), so the bytes were **not sent**, not lost.

**That missing counter was itself the defect in the instrument.** A sealed packet
this end cannot open was dropped in total silence: `unsealed_tags` counts *tag
failures*, so a refusal for "no root here" left every counter reading healthy
while the peer waited out a thirty-second deadline. It is now counted apart and
logged once with the stream id, so the next round starts from a measurement
instead of from a timeout.

Two experiments were spent ruling out the neighbours, and both are recorded
because they cost the time:

- **the echo is not the cause.** Decoupling `tests/common`'s echo — the same
  reader/queue/writer shape the bench backend got — moved the failure rate from
  4 of 5 to 3 of 6, i.e. not at all, and the change was reverted;
- **the in-process stripe harness is not an instrument.** The parked patch's
  `a_sealed_stripe_group_carries_a_transfer` stalls at **zero** bytes without
  wake-ups, at **128** bytes with them, and at **384** bytes with sealing
  *disabled* — so it never carried a transfer in any configuration, and it was
  deleted rather than left red. (Its lesson is worth keeping: a harness that
  steps `Conn` by hand must call `wake_readers`/`wake_writers` after every
  datagram, because in production the pump task does, and a missing wake-up reads
  exactly like a stalled layer.)

So the arrival path's largest measured lever is built, proved on the arithmetic
(one handshake per lane instead of one per visitor), and **not shipped**, because
the striped configuration deadlocks and stripe count grows under backpressure in
production. The next round's first job is the deadlock, with the switch as its
reproduction, not a re-derivation of the cipher.

### The arrival's chain is closed, and it lands on the per-stream handshake (2026-11-05)

Three stamps on one wall clock, joined by group id — one `SystemTime` read per event,
gated on the stats switch, which is the only way to time an interval that crosses two
processes. 1 201 groups of one staged cell, each with exactly one request:

| interval | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **control hop**: server sends the request → client's loop reads it | **0.056 ms** | 0.107 | **0.219** |
| **hand-off**: client's loop reads it → server pairs the visitor | 1.611 ms | 8.376 | **47.513 ms** |

And the server's own four stamps for the 188 pairings it calls slow:

| phase | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|
| `accept → pairing started` | **0.058 ms** | 0.123 |
| `pairing started → request enqueued` | 0.001 | 0.005 |
| **`request enqueued → first channel taken`** | **13.933 ms** | **122.455** |
| `first channel → forwarding command written` | 0.004 | 13.636 |
| total, `accept → paired` | 14.206 | 122.481 |

The two instruments agree to 0.4 % once the populations are matched — the cross-process
hand-off on those same 187 groups reads p50 **13.875**, p99 **122.430**. (The first
version of this entry called that a contradiction; it was comparing the hand-off's
median over *all* pairings with the server's median over the *slow* ones, which is the
population mistake this file keeps warning about and kept making.)

So the whole chain, in one column, for arrivals that are slow:

| | p50 |
|---|---|
| accept → pairing started | 0.058 ms |
| → the request is on the wire | 0.001 |
| → the client's control loop reads it | 0.056 |
| **→ the client has opened the stream and written its prologue** | **11.5 ms** |
| → the server takes the channel (prologue transit + push) | ~2 |
| → the pairing is woken and takes it | **0.004** |
| total | 14.2 |

**Every term is now measured, and the 11.5 ms is the per-stream mhd handshake** — the
same interval that reads `us == hs_us` with a share of 1.000, and the same one that
sealing deletes. The wake is 4 µs, the control plane 56 µs, the accept 58 µs, the
forwarding write 4 µs: none of them can be the tail any more, and no scheduling change
can touch a term that is four microseconds.

That closes the question this cycle spent four rounds on. The arrival is slow because
it performs a Noise handshake per stream, on a lane that is carrying bulk, and every
other explanation is now excluded by its own measurement. **The lever is sealing, and
its only blocker is the striped deadlock** — 3 of 6 runs, a repair loop with
`retransmits=1532`, narrowed but not yet cured.

### The tail is the pairing wait, and the arithmetic finally closes (2026-11-05)

The probe now splits its own round trip at the send. 555 arrivals of one staged cell:

| | p50 | p90 | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the whole round trip | 14.44 ms | 72.78 | **228.56** | 457.28 |
| connect + send | 0.193 ms | 0.271 | 0.452 | 1.403 |
| **waiting for the echo** | **14.19 ms** | 72.65 | **228.40** | 457.05 |

So the tool's accept path is fast and the tail is the wait for the reply. The first
version of this entry guessed the *kernel accept queue* and was refuted in one
experiment: `ss -ltn` inside the server's namespace, sampled 134 times across a run of
the same cell, read `Recv-Q = 0` **every time**. Nothing was piling up.

The same run's server-side windows then close the arithmetic exactly:

| phase (34 one-second windows, median of the window p50s) | |
|---|---|
| `accept → paired` | **10.232 ms** (p99 42.2) |
| `paired → first byte` | 0.022 ms |
| the echo (first byte → reply byte written) | 3.296 ms |
| **sum** | **13.550 ms** |
| the probe's own "waiting for the echo" | **14.19 ms** |

**The pairing wait is the tail** — 10.2 ms of the 14.2 — and everything after it is
microseconds plus a three-millisecond echo. That is the same conclusion the first stage
reached from a different direction (`paired_p99` 112 ms in the full-scale run); what is
new is that it is now the *whole* explanation of a warm cell, not a fragment of a
cold one.

So the arrival's cost is: server accepts, **asks the client for a channel**, the client
opens an mhd stream, the server pairs. The client's own phases are known — dequeue
~0, `spawn → first poll` 4–12 µs, handshake 1.34–1.38 ms — so of the 10.2 ms, about
1.4 is the open and the rest is the **control-plane round trip plus the pairing
hand-off**: the request crossing to the client's control loop, and the channel's
arrival waking the pairing.

That is the last interval in an arrival that has never been stamped, and it is
pre-registered for the next round: emit the server's send time and the client's receive
time for the same `CreateDataChannelFor` group id — both ends are on one host, so epoch
milliseconds are comparable — and split the 8.8 ms between the control hop and the
pairing hand-off. Whichever it is decides between the two remaining structural
candidates, a server-initiated stream (which deletes the request entirely) and a
direct hand-off (which deletes the wake).

### The carrier's whole round trip is fast, and the tail is outside it (2026-11-05)

The interval every previous instrument stopped short of now has a distribution: from
the request byte the server's forwarding loop read to the first byte it wrote back to
that same visitor — the carrier's two directions plus the client and the backend.

| | p50 | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| a visitor's echo after its own request | **538–708 µs** | 1.2–23.3 ms | 23.3 ms |

In the same rounds the cell reads **p99 104.3, 37.7, 116.5 and 7.6 ms**. The echo's
p99 never reaches the cell's, and its *maximum* in a second is below the cell's p99
over thirty seconds — so for these runs **the carrier's round trip is not where the
tail is**, and everything this cycle built for the arrival is confirmed as fast from
the other side.

What is left is the two boundaries the server cannot see, and they are the probe's own
view of the tool:

- **before the request byte**: the visitor's `connect()` and its `send`, i.e. the
  *tool's* accept path. `accepted_at` is stamped after `accept()` returns, so a
  connection that sat in the kernel's accept queue is invisible to every counter here;
- **after the reply byte**: the probe's own read, which on this host is a Python
  selector and a syscall.

That is a smaller remaining question than the ones this file has been asking, and it is
the first time the answer has been *outside* the carrier for a population this large.
The next instrument follows from it: stamp the listener's accept boundary — the time
between a connection being ready and this end taking it — and compare it with the
probe's own measured round trip. If the accept path accounts for the rest, the SLO is
being decided by the server's accept loop and not by mhd at all, which changes what
the release claim can honestly say.

### Every stage of the arrival is microseconds, and a second population is not (2026-11-05)

The dispatcher's admission of a new lane — registry lock, admission table, `Conn`, a
`Shared`, a spawned sender task, two insertions — costs **p50 27 µs, p99 39 µs**. That
was the last hypothesis about the receiving end, and with it every interval the
arrival crosses now has a distribution:

| interval | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|
| a datagram's wait for its stream's accept | 7–8 µs | 12–90 µs |
| a lane admitted inside the receive callback | 27 µs | 39 µs |
| a stream's first byte waiting for the wire (dwell) | 2–11 µs | 0.2–0.5 ms |
| the pump's post to the socket | 10–25 µs | 20–104 µs |
| the client's spawn → first poll (`started_us`) | **4–12 µs** | — |
| the client's dequeue → prologue (`cmd_us − ready_us`) | ~0 | — |
| the per-stream handshake, every open | 1.34–1.38 ms | 1.78 ms |
| the server's pairing (`paired`) | 1.5–1.9 ms | 2–6 ms |
| the server's first forwarded byte (`first`) | 19–22 µs | 37–46 µs |

Add the medians and an arrival costs about **three milliseconds**. The cell it was
measured in reports **p99 44.5, 50.7, 53.9 ms** in its three warm rounds (and 219 ms in
the round that starts the process) — ten to a hundred times the sum of every stage.

**So in these runs the tail is not in the arrival.** It is in what the probe does
after its request has been forwarded: the 64-byte echo has to come back through the client, the
backend and the carrier before the probe can stop its clock, and the probe's sample is
the whole round trip. The instruments above stop at "the server forwarded the first
byte" — which is why a cell can read tens of milliseconds while every one of them
reads microseconds.

That also reconciles the population sizes that have been nagging this file: the slow
*opens* are rare (13 in four minutes, about one arrival in four hundred, at 5–83 ms),
while the probe's p99 is slow in *every* round, so the two cannot be the same
phenomenon. One is a rare handshake, the other a common return path.

It is a statement about the runs that were measured, not about the carrier in general:
an earlier full-scale run had a server-side `paired_p99` of **112 ms**, i.e. a tail
inside the arrival. The two runs disagree about *where* the tail is because the tail
moves — which is the same lottery this file keeps meeting, seen from the other side.

**Pre-registered next instrument**: split the probe's own round trip at the boundary
this cycle has never timed — from the forwarding of the request to the visitor's echo
being read back. On the server that is `first_*` plus the return; on the client it is
the response direction's own path. The gate is the same as always: the interval's
distribution, then whatever it names, judged on its own A/B.

### The tail is a transport delay, and the timer only marks its boundary (2026-11-05)

The accept queue is not the wait: a stream waits **p50 7 µs, p99 12–14 µs** between
the datagram that names it and the loop that takes it (new instrument, reported as
`a stream waiting for its accept`). So the second of the two intervals this carrier
could not see is also fast.

The first version of this entry read one log line as "a fresh lane pays the
small-flight timer" — `window=13490` is `INITIAL_CWND`, so the lane had carried
nothing. **That inference is wrong**: `window` is `cwnd − flight`, and a lane whose
congestion window has stayed near its initial value reads the same number after a
megabyte. What the whole population says is better, and is the reason this entry was
rewritten rather than extended. Every slow open in one run, in order:

| open | remaining window | retransmissions |
|---|---|---|
| 5.5 / 6.0 / 10.9 ms | 21 584 / 13 490 / 22 933 | **0** |
| 15.2 / 15.8 / 16.7 / 20.6 ms | 13 490 each | **0** |
| 23.1 / 23.4 / 23.4 / 23.6 ms | 13 490 each | **1** |
| 27.6 / 33.4 / 39.7 / 45.6 / 66.4 / 83.4 ms | 13 404–20 144 | 1–3 |

Read down the middle: the opens climb from 5.5 to **20.6 ms with no retransmission at
all**, and only then does a cluster appear at 23+ with exactly one. So the
retransmission is not the cause of the tail — it is the *marker* of the 20 ms
`SMALL_FLIGHT_INITIAL_RTO` boundary, adding a duplicate and three milliseconds to
opens that were already late. **The delay itself is in the handshake's transport, and
it happens before any timer fires.**

That is a smaller claim than the one it replaces and it is the one the numbers
support: between 0.5 and 20 ms an open is slow with nothing lost and nothing refused
(`credit` 16.7 MB, `queued_streams=0`, `retransmits=0`), while every instrument the
carrier owns — dwell, post, accept, lock, park — reads microseconds.

**Pre-registered next experiment**: the remaining candidate is the dispatcher's own
batch. A datagram for a lane the listener has never seen is handled *inside* the
receive callback (registry lock, admission check, `Conn::new`, a `Shared`, a sender
task spawned, two map insertions) before the next `recv` of that batch, so bulk
traffic and a new lane's first packet share one task's critical section. Measure the
batch's processing time with its datagram count; if it reaches tens of milliseconds,
move the new-lane setup off the receive path and re-measure. Gate: the batch time
stays in microseconds and the arrival's p99 on the `cost` cell falls below the 20 ms
line that the timer cluster marks.

### Fewer wake-ups help, and do not touch the first stage (2026-11-05)

A lane carries four or five streams and a receive batch usually delivers bytes for
one, so the pump was waking every parked reader on the lane for each batch. It now
records which streams changed (`Conn::woke`) and wakes one reader per id; the
blanket wake stays for the events that really are connection-wide.

**On a staged cell with six bulk streams** (interleaved, three rounds, `--aa`):

| metric | change |
|---|---|
| `rtt_p99_ms` | **−79.35 %** |
| `rtt_p50_ms` | −51.70 % |
| `rtt_worst_1s_ms` | −75.52 % |
| `rtt_max_ms` | −66.27 % |
| `throughput_gbps` | **+16.79 %** (CI 1.28..2.08, entirely beyond its floor) |

Every latency metric moves the same way and throughput moves with them, which is
what fewer spurious wake-ups should look like — but the verdict is `directional`,
not `claim`, because at three rounds the cell's own A/A scatter is 48 % on p99.

**On the cell that decides the release** it does not fix the first stage. Full
scale, one arm, host quiet (load 0.24 / 0.75):

| stage | n | p50 | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `clean` (first) | 1 964 | **36.47** | **302.13** | 509.68 |
| `clean#2` (last) | 2 396 | **2.48** | **22.54** | 24.77 |

The last stage is the best it has ever read (22.54 against 23.60 and 23.65 in the
two previous runs), so the change is worth keeping. The first stage is the worst it
has ever read — and that is the finding: across four runs of near-identical code
the first clean stage has now read **25.79, 112.85, 146.03 and 302.13 ms** while the
last has read **22.5–23.7** every time. The *last* stage is a measurement; the
first is a lottery, and every lever tried against it so far (credit reserve, worker
count, scheduler order, wake scope) has left it a lottery.

Two things the four numbers do establish, and they are not the same problem:

- **the warm stage is 10× the control** — 22.5 ms against 2.28 — so even with no
  cold start there is a tail: about one arrival in a hundred pays twenty
  milliseconds inside a handshake whose own median is 1.0–1.45 ms;
- **the first stage adds a further factor of one to thirteen**, and which one is
  decided by something outside the arrival path: the same binary, the same host
  class, four different answers.

The intervals excluded by measurement so far are the send buffers (dwell p50 2–4 µs
client, 9 µs server), the pump's post (p50 11–20 µs, p99 20–35 µs), the server's
handshake processing (under 5 ms in 1 141 of 1 191 slow opens), the wire itself (the
asymmetry above), the credit reserve, the worker count, and the scheduler's order.
**What is left uninstrumented is the datagram's wait between the socket and the
dispatcher, and the spawn-to-first-poll of the per-stream task** — the server's own
clock starts *after* the stream exists, so neither interval appears in any counter
this cycle built.

**A discipline this cycle learned the hard way**, and it now costs a run each time
it is forgotten: a bench record is only comparable with one whose host was as idle.
The run that read 285.99 ms had a five-minute load average of 4.74 against 0.84 in
its reference; the one killed before it started had 5.71 and would have been the
same story. Check `meta.provenance.host.loadavg` before comparing two files, and
before believing that a change moved a first stage.

### The arrival's tail is not in the carrier's send path (2026-11-05)

Every instrument the carrier owns now reads microseconds at full scale, and the
arrival still reads a hundred:

| what | client | server |
|---|---|---|
| a stream's first byte waiting for the wire (dwell) | p50 **2–4 µs**, p99 ~0.5 ms | p50 **9 µs**, p99 0.14 ms, max 12–70 ms |
| the pump's post to the socket | p50 **11 µs**, p99 20 µs, max 0.18 ms | p50 20 µs, p99 **35 µs**, max 0.35 ms |
| a stream's reader parked for bytes | p50 131 µs, p99 **46 ms**, max **2 s** | p50 64 µs, p99 45 ms, max 2 s |
| the per-stream Noise handshake, every open | p50 **1.0–1.45 ms**, p99 **23–107 ms** | *(not kept on this side)* |

Read together with the earlier attribution — `us == hs_us` for every slow open,
share 1.000 — the handshake is still the whole of an arrival's cost, and its p99
(107 ms) is the arrival's p99 (112.85) to within a few percent. What is new is
that **the handshake's time is not being spent in either end's send path**: the
buffers drain in microseconds and the pump's post never exceeds a third of a
millisecond. So the wait is the interval between a handshake record being written
and the peer's reply being *read* — two task crossings per message, and the reader
parked across them (p99 46 ms, and a 2 s tail that is the keepalive interval to the
microsecond, i.e. a reader that missed its wake-up and waited for the pump's own
timer).

The same asymmetry says it is not the wire: of 1 191 slow client opens, only **50**
were slow on the server's own clock (its `selector + handshake + hello`, under 5 ms
in the other 1 141). Both directions would be slow if the path were; one side is.

Which makes the lever *fewer task crossings per arrival*, not a faster stage — and
that is what sealing does (it deletes both handshake messages and the round trip
they wait on), and why the scheduler work is secondary: a class-aware order cannot
help a packet that is already on the wire while its reader sleeps.

**And the second failed experiment is recorded.** The opening reserve, taken off
every bound, was measured interleaved against the build without it on a quiet host
(load 0.32): `clean` read **5.98 / 146.03 ms** with it and **2.35 / 25.79** without,
while `clean#2` was identical to 0.3 %. The comparison is order-confounded — one
round, two arms run one after the other, on a cell this file has measured at 25.79
and 112.85 for the *same* binary — so it is not a claim about the mechanism. It was
enough to revert, because a change with no demonstrated benefit and a large
apparent harm does not get to stay while someone looks for a better measurement.

### The sealed deadlock is a repair loop, and the instrument was lying twice (2026-11-04)

Two instrument defects came out of following the stall, and each of them had been
hiding it:

- **`note_rejected` collapsed every sealing refusal into `unknown`.** The
  label-to-counter map recognised `malformed`, `malformed_decode`,
  `malformed_lane` and `over_window`, and sent *everything else* — including
  `unsealed`, `unsealed_no_root`, `unsealed_no_tag`, `unsealed_no_key` — to the
  **unknown-stream** counter. So a run whose sealing was failing printed either
  `datagrams refused: unknown=N`, which reads as a routing defect, or (when only
  the sealing labels fired) nothing at all, because the print condition counted
  the four statics that cannot receive them. Sealing now has its own counter,
  matched by prefix so a fourth site cannot fall back to "unknown" again.
- **the stall line could not say *why* a stream with unsent bytes was passed
  over.** It now carries `worst_stream_reset` and `worst_stream_repair`: those
  two are the only ways the scheduler skips such a stream without building a
  packet for it.

With them, the sealed failure names itself:

```
mhd stalled: unsent_ms=0 unacked_ms=569 credit_blocked=false
  worst_stream=5 worst_stream_unsent=1136478 worst_stream_retransmits=1130
  worst_stream_next=2119826 worst_stream_written=2119826
  worst_stream_reset=false worst_stream_repair=true
```

`next == written` — that stream has put **every byte on the wire** — and it is
sitting on a **repair that is re-declared lost and re-sent 1 130 times**, with
no write ever refused (`credit_blocked=false`, `unsent_ms=0`). So the lane is not
stuck for want of room or for want of data: it is stuck spending its flight on
one range it will never see acknowledged, and the four streams whose selectors
the server timed out never got a turn behind it.

That is much narrower than "sealing plus stripes", and it is testable without
sockets: the question is *why a range that the peer has already read is declared
lost again*, which lives in the acknowledgement-to-frontier path, not in the
cipher. The next round starts there — and the first thing it needs is the same
line again, which now exists.

## Negative results: do not retry these blind

Every row was built (or measured) and reverted with its numbers. The archive has
the reasoning; this table exists so a future round does not spend it again.

| mechanism | result |
|---|---|
| yamux over an mhd lane | arrival p99 21.5 → 3.77 ms, but `bulk-n` −23.75 % and CPU/bit +29.37 % |
| a Noise record layer above the carrier | arrival p99 −74 % at three record sizes, and the bulk cell failed at all three |
| pre-opened channel stock | 6 400 arrivals; the stock of 4 is consumed by the first 4 |
| more lanes (4/8/16) | flat within the scatter; the tail is not lane queueing |
| larger `INITIAL_CWND` | first stage **doubled** (79.4 → 153.9 ms p99) |
| smaller `MIN_RTO` (200 → 20 ms) | every bulk cell failed |
| `MIN_RTO_SMALL_FLIGHT` / `SMALL_FLIGHT_INITIAL_RTO` at 5 ms | p99 22.6 / 22.1 against twins 22.3 / 20.3 |
| `TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS` 8 or 16 | monotone the wrong way; the lock is contention, not starvation |
| timer armed from the oldest packet (any kind) | `churn-16` p50 2.44 → 16.07 ms |
| timer armed from the oldest **data** packet | `bulk-n` −60 %; the flight outlives the RTO on this host |
| hole recovery by distance | neutral on every cell |
| eager credit advertisement | `churn-16` p99 +1 068 %; credit frames preempt data |
| `describe_hole` (send table for a receive hole) | answers about the wrong direction |
| per-datagram lock batching | +0.35 %, inside a 9.81 % floor |
| receive-region ownership / pinned pieces | RSS 376 MiB, but throughput 2.76 Gbit/s |
| chunk queue without a read cursor | `cpu_s_per_gbit` 46.7 |
| widening the pool for `soak` | 448 slots, same four stage failures |
| `warmup_rounds` to cure the first stage | a round's first stage is cold again; the probes restart per round |

## Environment

- **20 cores, 23 GB, kernel 6.12.** `/etc/machine-id` is absent, so `host_id`
  hashes CPU model + core count only; the hostname changes without moving it.
- **The cgroup is 13 GiB**, and `oom_kill` is a counter to read per run. Build
  with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`, prefer one release build over many debug feature
  permutations, and check `ps -eo rss,comm --sort=-rss` before a long run — a
  `rustc` for another project competes for the same memory.
- **The host is shared.** Its load swung between 1 and 87 in one afternoon, and
  `bulk-n` swings 3 ⇄ 11 Gbit/s and `capacity` 2 ⇄ 8 streams with no tree
  change. Every run records the load average; §10's "do not conclude across
  variance" is the operative rule.
- **`sudo -n` works, and it drops the environment.** The stats switches need
  `sudo -n env MOLEHILL_MHD_STATS=1 just bench …`; a run whose `server.log` has
  no diagnostic lines is a run with the switch off.
- **Do not run two chains or two bench runs at once.** The suites bind fixed
  ports and the bench holds network namespaces; a second run produces
  `ip netns exec` failures that look like product failures.
- **`/tmp` is periodically wiped.** Keep artifacts under `target/evidence/` or
  `~/tmp/`.
- **`timeout N` orphans the run**: it signals `uv run`, not the python child,
  which keeps going and holds the bench lock.
- **`iperf3` is installed at runtime**, so a container restart drops it
  (`command -v iperf3` first). It is version-sensitive in the fields the model
  reads.
- **Peers and the interop binary are cached** (`~/tmp/bench-peers`,
  `~/tmp/interop`), so a normal run needs no network. `just bench peers fetch`
  re-resolves each peer to its latest GitHub release and records the versions in
  the results meta. `just bench doctor` states what this host can and cannot
  measure before a run has to find out.
- **A baseline-less gate is the norm here.** Every stored baseline either has no
  `host_id` or predates the current method, so a fresh sweep is gated on its own
  absolute checks — coverage, the endpoint invariant, the SLO, drift, wedge and
  the ramp — and the gate names what it could not verify instead of assuming it.
- **A `sudo` bench run can leave root-owned files** in `.git/index` and
  `~/.cache/molehill-bench/venv`; both are repaired with `chown -R dsh:dsh` on
  the path named in the error.

## The archive

[HANDOFF-archive.md](HANDOFF-archive.md) holds every closed record, with a
contents list at the top. The section that matters most is
[the v1.0.0 cycle](HANDOFF-archive.md#the-v100-cycle-the-mhd-carrier-moved-2026-11-03):
the carrier swap, the cost investigation, all ~80 rounds of the arrival-tail
search, and the release ritual as it was run.

**No number in the archive may be quoted as a measurement of the current code**,
compared against a newer run, or used to gate anything. The live numbers are in
this page's "What is measured" section, and the method's home is
[docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md).

## Section 4 material consolidated on 2026-11-06 (round 136)

The six subsections below were superseded by later measurements (all of them by §4.19's
un-gated re-measurement and §4.12's join-key fix). They are kept verbatim: the value in
them is the record of how each instrument misled the investigation, which is why §7 lists
the rules that would have prevented each.

### 4.11 The data path's two ends disagree by five times, and that is the finding (2026-11-06)

The cell is the data path under concurrency (§4.10), so the next step was to split the server's
`wire` leg — the one part it cannot see is the far side's. A fourth histogram was added on the
client, `echo`, spanning the request's arrival from the carrier to the echo being read from the
backend. Both ends, same run:

```
server  wire   p50 1000 µs   p90 6000 µs   (n = 4300)
client  echo   p50 5000 µs   p90 6000 µs   (n = 2147)
```

**These span the same wall-clock interval from opposite ends and differ by five times.** One of
them is not measuring what it says, and until they agree nothing about the data path's
attribution is trustworthy — which is the same lesson as `ack_us` in §4.9 and the round before
it: an instrument that has not been cross-checked against another view of the same interval is
a guess with a number attached.

The obvious candidates on inspection: the server's `sent_ms` is stamped at the **first handoff**
while `got_ms` is stamped at the **first received frame**, and a group's first received frame is
not necessarily the reply to its first handoff — a group can receive the request's own frames
from a client that opened it, and the first round trip of a stripe group is not the first
exchange the group carries. The client's `echo`, meanwhile, starts at the first frame *from* the
carrier and ends at the first read *from the backend*, which is a different pair of events.

The next step is **A0t**: one line per group stating both ends' stamps for the *same* round trip
(group id, `sent`, `got`, `echo`), so the two numbers are defined in terms of the same two
events before either is used again.### 4.10 Sealing works now, removes the 1.7 ms handshake, and barely moves the cell (2026-11-06)

The mechanism phase A needs **already exists**: with `MOLEHILL_MHD_SEAL=1` the first stream's
handshake leaves a lane root behind, every later stream writes one derived selector byte, and
`open_channel_with_id` skips Noise entirely. It was off by default because sealing deadlocked
the striped transfer four runs in eight — and that deadlock's cause (the group's two-second
reorder deadline against an eleven-second carrier stall) was fixed in §4.6.

So it was measured again, and the open's own number collapses:

| phase | unsealed | sealed |
|---|---|---|
| `open_channel` | **1 693–1 743 µs** | **10 µs** |
| `hello_ack` | 0 µs | 129 µs |

**A hundred and seventy times faster on the phase that carries the handshake**, exactly as
§4.9 predicted. And the striped integration test now passes **6 of 6** with sealing on, against
11 of 12 unsealed — the stall that kept this switch off is gone.

**But the cell does not follow.** `churn-16` reads 9.29–10.26 ms sealed against 10.3–12.1
unsealed — about a millisecond, inside its own spread — and `rr-1` gets *worse*: 0.167–0.178 ms
against 0.151–0.163. The reuse cost is the per-packet AEAD that sealing adds to a 64-byte
request.

Two conclusions, and they are worth more than the speedup:

1. **the `churn-16` cell is not the open.** Removing 1.7 ms of handshake from every fresh
   connection leaves the cell where it was, so the seven to ten milliseconds it reports are the
   **data path under sixteen-way concurrency**, which §4.7's leg measurements put on the server
   side of the round trip (`wire` 1–5 ms, `up` and `down` zero, the client's legs zero).
2. **sealing stays off by default for now**, not because it is unsafe — it is not, any more —
   but because it buys nothing on the cell and costs thirteen percent on reuse. It becomes the
   right default the moment the data path is fixed, or if the target is open latency itself.


### 4.14 The pairing wait is not a request-and-response at all (2026-11-06)

The last unexplained piece was the five to six milliseconds a visitor waits for a data channel
to exist. The obvious model — the server asks, the client opens — has an instrument: the request
is written by `ask_missing`, and a stamp there joins, by group, with the client's arrival stamp.

**It never fired — and that was the instrument, not the system.** `ask_missing` is only the
pairing's **retry** path; the first request is sent directly, a few lines before the gather loop
(`data_ch_req_tx.send(stripe_request(...))` in a `for index in 0..stripes`). The stamp sat on the
retry and nothing ever retried, so it proved only that the first attempt succeeded.

**So the pairing *is* a request and a response**, as it always looked: request written, the client
opens a channel, the channel arrives, the visitor pairs. The five to six milliseconds contain
that open (1.7 ms, §4.9) plus whatever the request and the arrival cost, and the question the
section asked — how deep the client's inventory is — does not arise, because there is no
inventory: the channel is opened on demand.

The stamp belongs on the first request, in absolute epoch milliseconds so it joins with the
client's stamps for the same group. It was moved there and then reverted: the change kept landing
between `pair_striped_group`'s attribute and its body, and the function is at its line budget. The
next round makes it in one piece, as a helper above the attribute.

So the pairing is not a request and a response. The client keeps a speculative inventory of
data channels — unclaimed, opened ahead of demand — and `take_for(group)` adopts the next one that
arrives. **The five to six milliseconds are that inventory's arrival cadence**, not a round trip
that could be shortened by making a message smaller.

That is the same shape as everything else this cycle has measured about this cell: the visitor
is not waiting on the carrier's work but on *another task's schedule*. It is also the first
attribution the archive's rejected "warm pool" ever had — the objection was made without it, and
the question it raises is now specific and cheap: **how deep is the inventory, and what sets its
cadence?**

The next step is **A0v**: count, per second, how many unclaimed channels are waiting and how often
one arrives with none waiting. That number decides whether a deeper reserve would remove the wait
or merely move it.


### 4.15 The pairing wait, measured: a two-millisecond control hop and a 1.7 ms open (2026-11-06)

The stamp is on the first request at last, in absolute epoch milliseconds, and it joins with the
client's own arrival stamp for the same group. Six thousand four hundred groups:

```
control hop (server writes the request -> the client's stream delivers it)   p50 2.0 ms  mean 2.03  max 10
server `wait_us` for the same groups                                        p50 5.41 ms mean 5.59  max 9.2
```

**A0w corrected the label on that first term, and the correction matters.** `ask_ms` to the
client's `got_ms` is not a control hop: `got_ms` is a *data* frame on the group's lane, so the
interval already contains the open. Stamped where the client actually begins the open — absolute
epoch milliseconds, with how long the command sat in its queue:

```
command trip (server writes the request -> the client starts the open)   p50 0.0 ms  mean 0.02  max 2
client queueing before it starts                                        p50 0.00 ms
```

**The control session is not slow.** A command crosses it in twenty microseconds.

**The server's own share is smaller than that arithmetic predicted, and the rest has no owner.**
Two histograms inside `serve_mhd_stream` — task start to the hello decoded, and task start to the
channel delivered:

```
hello    p50 500 µs   p99 1 141 µs
deliver  p50 1 040 µs p99 2 320-2 387 µs
```

So the whole server-side setup is **1.04 ms at the median**, split into 0.5 ms of selector,
handshake and hello, and 0.54 ms of prologue and delivery. Against the pairing's 5.4 ms:

| term | measured |
|---|---|
| command across the control session | 0.02 ms |
| the client's channel open (§4.9) | 1.7 ms |
| the server's per-stream setup | 1.04 ms |
| **unaccounted** | **~2.6 ms** |

**The residual is one effect, and this cycle has now measured it from three directions.** The
line that would have said which branch the open took is silent, and its silence is the answer it
was built for: `log_slow_open` requires `reader_ready_at`, which is `None` when the acknowledgement
arrives **inside** the handshake rather than as stream data — so the carrying branch is the one in
use, its `hello_ack` is zero by construction, and the 2.6 ms cannot be a hello round trip.

That leaves one term in the whole cell: **a new stream's first exchange costs two to three
milliseconds, while the same carrier's later data costs 0.2.** The measurement has now hit that
same shape three times without ever naming a mechanism:

- the open's own round trip: 1.7 ms (§4.9) where an idle lane's is 0.1;
- the pairing's residual: 2.6 ms (§4.15) between a client's open and a server's task start;
- and, earlier, the 5–8 ms opens that sent twenty rounds after the handshake (§4.7).

Three independent intervals, all "the first thing on a new stream", all an order of magnitude
above the established path. That is a property of how this carrier starts a stream, not of any one
hop, and it is where the next experiment belongs: **first packet against second packet on the same
stream**, on the data path, with no handshake involved.

The whole cell, with every number now measured rather than inferred:

| term | value | shared? |
|---|---|---|
| visitor accepted and paired — control hop + open + arrival | **~5.4 ms** | ours |
| the first request's back-end echo | **~4.8 ms** | every arm pays it |
| the request and reply's carrier hops | ~0.4 ms | ours |

The next step is **A0w**: split the control hop — when the server's request leaves the control
session's sink against when the client's command loop reads it — so the two milliseconds are
attributed to a queue, a wake-up, or the mux layer above the carrier.


### 4.16 Every leg is measured and they do not add up to `wait_us` (2026-11-06)

The last named candidate — the server's spawn of the stream-serving task — is two microseconds:

```
spawn             p50 2 µs      p99 14-20 µs
server setup      p50 971-974 µs (selector, handshake, hello, prologue, delivery)
client open       p50 1 235 µs
carrier hops      ~200 µs        (established groups, §4.12)
control command   p50 20 µs
```

**Their sum is 2.4–2.9 ms. The pairing reports 5.4.** Nothing else is left to instrument on this
path, and a ninth stamp would be measuring one of these again.

So the discrepancy is in a **definition**, not in an interval: either `wait_us` begins somewhere
other than the moment the request is written (`pairing_started` is 22 µs after the visitor was
accepted, which is consistent), or one of the five numbers above is not the interval its name
claims — the likeliest being the client's `open`, which is measured at `open_data_channel`, the
service-level entry, while the lane's own open is measured deeper and the pool's placement between
them has only ever been sampled at a one-millisecond threshold.

The honest state of this cell: **every leg is measured, they are each microseconds to 1.2 ms, and
they do not account for the 5.4 ms a visitor waits.** The next step is to make one interval carry
both ends — a single line per group with the client's open start, the client's open end, the
server's task start and the server's delivery — and check that they are monotone and sum to the
pairing's own number. Until they do, the cell's ten milliseconds are attributable in order of
magnitude but not to the millisecond.


### 4.17 The missing 3.4 ms is a wake-up after delivery, on the server's own queue (2026-11-06)

Four stamps per group, all six thousand four hundred matched, and the order they came back in is
the answer:

```
client open               p50  1.0 ms
open-end -> server task   p50 -1.0 ms     (negative: the task starts before the open ends)
server setup              p50  1.0 ms
sum of the three          p50  2.0 ms
```

**The negative gap is correct and it corrects the model**: the server's stream task must run to
answer the handshake, so it starts *before* the client's open returns. From the client starting its
open to the server delivering the channel is therefore **2.0 ms**.

The pairing's own line says the rest:

```
accept_us 17-41 µs   enqueue_us 0   wait_us 5.1-5.5 ms   write_us 2-6 µs
```

and the command crosses to the client in 0.02 ms. So of the 5.4 ms the visitor waits, **2.0 ms is
the channel being opened and delivered and 3.4 ms is the pairing not noticing that it has been**.

That last stretch is a wake-up on this end's own in-process queue: `deliver` puts the channel where
`take_for` will find it, and the pairing task does not resume for three and a half milliseconds.
It is the same shape as the pump's parked writer (§4.11) and the stripe reader's deadline (§4.6),
and it is the only unexplained interval left in this cell.

The next step is **A0x**: stamp `deliver` and the `take_for` that follows it (absolute time, per
group), which turns "a wake-up" from an inference into a measurement — and, if it holds, makes the
pairing's wake the third member of a family this file can then fix once.


### 4.18 It was never a wake-up: the pairing takes somebody else's channel (2026-11-06)

`deliver` was stamped where it hands a channel to the pairing's own queue, and `take_for` where
the pairing takes it from there. Six thousand four hundred of the first, and **not one of the
second**:

```
mhd channel delivered   6 400
mhd channel taken           0
```

**The pairing never takes the channel that was delivered for its group.** Every visitor is served
from the **shared pool**, with a channel that was delivered for an *earlier* group — and its own
channel, arriving later, goes into that pool for the next visitor. The pool is a rotating belt.

So the three and a half milliseconds are not a wake-up at all. They are **the wait for the next
channel to arrive on the belt**, which is one whole open cycle: the previous visitor's channel has
to be produced, and the visitor behind it takes that one.

That is a structural limit, and it is the first one in this file that a *design* answer could
remove: the cell is not slow because any hop is slow, but because **the pool holds nothing and
every visitor queues behind production**. It also finally gives the archive's rejected "static warm
pool" its mechanism — the objection was that a warm pool changes behaviour without a measured
reason, and the reason was invisible until now: the pool is empty at every arrival.

The next step is **A0y**: the shared queue's depth at the moment a pairing looks, to see how often
it is empty (which the 5.4 ms wait predicts is always), and what the belt's period actually is.

## The mhd finalisation rounds (archived 2026-11-21)

The numbered rounds §4.389–§4.512, moved out of `HANDOFF.md` when its §0 grew
past what a state document can carry: the mhd engine's development through the
record layer, the pool's carrier policy, the striding and sealing work, and the
measurement accidents along the way. **The numbers are unchanged**, so a citation
written before the move still names the same round — it just names this file now.

What is current is in `HANDOFF.md`; what is here is the reasoning, the superseded
conclusions and the negative results, which is what an archive is for.

> **§4.509 (where the TCP carrier's bulk time goes: a third of it is the record cipher, and the faster one is already in the tree).**
> The same `perf` sample as §4.508, taken on the **kernel carrier** instead — `bulk-n`, clean, `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER=tcp`
> — because after the mix that is the path bulk actually rides. Splitting ~9 700 samples by image and symbol:
>
> | what | share of cycles |
> |---|---|
> | the kernel (unresolved under `perf_event_paranoid=2`) | **45.9 %** |
> | `ring_core…chacha20_poly1305_open_avx2` | **17.4 %** |
> | `ring_core…chacha20_poly1305_seal_avx2` | **15.4 %** |
> | everything else in user space (copies, yamux, stripe, pool) | 21.3 % |
>
> **So a third of this carrier's bulk CPU is one cipher**, and the tree already carries a measured faster one: `tests/primitives_test.rs`
> prices ring's AES-256-GCM at **671 ns** per 1 400-byte record against ChaCha20-Poly1305's **1 017** — the pair that made mhd's
> sealing affordable in P1, which is why the datagram carrier pays 12.6 % of its cycles for a cipher the kernel carrier pays
> 32.7 % for. **The next structural step is therefore a record-layer cipher change**: keep the Noise KK handshake exactly as
> it is (it is the authentication), derive two AES-256-GCM keys from the handshake hash with HKDF — the same shape the lane
> root already uses — and seal records with the faster primitive. **It is a wire change**, so it belongs to dialect 6.0 while
> that is unreleased, and it is not done here: at 33 % of the total it is worth roughly **+10 % throughput** on every encrypted
> path, which is real but does not close a 2.6× gap, and it is a change to the confidentiality path that wants a session with
> room to verify it rather than the end of one.
>
> **What that leaves as the honest account of the gap**: 46 % kernel and copies neither carrier can avoid, 33 % a cipher with
> a known-faster replacement, and the remaining fifth the mux/stripe/pool layers. None of those is a parameter, and all three
> are now measured rather than guessed.

> **§4.508 (two experiments this round: one kept, one refuted — and the profiler that made both possible).**
> **`perf` is installed now** (`apt install linux-perf`, 6.12.117, matching the kernel; the host had none, and
> `perf_event_paranoid` is 2 so user symbols resolve and kernel ones do not). The first clean-bulk sample put **56 %** of the
> cycles in the kernel and, in user space, **`mhd::recovery::Recovery::arm` at 9.4 %**: it walks the whole in-flight table on
> **every packet sent** to answer "is a small record in flight", which decides the retransmission timer's floor. Replaced by
> a counter exact by construction (insert +1, retirement −1, loss −1) with a test that drives a mixture through all three
> and pins the counter against the scan it replaced. **Clean `bulk-n`: 8.87 → 9.63 Gbit/s, 1.156 → 1.091 CPU-s/Gbit.**
> Kept (`a58e105`).
>
> **Refuted: a channel warmed ahead of the visitor.** The arrival's own round trip — the server asking for a channel and
> this end opening one — is the tail the record names (p50 37 µs, p99 2.7 ms), so the client was made to open one channel
> per TCP service at activation with **group zero**, which lands in that service's shared queue where `take_for` already
> falls back to it; the server labels it with the visitor's group on adoption and the client refills. It works: the
> integration suite passes 22/22 and the mechanism adopts and refills. **It does not help** — interleaved A/B, three rounds,
> clean path:
>
> | cell | no warm channel | warm channel |
> |---|---|---|
> | `churn-16` rtt p50 / p99 | 6.317 / 7.022 ms | 6.546 / 7.300 |
> | `churn-16` completed /s | 2 482 | 2 394 |
> | `rr-1` rtt p50 / p99 | **0.122 / 0.159 ms** | 0.165 / 0.202 |
> | `rr-1` completed /s | **7 514** | 5 685 |
>
> The arrival cell it was built for is unchanged (and 3–4 % worse inside its own scatter), and the single-connection cell is
> **24 % worse** — which the mechanism cannot explain by cost, so it is placement luck: with a channel parked in the queue,
> the visitor's first connection lands on the tunnel that was least loaded *at activation* instead of the one least loaded
> *now*. **Reverted.** What it teaches is worth keeping: the pairing wait this record has chased for many rounds is not
> what a fresh visitor pays any more — §4.505's open measurements (p50 37 µs) already said so, and this is the experiment
> that would have found it if it were.
>
> **And the isolation question, settled by the same method**: interleaved against itself, the carrier-keyed and
> tunnel-keyed variants are **indistinguishable** on the clean mixed cell (p99 4.56 against 4.95 ms, throughput 8.86 both),
> and the capacity ramp is **bimodal in both** — 39–70 ms at the second level in one round, 1.4–2.9 ms in the next. The
> **3 → 8 level improvement claimed in §4.507 was one lucky round**; the rule is kept because it is the property the cell is
> about, not because it is measured to win.

> **§4.507 (molehill(auto) against the peers, on the release-shaped sweep, twice — and the isolation defect the first one found).**
> **Method**: `--profile sweep` (the release ritual's shape: the eight-stage timeline plus the capacity ramp), rounds 1,
> every arm on the same host and path, nothing pinned. Run 1 was all five arms; run 2 repeated the three that matter after
> the fix below. Single-round numbers with no A/A, so **every difference smaller than a few percent here is scatter** —
> what follows is read at that resolution.
>
> **The staged timeline, after the fix** (interactive `rtt_p99_ms` / bulk Gbit/s):
>
> | stage | molehill(auto) | frp | rathole |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | clean | 2.4 / 7.99 | 5.7 / 6.07 | 2.3 / **24.31** |
> | rtt100 | 401.6 / 3.40 | 402.4 / 3.38 | 401.5 / 3.42 |
> | loss1 | 1 064.8 / 9.69 | 1 060.8 / 6.16 | 1 060.9 / **14.56** |
> | loss5 | **2 034.3** / 1.19 | 2 071.4 / 1.08 | 4 068.2 / 1.08 |
> | rate100 / rate20 | 195.9 / 433.8 | 196.5 / 426.5 | 197.6 / 430.4 |
> | jitter | 107.2 / 11.54 | 107.0 / 6.21 | 108.8 / **14.87** |
> | clean#2 | **1.9** / 10.21 | 18.5 / 6.05 | 2.4 / 24.42 |
>
> **Where that leaves the product**: **ahead of frp on every aligned cell** — the tail on `clean` (2.4 against 5.7), on
> `clean#2` (1.9 against 18.5) and on `loss5` (2 034 against 2 071), and bulk everywhere (7.99 against 6.07, 9.69 against
> 6.16, 11.54 against 6.21) — and **ahead of nps by two orders of magnitude on both axes** (nps: 101 ms and 0.13 Gbit/s).
> **Against rathole it is a split**: the tail is level within a millisecond on five stages and molehill wins the two where
> rathole collapses (`loss5` 2 034 against 4 068, `clean#2` 1.9 against 2.4), while **rathole owns bulk on every stage**
> (24.31 against 7.99 on `clean`, 14.56 against 9.69, 14.87 against 11.54).
>
> **The capacity ramp is where run 1 found a real defect.** Before the fix below, molehill's forwarding arm broke the
> interactive SLO at the fourth bulk level — 31.6 ms at L2, 44.8 at L3, **69.0 at L4, where the ramp stopped** — while the
> same product's L3 arm, which never multiplexes a claim's flows together, held **1.4 ms through L8**. The cause was the
> class preference being one-sided: bulk asked for the kernel carrier and conversational traffic asked for nothing, so an
> interactive open took the least-loaded tunnel, which after the mix is a kernel one full of bulk. **Both classes now ask**
> (`244dd90`), and the same ramp reads **every level from L1 to L8 inside the SLO, 1.5–2.9 ms**, carrying 12.6 Gbit/s at
> the eighth: capacity **3 → 8**, level with l3, frp and rathole, and with a tail far tighter than rathole's at that load
> (12.6 ms at L8).
>
> **The bulk gap is the data path, and its two measured components.** On a clean `bulk-n` cell, the same product arm reads
> **8.87 Gbit/s at 1.16 CPU-seconds per Gbit**; with the data plane unencrypted (`l4-plain`) **11.35 at 0.87**; with eight
> tunnels (`l4-mux8`) **10.87 at 1.08**. So **the AEAD costs 22 % and the pool width costs 22 %** — and rathole, at 24.31
> with **0.32 CPU-seconds per Gbit**, is still 2.2× ahead of the plain figure. What is left is molehill's own path: per
> byte it spends 3.3× rathole's CPU, and for a single stream 0.49 s/Gbit (kernel carrier) against 1.16 for eight — the
> cost grows with stream count, which is the signature of per-stream work (task wakes, copies, mux framing), not of the
> cipher. **Finding the rest needs a profiler and the host has none installed** (`perf` is absent, `perf_event_paranoid` is
> 2), so the next session starts by installing one, not by guessing.
>
> **What is not claimed**: these are single-round sweep numbers with no A/A twin, so no cell here is a claim in the sense
> the bench model uses — the run's own verdict says exactly that. The table is evidence of *position*, and the capacity
> change (3 → 8, with the tail measured per level) is evidence of a *fix*.

> **§4.506 (the plan is amended, and the default carrier stays mhd-first — for a better reason than before).**
> **The plan carries a sixth-version amendment** (`MHD-FINALIZATION-PLAN.md` §十一, untracked by design): the carrier
> choice is two-dimensional (path **and** workload), the decision is internal with no configuration key, §六's freeze on
> the TCP fallback is lifted for it, and — the point of the amendment — **the §一 criterion is corrected**: the `cost`
> cell answers the latency half, and the throughput half must be judged on two bulk cells in sequence, because `cost`
> opens every bulk channel before any class exists.
>
> **`carrier = auto` therefore stays mhd-first, and §4.503's conclusion survives with a different reason.** §4.503 kept
> the default because the alternative threw away the tail to recover bulk throughput a clean path already has, and said
> the real fix was a per-service key that this branch could not open. **The pool now does that job itself**: a session
> that carries both kinds converges on a split measured from its own traffic, so the bulk cost that argued for a key is
> recovered inside the session — 5.876 against 2.189 Gbit/s on the second bulk cell (§4.505). A key would now be a way
> for an operator to *override* a decision the product makes better than they can, which is the opposite of what the
> configuration surface is for.
>
> **What was changed to make convergence cheap**: up to two spares while the split is short (a three-tunnel move cost
> three cycles of "add, wait for one to empty, remove"), and at most one pool-size change per tick so `size` stops
> bouncing between two values while the split moves. Measured on the mixed cell at 1 % loss: two spares nineteen seconds
> apart, then two trims, ending at the configured count with the split the evidence asked for. Each step still costs one
> dial; whether that is worth a standing extra tunnel is untested and is written down as such.

> **§4.505 (the pool's carrier choice, judged — and the cell the objective named cannot answer the half it was asked for).**
> **The judgement, on the mixed `cost` cell the objective names** (two rounds, each run's own A/A twin, the condition on
> the leg the carrier crosses, nothing pinned, only `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER` distinguishing the two baselines):
>
> | `cost` | bulk Gbit/s | rtt p50 | rtt p99 | p99 range |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | `loss1`, pinned mhd | **2.632** | 41.4 ms | 98.5 ms | 97–104 |
> | `loss1`, the pool's own choice | 2.081 | 41.2 | **90.5** | 41–95 |
> | `loss1`, pinned tcp | **5.876** | 56.8 | 246.6 ms | 150–292 |
> | `loss5`, pinned mhd | 0.482 | 404.7 | 1 194 ms | 401–1 448 |
> | `loss5`, the pool's own choice | 0.522 | **401.7** | 1 437 | 401–1 505 |
> | `loss5`, pinned tcp | 0.480 | 633.4 | 2 606 ms | 1 756–2 948 |
>
> **The latency half is met on both conditions**: the pool's own choice tracks the datagram carrier (98.5 → 90.5 ms at
> 1 % loss; 404.7 → 401.7 ms at 5 %) and not the kernel one (246.6 and 633.4 ms). **The throughput half is not, and the
> cell cannot deliver it**: every bulk channel in `cost` is opened in the stage's first instant, before any megabyte has
> been carried, so the class does not exist yet when they are placed and no policy could have moved them. The 2.08 against
> 2.63 is that, not a regression — and at 5 % loss all three arms collide at 0.48–0.52 because the shaper dominates.
>
> **So the throughput half was judged on the cell that can express it**: two bulk cells in one session, the same service,
> back to back — `bulk-1` then `bulk-n`, three rounds:
>
> | one session, `loss1` | `bulk-1` | `bulk-n` |
> |---|---|---|
> | pinned mhd | 0.727 | 2.189 |
> | **the pool's own choice** | 0.713 | **5.876** |
> | pinned tcp | 2.168 | 7.684 |
>
> The first cell rides the datagram carrier because there is no evidence yet — the conservative prior doing exactly what it
> is for — and the second, whose channels are placed after the first has carried its gigabytes, carries **2.7× what the
> datagram carrier manages and 76 % of the pure kernel-carrier rate**.
>
> **What this means for the objective's own wording**: "the interactive p99 stays at mhd's level while bulk throughput moves
> to TCP's" is true, but not in one cell. The p99 half is `cost`'s; the throughput half needs a service whose channels are
> opened *after* its class is known, which in this model is a second bulk cell in the same round. **The measurement was
> corrected, not the claim.**
>
> **Two quality items recorded rather than hidden.** Convergence churns: each step adds a spare and trims one tunnel of the
> over-represented carrier, so reaching a 3-of-4 split costs three dials and waits for three idle tunnels (measured: three
> cycles in `cost`, six seconds in a quiet pool). And `cost`'s p99 at 5 % loss spans 401–1 505 ms across four samples, so
> the 1 437 against the pinned arm's 1 194 is inside that cell's own scatter — this cell cannot resolve a latency difference
> at that condition, which is why §4.500's latency claims were made on the `rr` cells.

> **§4.504 (the pool now decides a carrier per service, from what it carried — and its actuator is one slot short).**
> **The rule.** A service is **conversational** or **bulk**, read from what its channels moved: a channel reports one
> observation per megabyte it crosses (bulk) and one when it ends below 64 KiB (an exchange). Eight observations make a
> reading, two consecutive readings make a decision, and a service nobody has watched is conversational — which is the
> product's default carrier, so an unclassified service is placed exactly as it was before the rule existed. Placement
> takes the class as a *preference*: the matching carrier's tunnels move to the front of the candidate order and every
> other candidate stays behind them, so a pool that cannot satisfy it serves the open unchanged.
>
> **The mix.** A session that has shown both kinds owes the kernel carrier **a quarter of its tunnels** (at least one,
> never all) — the trade this exists for is only real when both are present, and a session with one kind keeps the
> endpoint's one answer. Repair dials whichever carrier the mix is short of.
>
> **What it does end to end, measured** (`cost`, loss1, the leg the carrier crosses, nothing pinned, one round): the
> bulk service's class flips 30 ms before the pool asks for the second carrier —
> ```
> pool-stats: a service's traffic class changed service=ServiceId([0,0,0,4]) from="conversational" to="bulk"
> pool-stats: this session carries both kinds of service; handing one tunnel to TCP mhd=4 tcp=0 mhd_target=3 tcp_target=1
> ```
>
> **What it does not do yet, and the next change.** That pool had **no slot to move**: the tunnel it chose held a
> long-lived bulk stream for the whole stage, so the drain never emptied, its budget expired and the pool resumed its
> ordinary repair — the log says nothing because a called-off move is a DEBUG line. A pinned pool is always full, so a
> mix needs one tunnel that can be freed; **the fix is a transient spare**: while the mix is owed and no drain can
> complete, grow to `count + 1` on the carrier that is short, then shrink back once a tunnel of the over-represented
> carrier empties. That is the next commit, and the mix's own judgement waits for it: the `cost` cell cannot show a
> completed move until the pool can make room.
>
> **Two guards worth stating.** The class is a *preference* and never a constraint, so a wrong guess costs throughput
> and never a visitor; and the whole policy is inert under `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER` because the handover's own choke
> point refuses to move a pinned carrier — which is what keeps the carrier A/B of §4.500 a clean measurement.

> flows — **11× tighter interactive p99 at 1 % loss, 3.8–4.2× at 5 %**, with 23–42 % more completed requests — and it carries

> `rathole` and `nps` have not been run against this build, so the published comparison on `docs/benchmarks.md` still describes

> **§4.500 (the carrier comparison, this time on the leg the carrier crosses: the interactive tail is 4–11× tighter and bulk is behind).**
> **§4.498/§4.499 are retracted as carrier evidence.** Both batches shaped the **visitor** leg — `--condition-leg` defaults to
> `visitor` (`bench/src/bench/cli.py:1276`) and the runs recorded `condition_leg: "visitor"` in their own `method` block — and both ran
> with **`MOLEHILL_MHD_STATS=1`**, which `MHD-FINALIZATION-PLAN.md` §五 forbids for a performance conclusion. The leg the carrier does
> not cross is the one thing a carrier comparison may not use. The tell is in the numbers: the visitor-leg `loss1` batch read **rr-1 p99
> 245.2 ms on both arms**, and the tunnel-leg TCP arm below reads **247.0** — the first batch was measuring the visitor's own kernel TCP.
>
> **Method now.** Build `8fd13c5`, one `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER` pin per run, **no stats switches**, `--condition-leg tunnel`, `dev` profile
> (5 s bulk samples), 3 rounds plus each run's A/A twin, three scenarios.
>
> | `loss1` (10 ms, 1 %) · tunnel leg | mhd | tcp |
> |---|---|---|
> | bulk-1 Gbit/s | **0.733** (0.715–0.756) | **2.077** (1.878–2.171) |
> | bulk-1 CPU s/Gbit | 1.71 | **0.44** |
> | bulk-1 RSS MiB | 124 | **25.7** |
> | bulk-1 wire bytes / visitor byte | 1.072 | **1.002** |
> | rr-1 rtt p50 / p99 (ms) | 20.44 / **22.66** | 20.66 / **247.0** |
> | rr-1 completed /s | **48.7** | 39.6 |
> | rr-16 rtt p50 / p99 (ms) | 20.26 / **24.80** | 20.39 / **49.28** |
> | rr-16 completed /s | **777** | 704 |
>
> | `loss5` (100 ms, 5 %) · tunnel leg | mhd | tcp |
> |---|---|---|
> | bulk-1 Gbit/s (5 s samples) | **0.0874** (0.080–0.111) | 0.0678 (0.018–0.129) |
> | bulk-1 Gbit/s (10 s samples) | 0.1084 (0.0958–0.1251) | **0.1332** (0.0632–0.1600) |
> | rr-1 rtt p50 / p99 (ms) | 200.47 / **287.9** | 200.71 / **1 095.7** |
> | rr-1 completed /s | **4.9** | 3.9 |
> | rr-16 rtt p50 / p99 (ms) | 200.28 / **206.3** | 200.83 / **865.5** |
> | rr-16 completed /s | **79.5** | 55.9 |
>
> **What it says.** The interactive tail is the carrier's case and it is now measured on the right leg: **11× tighter at 1 % loss and 3.8–4.2×
> tighter at 5 %**, with 23–42 % more completed requests. The mechanism is visible in the numbers — TCP's p99 of 247 ms on a 20 ms path is
> its 200 ms minimum retransmission timeout, so one lost segment costs a request ten round trips, while mhd repairs inside the next one.
> **Bulk is the opposite story**: 2.8× behind at 20 ms and 19 % behind at 200 ms (10 s samples; the 5 s sample has mhd ahead, which is the
> slow-start artefact the plan's budget rule warns about). Both are far outside each run's own A/A scatter (`throughput_gbps` 4–6 %,
> `rtt_p99_ms` 0.4–23 %).
>
> **So the carrier's reason to exist is latency, not throughput**, and the clean batch (§4.498, valid — a clean leg is the same leg) says
> TCP wins there on every axis. A `carrier = auto` policy that wants both has to choose per workload, which the product does not let it do
> today (the carrier is per data endpoint, not per service).

> **§4.501 (the bulk gap was the window, and the fix is refuted — the eighth member of the same family).**
> **The diagnosis.** A `MOLEHILL_MHD_STATS=1` diagnostic of `bulk-1` on the 1 %-loss tunnel leg (a diagnostic, never a
> performance claim) reads the sender's window at **1 121 076 bytes against its own 5 242 880-byte ceiling**, **1 906 writes a
> second refused for want of window**, and **3.42 MB** of the writer's bytes queued with nothing to carry them:
> `slow_start=false`, `grow=104 598` bytes/s, `srtt` 20.1 ms against `min` 20.0 ms. The growth phase had ended at the
> connection's first loss, and the additive rule that follows opens the window at **≈65 KB/s** on a 20 ms path — 76 seconds to
> double. **Ending the growth phase on a loss is a TCP inference** ("the path dropped, so its capacity was found") and this
> carrier's own doctrine says a loss is not capacity, so the experiment was to end it only when the loss came with a standing
> queue (`smoothed > 1.25 × min`), the only evidence in the tree that a queue exists.
>
> **What it bought (10 s samples, 3 rounds, same run length).** `loss5` tunnel `bulk-1` **0.1084 → 0.1799 (+66 %)**, above both
> the other carrier's 0.1332 and the plan's 0.11; that cell's `rr-1` p99 **287.9 → 206.5 ms**; `loss1` bulk 0.7349 → 0.7712
> (+4.9 %, inside noise); clean bulk unchanged (3.70 Gbit/s); the `rate100_shallow` A/B against the pre-change binary
> indistinguishable (0.0812 vs 0.0801 Gbit/s, 8 881 vs 8 439 drops, both arms' own scatter).
>
> **What it cost, and why it is reverted.**
>
> | reading | guarded build | pre-change build |
> |---|---|---|
> | soak `rtt100` interactive failures | **16.0 %** | 1.74 % |
> | soak `loss5` interactive p99 | **3 916 ms** | 391 ms |
> | soak `loss1` interactive p99 | 77.1 ms | 40.9 ms |
> | soak `wedge_count` / `wedge_max_s` | **9 / 50.0** | 5 / 60.2 |
> | step grid (`step_recovery_ms`, first arm) | **1 360 / 1 661 / 905** | 131 / 2 |
>
> **The mechanism is the one this record already carries**: with no rate decision above it, a window that only opens turns every
> shaped path into a standing queue, and the interactive stream drowns in it — 16 % of a soak's pings timing out is the same
> defect as §4.298's second-long tails, at a larger window. The isolated loss cell rewards a big window; the rotating path
> punishes it, and the rotating path is the one a deployment runs on.
>
> **So the window keeps ending its growth phase at the first loss**, and the +66 % on one cell is recorded as unavailable at
> that price. That is the eighth member of the `cwnd`/rate family (§九) and it failed the same way as the first seven: **the
> carrier has no send-rate policy, and every attempt to give it one inside the window's arithmetic is a trade between cells
> rather than an improvement.**
>
> **A method finding of its own**: `step_recovery_ms` cannot resolve a build difference at three rounds. In the interleaved A/B
> the guarded build's *own twin* read **8 and 26 ms** in the same run where the first arm read **1 360–1 661**, so the cell is
> dominated by arm position and by whether a round hits its six-second cap. Any future claim on that grid needs more rounds and
> a balanced order, and §4.489's 22 ms is a lucky draw rather than a stable reading.

> **§4.502 (the shallow-queue cell's drop count no longer matches its P2 record, and nothing in this goal changed it).**
> P2 recorded `rate100_shallow` at **0.0932 Gbit/s with 14–18 drops** (§4.292's table). On this build the same cell reads
> **0.081–0.084 Gbit/s with 8 400–8 900 drops**, and the pre-change binary reads the same **8 439** — so the change is not
> the cause and the regression happened somewhere between P2 and `8fd13c5`. The twin in one run read **2 261** drops against the
> product arm's **8 881** with the *same binary*, so the cell is also far noisier than the record implies. Recorded, not
> investigated: the plan demoted `dropped_packets` from a gate to a health reading (§一), and this cell has no other claim
> attached to it. **Whoever picks this up should first run it with six rounds and a twin, because at three rounds the same
> binary spans 2 261–8 881.**

> **§4.503 (the carrier choice, decided on the measurements: the default stays, and the key that would fix it stays unopened).**
> The three mechanisms that decide a carrier were read against §4.500's numbers.
>
> - **The fallback** (`carrier.rs`) fires only when an mhd session **cannot be established** — UDP blocked, a middlebox
>   eating it, the attempt's two-second budget spent. A path that carries UDP and *loses* packets never leaves mhd, so a
>   deployment moving bulk over a lossy path stays on the carrier that carries 0.74 against the other one's 2.10. That is
>   by design: the fallback answers "can this path carry the carrier at all", not "which one is faster".
> - **The pool's carrier rule** (`MOLEHILL_TUNNEL_CARRIER_RULE`, off by default) hands a tunnel to TCP when its
>   retransmit share clears **4 % for three windows**. Measured, mhd's share on a 1 %-loss path is **3–7 %** (`rep`), so the
>   threshold sits inside a real deployment's own noise — the rule would flap between carriers on exactly the path where both
>   work. It is also one-sided by construction (a TCP tunnel's retransmits live in the kernel), so it can only ever move
>   mhd → TCP, which would take the interactive tail down with the bulk it was trying to rescue.
> - **The L3 lane policy** moves lanes between *claims*, not between carriers; it does not touch this question.
>
> **The decision: the default stays mhd-first.** The plan's priority is latency (§六), the interactive tail is the one axis
> where either carrier is decisively better and it is better by 4–11×, and the alternative — TCP first — throws that away to
> recover bulk throughput that a clean path already has. A deployment that knows its path is clean and its traffic is bulk
> pins `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER=tcp`, which is documented as the measurement switch it is.
>
> **What would actually fix the trade is a per-service carrier key**, because the trade is a property of the *workload* as
> much as of the path: a service is interactive or bulk by its nature, and the config already knows which service is which.
> The product deliberately refuses that key — "which carrier works is a property of the network, not of the deployment" —
> and §4.500 is the first measurement that says the sentence is incomplete. **Reversing a configuration-surface decision is
> not this branch's to make**, so the key is not added here; the evidence for it is this section and the table it cites.
