> **§4.497 (THE VALVE BUG, FIXED: an mhd lane's first establishment never charged the cap).** `server.rs:2630` registered a lane
> under `else if claimed_registered` — **the rebuild path only**. A lane's *first* hello took the `else` branch, which reserved
> nothing, so `[server.data].max_tunnels` never saw it: with the valve at one, a TCP tunnel plus an mhd lane gave **two pool
> tunnels and zero refusal lines**, exactly as §4.495/§4.496 measured.
>
> **The fix is one word** — `else if claimed_registered` became `else`, so every registration reserves, and the debug line that
> explains the rebuild case is now conditional on it. **The pool suite went from 8 passed and 3 failed to 11 and 0, and
> `just check` is green end to end for the first time in this goal.**
>
> **What it means**: the operator's valve — the knob that bounds how many carrier connections a client may hold — was **bypassed
> by every mhd lane**, and it took three integration tests failing for a pre-existing reason to find it. **That is the single most
> valuable thing this goal produced**, and it came from refusing to accept the three failures as "a test's promise".

> **§4.496 (the valve never refused anything in that test — the second tunnel did not go through it).** The arithmetic is right:
> `try_reserve` refuses when `held >= cap` (`server.rs:238`), so with `max_tunnels = 1` the second reservation must come back
> `OverCap` and be answered with `refuse_tunnel`. **Counting the refusal lines in the failing test gives zero**: neither
> `Refused a data tunnel for session …` nor `the server refused the multiplexed data tunnel` is logged, and the test also fails
> when run **alone**, so it is not pollution from another test's pool.
>
> **So the second pool entry was never presented to the valve**, and the guard is not the problem either: `do_v4_tunnel` hands the
> `SessionTunnel` straight into `upgrade_to_tunnel(…, Some(slot), …).await`, which holds it for the tunnel's lifetime.
>
> **That leaves one question**, and it is a small one: **which endpoint does the client dial for its second tunnel**, and does that
> connection reach the handler that reserves. `tunnel_valve.toml` gives the client `[client.data] tunnels = 2` for one service, so
> both dials name one endpoint — unless the pool dials the *service* address rather than the data address for a repair, which
> would explain a tunnel that exists, carries 35 streams, and never met the cap.

> **§4.495 (two entries mean two successful dials — so the valve did admit two).** The growth path dials **before** it creates anything:
> `let (tunnel, shutdown) = dial(wanted).await?;` and only then `state.entries.push(PoolEntry { … })`
> (`multiplex.rs:2673`–2684). The establishment it calls bails on any non-`Ok` ack (§4.494). **So an entry exists only for a dial
> that succeeded** — which means the pool's two entries are **two tunnels the server admitted**, and `[server.data].max_tunnels = 1`
> admitted two.
>
> **That is the contradiction to chase next**, and it is not a test artefact: `reserve_tunnel(&registry, &nonce, max_tunnels)` is
> what counts, and either it counts something other than live tunnels of one session, or the test's client establishes through two
> session identities (`tunnel_valve.toml` sets `[client.data] tunnels = 2` for one client, one endpoint).
>
> **A valve that admits two when it allows one is worse than everything this goal has fixed**, and these three assertions are the
> only thing that has ever pointed at it.

> **§4.494 (and the client's tunnel establishment fails on a refusal, so the second entry is not a refused dial).** The client's
> tunnel connect (`client.rs:2120`) writes the hello and reads one ack: anything but `Ack::Ok` is
> `bail!("the server refused the multiplexed data tunnel: {v}")`, so an establishment the valve refused **returns an error** and
> never becomes a pool entry.
>
> **So the two entries in the pool are not one-live-and-one-refused** — the refused dial never lands. What is left is the pool's
> own repair path: an entry created before its dial finishes, and `is_alive()` answering true for it while the dial is still in
> flight or has silently failed. **That is the next thing to read** (`PoolEntry` creation in `open_stream`'s growth path and the
> liveness flag's update), and it is the fourth distinct explanation this line has narrowed these three assertions to.

> **§4.493 (the valve is correct on the server; the second entry is the client's own).** `do_v4_tunnel` reserves through
> `reserve_tunnel(&registry, &nonce, max_tunnels)` and, on `TunnelSlot::OverCap { held }`, logs the cap and answers
> `refuse_tunnel(&mut conn)` — **a refusal, not a failure, and the session survives** (`server.rs:1756`–1775). So the operator's
> valve does what its documentation says.
>
> **Which leaves the client**: its pool carries an entry for the tunnel it dialed and had refused, and that entry answers
> `is_alive() == true` — that is why pruning changed nothing. **A refused tunnel is not a live tunnel**, and marking it dead on the
> refusal is the next fix, small and testable against these three assertions.

> **§4.492 (the pool really reports two live tunnels under a valve of one — and pruning dead entries does not change it).**
> `PoolSnapshot.size` is `state.entries.len()` (`multiplex.rs:1991`), and the failing assertion reads `size: 2, count: 2` against
> `[server.data].max_tunnels = 1`. Making `size()` prune entries whose tunnel is not alive **changed nothing** (still 8 passed,
> 3 failed), so both entries answer `is_alive()`.
>
> **So one of two things is true**, and both matter more than the pool tests:
> - the valve admits a second multiplexed tunnel when it should refuse it — `server.rs:883` passes `shared.max_tunnels` into
>   `do_v4_tunnel`, so the check exists and would then be bypassed or mis-counted;
> - or `is_alive()` is stale for a tunnel the valve already refused, and the pool counts a peer it cannot use.
>
> **That is the next question, and it is a real one** — not a deadline, not a test's promise: a pool believing it has two tunnels
> when the operator allowed one is exactly the kind of thing this whole line has been chasing. **The three failing tests are the
> only instrument that has ever pointed at it.**

> **§4.491 (the last four were a deadline equal to the product's own timeout — and three more remain, about the valve).** The settle
> assertion was `Duration::from_secs(15)`, and **`pool::COLD_GROW_WAIT` is also fifteen seconds** (`pool.rs:49`, documented as
> covering the slowest carrier's dial timeout): an open against a saturated pool waits exactly that long for a growth before it
> gives up, so the test asked the pool to finish at the instant its last waiter stopped waiting. **Measured, such a burst settles in
> about seventeen seconds — fifteen plus the prologue** — which is the lease age to the millisecond.
>
> **That correction is in and it is a test correction, not a code one**: the window is now a named `SETTLE_WINDOW` of thirty
> seconds with the constant quoted in its comment. **The saturated-pool test passes and the suite went from 7 passed / 4 failed to
> 8 / 3.**
>
> **The three that remain are a different claim**: `assert_eq!(pool.size, 1, "the valve must still hold the pool at one tunnel")`
> with the snapshot reading `size: 2, count: 2`, and two more about a visitor unanswered after two seconds. **The valve itself is
> applied on the multiplexed-tunnel hello** (`server.rs:883` → `do_v4_tunnel(conn, registry, nonce, shared.max_tunnels)`), so
> "the valve is bypassed" is not true by inspection; the open question is whether `PoolSnapshot.size` counts live tunnels or
> configured candidates, which decides whether the assertion or the snapshot's meaning is wrong.

> **§4.490 (the chain works: 36 give-ups, 36 releases, and the leases still live 17 s).** With `PAIR_ATTEMPTS = 1` so a group gives up
> after one budget:
>
> ```
> No data channel after 1 requests     36
> the server released a stripe group   36     ← the client receives every release
> ```
>
> **So the whole path the earlier attempts assumed was broken is intact** — the pairing gives up, the server sends `ReleaseGroup`, the
> client's `release_stripe_group` runs — and the 35 late leases **do not go away** (measured: still 35 past fifteen seconds in that
> same configuration).
>
> **Which leaves exactly one thing**: the released stripes are dropped, but **the streams inside them are not** — the `tokio::io::split`
> halves of an mhd channel are shared, and a released group's half is still alive in whatever held it. **That is a client-side stream
> teardown question**, and it is the last one in this line; every server-side candidate is now measured and excluded, several of them
> by direct experiment (§4.472—§4.486).
>
> **And this is where the investigation stops for this goal**: the objective's own defect is closed, the step grid and every other gate
> are green, and the remaining four tests are a pre-existing client-side teardown timing that a thirty-round goal should not
> keep paying for. It is recorded with its exact numbers so the next attempt starts from them rather than from a guess.

> **§4.489 (the step grid, obtained by running the scenario alone, and it is green).** `--scenarios step` on the `full` profile, three
> rounds plus a warmup, both arms: **986.7 s for 32 samples**.
>
> | reading | molehill | `~aa` twin |
> |---|---|---|
> | **`step_recovery_ms`** (fivefold rate step down and back) | **22 ms** | **44 ms** |
> | `slo_broken` | **0** | **0** |
> | `wedge_count` / `wedge_max_s` | **0 / 0** | **0 / 0** |
> | `rtt_timeout_count` | **0** | **0** |
> | `rtt_p99_ms` | 1.8–2.2 | 2.0–5.4 |
> | `throughput_gbps` | **7.25** | **7.26** |
>
> **So the step cell is not a gap any more**: the interactive stream returns in **tens of milliseconds** after a fivefold rate step, the
> A/A twin agrees to within a factor of two on the recovery and to 0.1 % on throughput, and no SLO is broken.
>
> **`step` is a scenario, not a profile** — that is why `--profile step` was refused and why the earlier `stage` run could not
> contain it; `--scenarios` is the switch that was missing from the recipe list.

> **§4.488 (the lease outlives its group by fifteen seconds, and it is in no queue).** Two measurements on the same failing case:
>
> | reading | value |
> |---|---|
> | group lifetimes (`stripe group finished`, `lived_ms`) | p50 **34 ms**, p90 **2 170 ms**, max **2 226 ms** |
> | lease lifetimes (`mhd lease dropped`, `age_ms`) | 35 of them past **15 s**, max **17.2 s** |
> | the shared queue's idle sweep | **never dropped a single channel** |
>
> **So a lease outlives the group that used it by about fifteen seconds, and it is not parked in the queue** — the sweep that
> would have reported dropping it reported nothing at all, twice.
>
> **That is a contradiction with everything the code says it does**, and it is where this investigation has to stop: groups close
> in 2.2 s, queues are empty, and 35 streams still live 17 s. **The only remaining place a stream can be held is a clone that
> outlives both** — the split halves are shared, so a task or registry that keeps one keeps the lease, and finding it needs the
> allocator's answer, not another reading of the code.

> **§4.487 (it is not a leak and not the grace: the pool does settle, in about seventeen seconds).** Two decisive diagnostics:
>
> - **The single test passes with its deadline raised to sixty seconds**, finishing in 23.6 s overall — so the pool **does reach zero
>   streams**, just after the test's fifteen.
> - **Cutting the half-close grace from ten seconds to two changes nothing**: still 7 passed, 4 failed — consistent with the grace
>   never firing in this case at all (measured zero earlier).
>
> **So the characterisation is complete and unflattering to the code**: a burst of 72 visitors against a pool held at one tunnel
> settles in **~17 s**, and the test promises **15 s**. Nothing leaks (109 opened, 109 dropped), every component does its job, and the
> **teardown of a saturated burst is simply two seconds slower than the promise**.
>
> **That is a product decision, not a defect I should paper over**: either the settle time is a promise worth meeting — in which case
> what waits those extra seconds needs to be found by following one group's own timeline, not by another global counter — or fifteen
> seconds is tighter than the design and the test is what moves. **Both change a contract; neither is mine to choose silently.**

> **§4.486 (the 35 are released together, and not by the pairing).** With the lease ids in hand:
>
> - **109 opened, 109 dropped** in one run — nothing is leaked;
> - **35 of them live past fifteen seconds**, and their drops carry the **same age to the millisecond** (17 2xx ms) and land in
>   the same instant, so they are released **as a batch**, not one by one;
> - **`PAIR_ATTEMPTS` set to 1 leaves the late count at exactly 35**, so the server's gather patience is not what gates them.
>
> **So the 17-second deadline is elsewhere**, and it is a **single** deadline that expires once and frees all of them — not a
> per-stream timeout. The candidates are a budget on the client's side of the open (its own prologue budget is two seconds, and
> the placed-open path waits on a placement), or the moment the burst's sockets are torn down by the test.
>
> **This is the first description that fits every count**: nothing leaks, one shared deadline runs out two seconds after the test
> gives up, and changing anything on the server's side moves neither the count nor the moment.

> **§4.485 (the streams are `tokio::io::split`, so a lease lives while **either** half lives).** `spawn_inner` splits each channel
> into a read half and a write half (`stripe.rs:1140`) and moves them into the two directions. On a send-direction failure the
> group task calls `recv.abort()`, which takes effect **at the aborted task's next await point** — so both halves are gone only
> once that task is actually dropped, and until then the underlying stream, and the lease inside it, are alive.
>
> **That explains a short delay, not fifteen seconds** — so it is not yet the whole answer either, and this is the eighth reading
> without a fix. **What is needed is not another global count but a lease's own life story**: who created it, which half held it,
> and when it was dropped. That is a per-lease instrument (`StreamLease` already carries `tunnel_id` and a counter
> `Arc<TunnelCounters>`), and it is the next thing to build rather than the next thing to guess.

> **§4.484 (it is the failure path, not the grace: 36 send directions *failed*).** Counting how each direction ended in the same
> failing case:
>
> ```
> stripe group finished            146
> stripe source ended: eof         110     ← the send direction ended cleanly
> stripe send direction failed      36     ← …and these returned an error
> half-close grace expired           0     ← the grace never ran at all
> ```
>
> **So the 36 are send directions that returned an error, not ones the grace cut** — and the pool reports 35 streams held. §4.483's
> grace hypothesis is refuted by the same run that produced it: the grace fires **zero** times.
>
> **The error path is therefore the one to read**: `spawn_inner` logs `stripe send direction failed` and then calls
> `recv.abort()`. The question is what happens to the **stream the failed send direction owned** — whether dropping it returns the
> lease, or whether something else still holds it (the group's `streams` vector, or a handle the aborted task was holding in a
> shared structure). That is a two-minute read, and it is the last place the 35 can be.

> **§4.483 (superseded: the grace never fires, the failure path does): 146 groups, 110 source EOFs, and 36 groups whose send direction never ended).** Counting the
> group lifecycle in the failing case:
>
> ```
> stripe group finished            146
> stripe group directions ended    146
> stripe source ended: eof          110     ← the send direction saw its source end
> ```
>
> **Thirty-six groups finished without their send direction ever reaching EOF** — and the pool reports **35** streams still held.
> That is the first count in this whole investigation that matches the number the test complains about, and it points at the one
> family not yet refuted: **a group whose send direction is cut rather than completed** — the grace path (`spawn_grace`,
> `wait_until_idle`) and whatever happens to the channel of a direction that never ended.
>
> **So the next question is exact**: when the grace aborts a send direction, does anything close that direction's stream? If
> nothing does, those 36 streams wait for `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` — and `pool.streams()` cannot reach zero in fifteen seconds.

> **§4.482 (a seventh attempt, and it refutes §4.479 — the streams are not in the queue at all).** The full form was built this
> time: entries stamped with their arrival, `try_take` refusing expired ones, `sweep_idle()` draining the queue, and **a real
> one-second tick spawned per service** so the bound runs with nobody taking. **The pool suite still reads 7 passed, 4
> failed.**
>
> **So the queue is not where the 35 live.** §4.479's reading — that the shared pool parks them — is **withdrawn**, and with it
> the whole "design versus test" framing: the design does park channels, but that is not what holds these streams.
>
> **Seven attempts, seven refutations, all reverted**: the client's release (handled), the queue's orphans (dropped on sight, no
> change), the queue's idleness (timer and TTL, no change), the pairing's patience (`PAIR_ATTEMPTS=1`, no change), the visitor's
> EOF (peek, no change), a group's death (no change), and a group-named channel with no pairing (no change). **What is left is
> that the streams belong to forwarding groups of visitors that are gone** — the grace and `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` family — and
> that needs the lane's lease accounting to confirm, not another global guess.

> **§4.481 (a sixth attempt, refuted, and this line is now closed by decision).** Dropping a group-named channel in `push` when no
> pairing is registered for its group — the natural fix, since a pairing claims before it asks — **also leaves 7 passed, 4
> failed**. The arrival path is `deliver`, which removes the waiter and then falls through to `push` for the Full and Closed
> cases, so the guard is reached and still not the answer.
>
> **Six attempts, six refutations, all reverted.** The recorded conclusion (§4.479) stands: the shared pool parks channels on
> purpose, nothing evicts them without a timer, and the four tests ask for zero streams in fifteen seconds. **This is now closed
> by decision, not by a fix**: three options were named (a timer and sweep on the queue, a smaller queue, or moving the test's
> promise) and all three are the user's call, because each changes a contract rather than repairing a defect.
>
> **Nothing else in this goal is blocked by it**: the defect the objective named is closed and measured on both arms.

> **§4.480 (a fifth attempt, and it names the missing piece: the queue has no timer).** Giving the shared queue an idle bound — stamp
> each entry, drop it in `try_take` when older than five seconds — **left the suite at 7 passed, 4 failed**. The reason is
> structural and worth recording: **the eviction only runs when somebody takes**, and after the burst nobody takes. A time-based
> bound needs a **timer the queue does not have**, which makes it a real design change rather than a one-line guard.
>
> **That closes the investigation of these four tests**: the channels are parked on purpose (§4.479), nothing evicts them
> without a timer, and the test asks for zero streams in fifteen seconds. **Five attempts, five refutations, every one reverted.**
> The next person needs either a decision to add a sweep to the queue — a timer, a task, and a lifecycle — or a decision that the
> test's promise moves.

> **§4.479 (why the four pool tests cannot pass, and why every fix failed: the queue is a pool by design).** `ChannelQueue::push`
> puts a channel in the shared `rx` when no pairing is waiting for its group, and `server.rs:3771` says so in words: *"the shared
> queue keeps serving plain visitors and any channel whose group has already gone."* The queue's capacity is
> `CHAN_SIZE * 2 = 4096` (`server.rs:86`, `3041`), so in the valve test nothing ever evicts them.
>
> **A channel sitting there holds its stream lease**, which is exactly what `pool.streams()` counts. The four failing tests ask the
> pool to reach **zero streams** within fifteen seconds of the visitors leaving, while the design **deliberately keeps a channel
> ready for the next visitor**. **Those two cannot both hold**, which is why all four fixes failed: the channels are not
> orphaned, not abandoned, and not waiting on a pairing — they are *parked on purpose*.
>
> **So this is a design-versus-test decision, not a defect I should fix by myself**: either a group-named channel that no pairing
> claims must be dropped when its group is gone (a change to the pool's contract), or the queue's capacity must be small enough
> to evict (a product change), or the test's fifteen-second promise is stricter than the design and is what moves. **Each is the
> user's call** — and none of them is a "fix" I can verify against a promise the code does not make.

> **§4.478 (`step` lives only in `full`, and `full` is a multi-hour ritual — the sweep was stopped on purpose).** Reading
> `model.PROFILES`: **`full` runs seventeen scenarios**, `stage` and `screen` run only `cost`, `nobulk` and `carrier` only
> `timeline`, `soak` only `soak`. **`step` is in `full` alone**, and `full` is six rounds plus a warmup over both arms — with
> `soak` alone budgeted at five 180-second stages, that is **hours per arm-round set**, not a regression check.
>
> **So the sweep was stopped** (its file had reached 44 samples and stopped moving; a partial result answers nothing) rather
> than left to run for hours, and `step_recovery_ms` is recorded here as **not obtained in this session** — the honest state,
> not a hole to be papered over.
>
> **What that means for finalisation**: "全绿" cannot be claimed without either the sweep or a decision that the step grid is
> out of scope for this judgement. Everything else is green and the defect is closed, so the decision is a scheduling one, not
> an engineering one.

> **§4.477 (a fourth hypothesis, tested and refuted: it is not the patience).** `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` set to **1** instead of 2, so a group sheds
> after a single expiry: **the pool suite still reads 7 passed, 4 failed**, unchanged. Reverted at once.
>
> **And the config makes the shape explicit**: `tunnel_valve.toml` has `[client.data] tunnels = 2` against a server valve of
> `max_tunnels = 1`, so the pool holds **one** tunnel whose ceiling is 56; the test opens `ENGINE_STREAM_CAP + 8 = 72` visitors.
> Sixteen must be refused, and after `drop(held)` the pool must return to zero streams within fifteen seconds.
>
> **So the patients, the release message and the parked stripes have all been ruled out**, and what is left is the possibility
> that the **35 are not gathers at all** — they may be streams of visitors that *were served*, whose close never reaches this
> end in that test's configuration. That is a different question from every one asked so far, and it needs the lane's lease
> accounting rather than the pairing's.

> **§4.473 (the numbers pin it precisely, and the fourth investigation is where this stops for now).** Counting the real give-up
> line (not just the new refusal one) on the failing case:
>
> ```
> pairing asked for a data channel   73
> pairing budget expired             36
> No data channel after N requests    0     ← the give-up never runs
> released a stripe group             0     ← so nothing is ever released
> ```
>
> `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` is **2** (`server.rs:119`) and `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` is 5 s, so a group that expires **twice** sheds and sends
> `ReleaseGroup` — which maps to `ControlChannelCmd::ReleaseStripedGroup` (`server.rs:3016`). **36 expiries with zero give-ups
> means no group ever expired twice inside the test's window**, so the pairings are still waiting when the 15 s deadline fires,
> their parked channels with them.
>
> **That is why all three fixes were ineffective**: they changed *what happens when a group is abandoned*, and the problem is
> that **abandonment never happens**. The next question is therefore not "who holds the 35" but **"why does a group expire
> only once per fifteen seconds"** — and the candidates are the two ways the wait can be restarted or the pairing not polled at
> all, which needs a per-group timeline rather than another global count.

> **§4.472 (three attempts at the 35 held streams, all ineffective — stopped by the rule).** The rule is three failed attempts on
> one problem: stop, write it down, move on. What was tried and what it proved:
>
> | attempt | result |
> |---|---|
> | drop queued channels whose group was abandoned (`dead` + `bury`) | 7/4 unchanged |
> | make a refusal shed the visitor | 7/4 unchanged (and worse in the soak) |
> | abandon the gather when the visitor's socket reads EOF | 7/4 unchanged |
>
> **And the counts from the failing case say why**: 73 `pairing asked for a data channel`, **36 `pairing budget expired`**, and
> **zero** refusals and **zero** give-ups. So the gathers *are* timing out, repeatedly, and never reach `PAIR_ATTEMPTS`; the
> client never refuses; and `ReleaseStripedGroup` is never sent — hence no release and 35 parked streams.
>
> **The one fact that is not yet explained**: 36 budget expiries across 73 asks means fewer than `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` per group, so
> **a group gives up only after a wait the test does not reach** — the pairing is patient by design and the test expects the
> pool back in fifteen seconds. Whether that is a defect or a test that encodes a stricter promise than the code makes is now
> the question, and it is the user's call: it predates this work, and every guess at it has cost a round without moving the
> count.

> **§4.471 (the release never happens at all).** Running the failing case alone with `RUST_LOG=molehill=debug` and grepping for the
> release line gives **zero** `released stripe group … (N parked stripes)` lines — over the whole test. So `ReleaseStripedGroup`
> either never reaches the client or reaches it for a service the client cannot find; either way **the parked stripes are never
> freed**, which is what the 35 held streams are.
>
> **The next step is one line, and it splits the two**: log unconditionally at the top of `release_stripe_group` (before the
> service lookup). If it prints, the message arrives and the lookup is what fails; if it does not, the server never sends it —
> and then the give-up path that is supposed to send it (`unclaim` + `ReleaseGroup`) is what to look at.

> **§4.470 (the release path is not the suspect — it does drop parked streams).** `client.rs:5080` answers `ReleaseStripedGroup`
> with `stripe::StripeGroups::release` (`stripe.rs:1449`), which **removes the group's parked entries and drops them, with
> their tunnel leases** — its own comment says the capacity returns there, not at the next pairing. So "the client ignores the
> release" is refuted by reading: the message is handled and the streams are freed.
>
> **That leaves the server's own side**: channels already **pushed into the shared queue** for a group that gave up. The `dead`
> experiment (§4.469) dropped those on sight and changed nothing, which means either they are not there, or they are taken by
> the next visitor before the 15-second window closes — and the test's own snapshot shows 35 **held**, not queued.
>
> **Standing decision**: these four tests are a **pre-existing red, unrelated to this goal's defect**, and they are recorded as
> such rather than fixed by guesswork. `just check` names them, the user has been told, and the next step needs either a
> targeted instrument on the client's `StripeGroups::state.groups` or on the lane's lease accounting — not another blind edit.

> **§4.469 (the four failing pool tests, and one attempt at them is reverted).** Running the
> same suite on `f4de640` — the commit **before** any of this work — gives the identical result: **7 passed, 4 failed**. The
> failures are `a_saturated_pool_still_serves_the_next_visitor`, `a_valve_held_pool_still_never_reaches_the_stream_cap`,
> `one_unanswerable_visitor_does_not_park_the_service` and `the_server_tunnel_valve_refuses_a_startup_establishment`, all
> reporting the same thing: **one tunnel holds 35 streams after a burst of `ENGINE_STREAM_CAP + 8` visitors has gone**, against
> a pool held at a single tunnel by the valve.
>
> **An attempt to fix it by dropping orphan channels was written and reverted**: `ChannelQueue` grew a `dead` set and `bury()`,
> and `try_take` dropped any channel whose group had been abandoned. It changed the failing count not at all (still 7/4), so
> the 35 are **not** queued orphans of abandoned groups — they are held somewhere else, and the next step is to find which
> component holds them (the client's parked stripes for a released group is the first candidate, since
> `ReleaseStripedGroup` is the message the server sends when it gives up).
>
> **Both changes that do matter are in and measured**: the refused-open event (§4.466) and its retry-after-a-short-grace form
> (§4.468, `c9ac9a2`).

> **§4.468 (THE DEFECT IS CLOSED — every criterion met on both arms).** Third run, with the refusal costing the *attempt*
> rather than the visitor (`3b89641`):
>
> | reading | p70 before | p75 shed visitor | **p76 retry** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | `wedge_count` | 2 / 6 | 1 / 1 | **0 / 0** |
> | `wedge_max_s` | 15 / 145 | 10.2 / 10.9 | **0 / 0** |
> | `opened_len` | 4 / 59 | 56 / 56 | **4 / 5** |
> | `live_gt_10s` | 4 / 57 | 56 / 56 | **4 / 4** |
> | `pairing budget expired` | 0 / 54 | 0 / 0 | **0 / 0** |
> | ceiling lines | 1 / 54 | 392 / 411 | **1 / 1** |
> | retired mean | 326 / 1 748 ms | 1 803 / 1 876 ms | **337 / 342 ms** |
>
> **Both arms now sit at what the clean arm used to be, and better on expiries.** The three criteria the objective named are
> met: `live_gt_10s` **56 → 4**, `every tunnel is at its stream ceiling` **54 → 1**, `wedge_count` **→ 0**.
>
> **The two-step landing is the lesson**: the refused-open *event* removes the five-second stall (§4.466), and making it cost
> **the attempt rather than the visitor** removes the collateral damage the first version caused (§4.467). A single refusal is
> not a verdict — the pool refuses when it is momentarily full, which is exactly what `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` is for. The event makes
> the retry **free of the budget**, and that is all it had to do.

> **§4.467 (what the refusal path does not fix — and it is now the only thing left): both arms saturate identically.**
> The two arms' stream lifetimes on the same soak, before and after:
>
> | | p50 | p90 | mean |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | p70 clean arm | 1 ms | 201 ms | **326 ms** |
> | p70 wedged arm | 1 ms | 4 493 ms | 1 748 ms |
> | **p75 both arms** | 1 ms | **7 066 / 7 731 ms** | **1 803 / 1 876 ms** |
>
> **The divergence is gone** — the two arms now measure the same thing, which is what an A/A run is supposed to show — **but
> both sit where the wedged arm used to.** And the occupancy is 56 on both, with `live_gt_60s` only 3, so ~53 streams are
> ten to sixty seconds old on a workload whose requests take milliseconds.
>
> **The mechanism is a feedback the old stall was hiding**: a refused visitor used to occupy its pairing for five seconds, and
> that stall *was* the backpressure. Making the refusal instant removes the stall, so the churn loop cycles faster, offers
> more concurrent work, and the pool saturates harder — the ceiling line fires 392 times where it fired once.
>
> **So the refusal path is right and insufficient**: it removes a five-second stall and an unbounded wedge (worst 175 s → 10.9 s)
> while removing the backpressure that kept the pool under its ceiling. **Explicit admission is the missing piece** — refusing
> the visitor at the listener when the pool cannot serve it, instead of accepting and then failing fast.

> **§4.466 (the refusal path works, measured): the five-second stall is gone.** With both halves in (`9098125`, `9983658`), a
> soak whose arms both run the refusal path:
>
> | reading | before (p70) | after (p75) |
> |---|---|---|
> | `pairing budget expired` | 0 / **54** | **0 / 0** |
> | `shedding the visitor` on a refused group | — | **391 / 410** |
> | `every tunnel is at its stream ceiling` | 1 / 54 | 392 / 411 |
> | wedge count / worst | 2 / 6, up to 15 s | **1 / 1, 10.2 / 10.9 s** |
> | `live_gt_10s` | 56 | 56 |
>
> **The budget expiry is at zero on both arms** — the five seconds per unsuccessful gather no longer exist, because a refusal
> is now an event the gather sees and it sheds the visitor at once. The ceiling and shed counts rose **because the cycle is
> fast now**: the same offered churn produces many more, much shorter, refusals instead of a few five-second stalls.
>
> **What did not change is the occupancy**: `live_gt_10s` is still 56. That is a different fact — the pool really is at its
> ceiling for this workload — and the fix was never going to change it. It changed the **cost of a refusal** from five seconds
> of a held visitor to microseconds, and the worst wedge on either arm from 15–175 s to 10.9 s.

> **§4.465 (the server half of the refusal path is in; the client half is the last piece).** `9098125` adds
> `SessionCmd::ChannelRefused(ServiceId, [u8; 4])` with a roundtrip test, a `refused` set and `Notify` on `ChannelQueue` with
> `refuse()` / `refused(group)`, the queue filed per service in `SessionCtx` (via a new `ControlChannelHandle::channels()`),
> the dispatch arm that calls `refuse`, and the pairing's select arm that **sheds the visitor at once** instead of waiting out
> the budget. Both clippy builds are 0 and the 410 tests pass. **Behaviour is unchanged until the client sends it.**
>
> **What the client half needs, precisely**: `RunDataChannelArgs` has no session sender, and the only place that can write a
> session command is the control session loop, which owns `wr` (`client.rs:4225`). So:
> 1. create an `mpsc::UnboundedSender<(ServiceId, [u8; 4])>` where the session loop starts and hold the receiver there;
> 2. add a select arm to that loop that writes `SessionCmd::ChannelRefused(..)` with `wr`;
> 3. carry a clone of the sender into `RunDataChannelArgs` through `activate()` (`client.rs:4882`, built at `4937`);
> 4. send `(service_id, group.to_be_bytes())` where the prologue fails (`client.rs:1657`) and where `open_stream` is refused.

> **§4.464 (the protocol path's ordering constraint, found by trying to add the variant first).** Adding
> `SessionCmd::ChannelRefused` alone **does not build**: the server's `handle_session_cmd` match is exhaustive
> (`server.rs:1303`), so the variant needs its consumer in the same commit. And that consumer is not reachable today —
> `pair_striped_group` selects on `data_ch_rx`, but **the `ChannelQueue` is created at `server.rs:3008`, after the session loop
> at `1245`, and `SessionCtx` does not hold it**.
>
> **So the order of work is forced**:
> 1. make the queue reachable from the session task (share it before the loop, add it to `SessionCtx`);
> 2. add `refused: Mutex<HashSet<u32>>` + `Notify` and `refuse(group)` / `refused(group)` to `ChannelQueue`;
> 3. add `SessionCmd::ChannelRefused(ServiceId, [u8; 4])` with a roundtrip test;
> 4. the server arm: `ctx.data_ch_rx.refuse(group)`;
> 5. the pairing's select arm: a refused group **sheds the visitor at once** — a refusal is definitive, unlike a slow
>    channel, which is what `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` is for;
> 6. the client sends it: `RunDataChannelArgs` has no session sender, so one has to be threaded in.
>
> **Step 3 alone was written and reverted** rather than landed as an unhandled variant — a variant with no consumer is a dead
> path, and the tree is green as it stands.

> **§4.463 (the tree at the end of this goal, verified).** On `47df18b`: **both clippy builds at 0 errors**, **410 lib tests pass**,
> **`git status` clean**, `just interop` 3/3, `just l3-accept` PASS through its sudo entry point. The only red in the chain is
> §4.461's advisory, which predates this branch's last dependency change.

> **§4.499 (the carrier's case, measured: it loses on a clean path, ties under loss, and leads under jitter).** Same build, same host,
> `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER` pinning one carrier per run, three rounds each; the clean batch is §4.498 (four scenarios), the impaired
> batches are three scenarios with `--condition loss1` and `--condition jitter` on the visitor leg (1186 s, 1185 s, 1516 s, 1516 s).
>

> |---|---|---|---|

> | bulk-1 CPU per Gbit (s) | 0.76 / **0.48** | 0.77 / **0.46** | 0.77 / **0.48** |
> | rr-1 rate (req/s) | 6 278 / **10 213** | **40.7** / 39.5 | 24.7 / 24.6 |
> | rr-1 rtt p50 (ms) | 0.147 / **0.088** | 20.70 / 20.69 | **40.31** / 40.76 |
> | rr-1 rtt p99 (ms) | 0.187 / **0.121** | 245.2 / 246.7 | **57.47** / 57.57 |
> | rr-16 rate (req/s) | 22 305 / **27 631** | 603 / 614 | 394.2 / 394.4 |
> | rr-16 rtt p50 (ms) | 0.645 / **0.518** | 20.42 / 20.57 | 40.53 / 40.51 |
> | rr-16 rtt p99 (ms) | 1.673 / **1.363** | 246.1 / 245.9 | 57.69 / 57.67 |
>
> **Reading it honestly**: on a clean loopback TCP is ahead everywhere. **Under 1 % loss the two converge to the impairment's own floor**
> (p50 ≈ 20.7 ms, p99 ≈ 246 ms on both) and the carrier stops mattering — the interactive rate is a dead heat (40.7 against 39.5).
> **Under jitter mhd leads**: bulk **+6 %** (3.44 against 3.24 Gbit/s), interactive p50 40.31 against 40.76 and p99 57.47 against
> 57.57, with the sixteen-connection rate equal (394.2 against 394.4).
>
> **So the carrier's reason to exist is real but narrow**: it never loses when the path is impaired, ties under loss,
> and its advantage under jitter is a few percent — while it costs **2.1–3.4× the CPU** and **3× the RSS** on every path, clean or not.
> That is the honest summary, and it is the first time this repository has it measured in one batch across three conditions.

> **§4.498 (mhd against TCP, same build and host, one batch): TCP is ahead on every axis on a clean loopback path.** Both runs use the
> `dev` profile's four scenarios, three rounds, one arm (`molehill`), with `MOLEHILL_DATA_CARRIER` pinning one carrier per run — the

> | churn-16 | CPU per Gbit | **405 s** | **196 s** | ×2.1 |
>
> **What this says and does not say**: on a **clean loopback** path the userspace carrier is 19–39 % behind in completed work, 23–67 %
> behind in latency, **2.1–3.4× more expensive in CPU** and **3× in RSS**, while spending 5 % more bytes on the wire in bulk. That is
> the expected direction — kernel TCP on loopback has no packet loss to repair and no userspace copies to pay for — and **it is not a
> verdict on the carrier's reason to exist**: mhd's case is jitter, loss and reordering, which this batch did not impose. A
> comparison under `--condition loss1` / `jitter` is the measurement that would decide it, and it has not been run.

> **FINAL STATE OF THIS DEFECT (round 38 of this goal; supersedes the block below and every earlier closing note).**
>
> **One sentence**: when the client's stream pool is at its ceiling, **a channel request that is refused produces no event the
> server's gather can see**, so the gather waits out `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` (5 s) per attempt (`server.rs:4618`, budget at
> `server.rs:96`, `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` of them), holding the visitor's connection and every channel that did arrive.
>
> **Why it fills the pool**: each refusal costs five seconds of held capacity, which causes the next refusal. That is a positive
> feedback loop, not a leak — and it is why nothing in isolation looked broken.

## The open-problems record (archived 2026-11-21)

§4.1 through §4.512 as they were written while they were open: symptom, what was
unknown, the experiment, and what the run answered. **A question that is still open
is in `HANDOFF.md` §4**; what is here is closed, superseded or abandoned, with the
numbers unchanged so an older citation still names the same round.

### 4.1 A visitor pays for a Noise handshake that TCP does not

- **Symptom.** Clean p99 22.5 ms against 2–3.5 ms for the TCP peers (§3.1), and
  the earlier cycle measured `open_us` p90 45.8 ms / max 101.5 ms on individual
  opens — a per-stream tail, not a throughput problem.
- **Where it is, measured (A0 done).** The client already splits an open into
  `started_us` (spawn) / `open_us` (the carrier's stream open) / `ready_us`
  (prologue) / `cmd_us` (command), and the carrier splits the open again into
  `hs_us` (handshake) and `ack_us` (hello acknowledgement). In the failing
  samples **all of the wait is `hs_us`**:

  ```
  started_us=2..16   open_us=8005..21924   ready_us=open_us+2..4   cmd_us=ready_us+3..17
  mhd slow stream open: lane=0 us=21924 hs_us=21820 ack_us=0
  ```

  So the whole clean tail is the **per-visitor Noise handshake**, and a stream
  open costs 5–22 ms where a loopback round trip costs 0.1.
- **Two hypotheses already refuted, both one-constant A/Bs on the `dev` profile**
  (`churn-16`, A/A in the same run, noise ±0.5 ms): the small-flight RTO clamp
  (`MIN_RTO_SMALL_FLIGHT` 20 → 2 ms) and the unmeasured small-flight timer
  (`SMALL_FLIGHT_INITIAL_RTO` 20 → 2 ms). `churn-16` read **10.2 ms** at the
  baseline, **9.95 ms** and **9.5–10.7 ms** after — no change, both reverted. The
  20 ms is therefore **not** a retransmission timer, even though the code contains
  two constants of exactly that value on the same path. (A number matching a
  constant is a reason to look, not a finding.)
- **A proviso on that second A/B.** I rebuilt the binary *while its run was still
  going*, so only that run's first four rounds belong to the 2 ms build (9.720,
  10.472, 7.373, 10.733 ms); the rest measured a mixed binary and are not used.
  The conclusion does not change — the first four are the whole of the evidence —
  but the rule is worth restating: **build, then run, then read; never rebuild
  under a measurement.**
- **Unknown.** Where inside `open_channel_carrying` the time goes: the first
  Noise message's write, the pump's post of it, or the wait for the reply. The
  instrument that answers it is three timestamps inside that call.
- **A0b/A0c, done — and they reframe the question.** Two instruments and three
  runs (`churn-16` and `rr-16`, ~2 000 opens, same-run A/A) say:

  1. an idle write reaches the wire inside five milliseconds — `mhd idle write
     waited for the pump` fired **zero** times;
  2. the server's own path is microseconds — `accept_p50 6 µs`, `post_p50 12 µs`;
  3. in the churn scenario **no open exceeded 5 ms at all** — the
     `mhd open round trip` line never fired.

  So the 21.8 ms `hs_us` that A0 found is **not** the clean path's cost: it is an
  open measured **under contention** (during bulk), which is phase C's problem,
  not the handshake's.

  What the plan's completion condition compares against TCP is the bench's
  `churn-16` cell: `kind="rr"`, sixteen connections each carrying four hundred
  requests, every connection fresh, and the cell is **the round trip of the first
  request on each new connection** — its own claim says so, and that the connect
  itself is `setup_p50_ms` because the server accepts before it pairs. That cell
  reads **10.4 ms** here against 2.1–3.5 ms for the TCP peers.

  The carrier's share of it is now bounded from both ends: the channel open never
  reached 5 ms in these runs (point 3), and the server's accept and post are
  microseconds (point 2). So the residual ~10 ms is in the **forward and echo
  path** — the pair, the backend round trip, the response leg — and that is where
  the next instrument goes. (The probe now states the same connect/echo split on
  its churn line that it already stated for the interactive one; `churn-16` itself
  is an `rr` scenario and does not use that probe.)

- **Unknown.** Whether RACK-style loss detection plus a separate PTO — the split
  MsQuic makes in `core/loss_detection.c` — removes both the age gate and the
  full-flight retransmission storm without reintroducing spurious repairs.
- **Next experiment.** Phase B below.
- **Pass.** A single lost opening recovers at low latency; bulk never re-sends a
  healthy flight; `churn-16`, `rr-16`, both clean stages and `loss1/loss5/rtt100`
  each judged alone; retransmission volume and CPU compared in the same round.
- **Rollback.** Any healthy full-flight retransmission storm, or a first-stage
  throughput drop.

### 4.3 A new stream queues behind bulk

- **Symptom.** `conn.rs` schedules one packet per stream round robin, so a
  44-packet GSO run can belong entirely to mature bulk streams while an opening
  waits its turn.
- **Unknown.** Whether bounded per-class quanta (control/repair/opening,
  new-stream, bulk by byte deficit) move the clean tail without costing single
  stream throughput.
- **Next experiment.** Phase C below.
- **Rollback.** p99 improves while throughput falls; or fairness arguments end up
  starving new streams under an adversary that keeps opening them.

### 4.4 The window only grows, and it grows from a proxy

- **Symptom.** `cwnd` never decreases on loss and slow start never returns; the
  flight total is measuring *received* bytes rather than *delivered* ones, which
  this cycle showed is load-bearing: freeing it on what the peer holds made the
  transfer four to five times worse.
- **Unknown.** Whether a delivery-rate/BDP controller (a simplified BBR: startup,
  drain, probe-BW, app-limited sampling) makes the clean stage stable and the
  shaped stages recoverable, and whether its pacing avoids adding a new
  sub-millisecond wait.
- **Next experiment.** Phase D below.
- **Rollback.** Less stable than today's cwnd on a clean host; keep the recovery
  and scheduler work, revert the controller alone.

### 4.5 The runner's summary prints dashes over real data

- **Symptom.** The sweep summary shows `run: -` and `L1..L8: -` for every arm
  while the results file holds those samples; `just bench gate` reads them fine.
- **Unknown.** Which metric the summary selects per cell — a display bug, not a
  data one.
- **Next experiment.** Fix the summary to name the metric it prints, so a future
  reader cannot mistake "no metric chosen" for "no measurement".

### 4.6 Evidence has been lost to its own clean-up

- **Symptom.** A clean-up glob `m[0-9]*-*` matched the result files as well as the
  scratch directories and deleted `~/tmp/m2*.json`, including the aggregate of the
  gate-passing sweep (§7). The raw per-sample artefacts of that run survive under
  `~/tmp/bench-20261105-230248/`, and the gate output is quoted here.
- **Rule for next time.** Clean up by **directory type** (`bench-<date>-<time>/`,
  `m<round>-<topic>/`), list what will be deleted and count it first, and keep
  result JSONs in a directory that no clean-up pattern covers.

### 4.382 One pairing waits ten seconds while the probe's own timeout is five (2026-11-14)

The expiry line carries `attempts`, `gathered` and `waited_ms`, and the same `group` appears twice — for 7812:

```
attempts=1 group=7812 gathered=0 waited_ms=5000
attempts=2 group=7812 gathered=0 waited_ms=10001
```

**So a pairing that gathers nothing waits `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` (5 s), retries, and waits another five — ten seconds — while the
visitor's own connect timeout is five.** The visitor has given up by then, and the wedge durations this record has been
reading are exactly that arithmetic: 10.01 s, 15.015 s, 25.024 s are one, one and a half, and two and a half pairings.

**Two consequences, both worth acting on:**

1. **The gate's number is a pairing budget, not a carrier stall.** `wedge_max_s` ≥ 10 s is what two attempts of a
   five-second budget looks like when nothing answers.
2. **Retrying to ten seconds when the visitor leaves at five is work spent on a visitor that is gone** — the second
   attempt cannot help anyone, and it holds the group (and its slot) for five more seconds.

**And the cause is still that nothing answers the ask.** Both attempts gather zero, so the client never delivered a
channel for 7812 either time; the ask, its receipt and its answer remain the three timestamps nobody has taken.

### 4.381 The stale claim is real and rare, and it was not the cause (2026-11-14)

§4.380 called the refusal at `server.rs:2603` the root cause. The fix landed (`2da9cee`, 410 tests green) and the
next soak says otherwise:

| reading | before the fix | after it |
|---|---|---|
| twin's wedges | 6 (15.015 s) | **6 (10.01 s)** |
| twin's pairing expiries | — | **37** |
| twin's `opened_len` max | 56 | **56** |
| the new line ("registering it from the stream's own prologue") | — | **4** |

**The stale-claim case happens four times in a run, and the pairings still expire thirty-seven times** — so the
refusal was never the mechanism behind `gathered=0`, and §4.380's causal claim is withdrawn. The fix stays: it is
correct on its own terms (a claim with no acknowledgement must not be refused), it is test-covered, and it removes a
real if rare failure — but it was not this defect.

**What the four-versus-thirty-seven does say**: a pairing expires for reasons that are ten times more common than a
stale claim. The pairing waits for a channel that was **asked for** — the server's request to the client for a
channel — and gathers nothing, while the client opens thousands of channels per run. So either the request does not
reach the client, or the client's channel for it arrives after the budget.

**The next instrument is on that request**: log, on the server, when it asks for a channel (group, service, time) and,
on the client, when it receives the ask and when it answers. Three timestamps per pairing say which of the two it is,
and they are the only thing in this line that has never been timed.

### 4.380 The root cause: the server refuses a stream whose claim says "registered" while it holds no registration (2026-11-14)

§4.379's claim mismatch, located in the code (`server.rs:2603`). When a data channel's selector is
`REGISTERED_SELECTOR` or `DERIVED_REGISTERED_SELECTOR`, the server sets `claimed_registered` — and then, at the
session state:

```rust
if let Some(existing) = registered.as_ref() { … } else if claimed_registered {
    // **The claim this end cannot honour.** …
    // So the *stream* is refused, not the lane
```

**The stream is refused.** Not the lane — the single channel — so the pairing that was waiting for it gathers
nothing, expires after `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET`, and the visitor is dropped.

**That is the defect, and it now explains every reading in this line at once:**

| reading | explanation |
|---|---|
| 43 pairings expired with `gathered=0` | the channel was refused, not paired |
| 14 547 channels accepted, selectors all read | the stream *is* accepted and its selector read; the refusal happens after |
| the pool's four lanes at 56 | each refused channel still charges the lane until the client gives up |
| a 1 % tail of 5-second hangs | those are the refused channels |
| no error counter anywhere | the refusal is a `bail!` on a *stream*, and the pool treats it as a failed open and rebuilds |
| clean on one run, wedged on another | it depends on whether that session's registration is present when the claim arrives |

**The condition** is that the client claims "registered" while the server holds **no** registration for that session:
the client's belief is stale — it derives the claim from its own lane root, which outlives the server's registration.

**The fix is a decision, not a patch**, and it is the next thing to make: either the client stops claiming registered
when its registration has not been re-confirmed on this lane, or the server re-registers from the stream's own
prologue instead of refusing it. The second is the one that removes the failure mode rather than narrowing it, and it
is what a protocol with no acknowledgement for this claim needs.

### 4.379 Every expired pairing gathered *zero* channels, while the server accepted every channel (2026-11-14)

The discriminator §4.378 needed, from the logs already on disk — the pairing-expiry line carries `gathered`:

| arm | pairing expiries | `gathered=0` |
|---|---|---|
| product (4 wedges) | **43** | **43** |
| twin (clean) | **0** | — |

**All forty-three expired with no channel at all**, on an arm where the server accepted **14 547** channels from the same
client. So the channels arrived — the frames were parsed, the streams created, the selectors read (§4.378) — and
**not one of them was attached to a pairing that was waiting for it**.

**That is a claim mismatch, not a transport loss.** The channel reaches `handle_data_channel`, is claimed under its
selector, and instead of joining the group that is parked waiting (`pair_striped_group`), it is treated as a new
visitor — so the pairing sits until `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET`, expires with `gathered=0`, and the visitor is dropped. From the
probe's side that is a five-second hang and then a refused dial, which is the wedge.

**This is the first finding in this line that points at a specific code path rather than a distribution**: the selector
a channel carries, and the group the pairing is waiting on, do not meet. The sealed-open claim (§ earlier in this
record) is the mechanism that decides which path a channel takes — `DERIVED_REGISTERED_SELECTOR` with a lane root, or
`REGISTERED_SELECTOR`/`PLAIN_SELECTOR` without one — and a channel whose claim says "registered" while the pairing
waits under a different claim lands on the wrong side.

**The next read is the claim's write and its parse, side by side**: what the client writes into the selector for a
pooled channel, and what `handle_data_channel` compares it against.

### 4.378 The server reads every selector, so the hang is after it (2026-11-14)

§4.377 left one question: what a hung request waits for. The answer's first half, from the wedged arm's own log —
joining the streams whose first packet arrived against those the accept loop read:

| reading | count |
|---|---|
| distinct streams with a first packet | **14 547** |
| distinct streams the accept loop read a selector from | **14 548** |
| **first packets never read** | **0** |

**Not one channel was left unread.** So the packet path is clean — the frame arrives, the lane creates the stream, the
accept loop picks it up and reads the selector, for every single open of the run — and a request that hangs hangs
**after** its selector.

**That kills the two candidate explanations on this side**: the packet never arriving, and the accept loop never being
scheduled. What remains is the server's answer: the hello that follows the selector, the pairing it waits on, and the
reply it writes. `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` is five seconds and the probe's own timeout is five seconds — **the same number**,
which is why a hung request and an unanswered pairing look identical from the probe and why the record could not tell
them apart for fifty rounds.

**The next instrument names which of the two fired**: on the server, log when a pairing's budget expires with the
stream id it belonged to, and on the client, when its five-second wait ends — then the two lines either match (the
pairing) or do not (the reply).

### 4.377 Every open is a visitor open, and thirteen a second times four seconds is fifty-six (2026-11-14)

The tag instrument (`3df5adb`) on a run where the product arm wedged (4 wedges, 10.01 s) and its twin did not:

| arm | `opens_open` | `opens_striped` | `opens_other` | `opened_len` max | wedges |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| product | **14 548** | 0 | **0** | **56** | 4 |
| twin | 10 995 | 0 | **0** | 4 | 0 |

**No second dialler exists.** Every channel this campaign ever opened came through the plain visitor path — the
hypothesis that something other than a visitor dials is refuted, and so is a per-visitor retry.

**And the arithmetic now closes**: 14 548 opens over ~1 080 s is **13.5 a second**, and a lane holding 56 of them
means each lives **~4 seconds** on average. The median request is 1.3 ms, so those four seconds are not the typical
request — they are the tail that hangs until its **5 s timeout**.

**So the fifty-six are hung visitor requests**, and the lane's ceiling turns "a few requests hang" into "the pool has
no channel to give". The two facts this line has chased separately — a hanging request and a full pool — are the same
event seen twice, and the first is the cause.

**What is left is exactly one question, and it is now narrow enough to instrument directly**: what a hung request is
waiting for. Its channel was opened, its selector written, and the reply never came back within five seconds; on the
client that is `handle_data_channel` waiting for the first selector byte, i.e. the server never read it.

### 4.376 The churn loop is sequential, so the probes account for two channels out of fifty-six (2026-11-14)

`run_churn` (`probes/series.py:191`) is a `while` loop that calls `ping()` and emits — **one connection at a time**, no
workers, no keep-alive. The interactive probe is likewise one. So the two probes ride on **at most two channels
between them**, and the budget's other paths (bulk, rr) are not in this profile.

**Fifty-six dialled channels against two accounted for.** §4.375's two candidates are now one: not "a worker pool opens
more than one per visitor" — there is no worker pool — but **something else calls `open_stream`**.

**`client.rs` has two call sites** (`1597` for a plain visitor channel, and the striped path), and both are per-request
with no retry. So either a request is forwarded more than once, or a channel is dialled for something that is not a
visitor at all.

**The next instrument is the caller tag §4.371 named**, and the cheap routes are now exhausted: a `&'static str` on
`Conn::open` for the call site, counted per opening and printed beside `opened_len`. One run then says whether the
fifty-six are visitor channels, striped groups, or a third thing — which is the question the last six rounds have
circled without being able to ask.

### 4.375 All fifty-six are dialled here, and that is more than the probes can hold (2026-11-14)

The origin instrument (`opened_here`, `4f08d9d`) on a run that wedged (twin: 6 wedges, 15.015 s):

| arm | `opened_len` max | `opened_here` max | wedges |
|---|---|---|---|
| product | 5 | **5** | 0 |
| twin | **56** | **56** | 6 |

**Every stream is one this end dialled** — no peer-created channel is in the table. So the client opened 56 channels to
one lane and holds them all.

**And that is more than the workload can ask for.** The soak's probes run at 16 concurrent (churn) and 16 (rr), the
bulk stages at 8, the interactive at 1. Their sum is well under 56, and each probe's *own* measured concurrency is
single digits (§4.371). **So the count exceeds what any probe claims to be using, on a lane that was dialled 56
times.**

**That is now the whole of the question, and it is a countable one**: either a probe's worker pool is larger than its
nominal concurrency (16 workers each opening more than one channel), or something re-dials when a channel is not
answered — a retry that leaves the previous channel open. The second would explain the growth over minutes and the
absence of any error counter, and it is checkable in one place: **whether `open_stream` is ever called again for a
visitor that already has a channel.**

### 4.374 The soak profile runs no capacity ramp, so §4.373's candidate dies too (2026-11-14)

The soak profile's scenario list is `("soak",)` (`model.py:1834`) — the five-stage timeline and the probes that ride
it. **`capacity` is a different profile and never runs here**, so nothing in this campaign opens streams until the
pool refuses. The eleventh candidate goes the way of the other ten, and it goes cheaply: one `grep` of the profile
table instead of a forty-minute run.

**What that leaves is the starkest statement in this record**: during a soak, the client holds **224 streams** (four
lanes at 56, `opened_len`, each with a live handle — none abandoned) while **every probe's own concurrency is single
digits** and every latency distribution is healthy except a one-percent tail.

**Those two cannot both be about the same connections.** Either the probes under-report their own concurrency, or the
224 handles are held by tasks that are not serving a visitor. The instrument that separates them is the one §4.371
named and this line has not built: **count the streams by what is on the other side of them** — a visitor socket, a
peer's fin, or nothing at all. That is a per-stream tag set at `open()` and printed as a histogram, and it is the only
remaining measurement that can tell "224 visitors are waiting" from "224 tasks are holding a channel each and doing
nothing".

### 4.373 The pool is a lease pool, so nothing is prefilled — and the capacity ramp is what fills it (2026-11-14)

§4.372's hypothesis, read in the code: `Multiplex::open_stream` returns a **`StreamLease`** (`multiplex.rs:2064`), a
lease that releases its stream when dropped. There is no prefill list, no idle set, no pinned-and-unplaced channel.

**So every one of the 56 is held by something that wants it** — hypothesis dead, the tenth in this line to go that way.

**And the thing that wants them is in the benchmark's own design**: `run_capacity` (`workloads.py:1799`) **ramps levels
and opens streams until the pool refuses**, which is exactly how it measures `capacity_streams`. That scenario forces
the pool to its ceiling by construction — 4 lanes × 56 = the 224 this line has been counting — and the reading it
produces is the one already in the record: **`capacity_streams` median 4 against the control's 8**.

**So the shape to test is**: does the capacity ramp's occupancy come back down before the next scenario dials? If it
does not, every later scenario in that arm — churn, interactive — inherits a full pool, and the "wedge" is the ramp's
tail rather than a transport defect at all. The bench already prints the capacity cell's `sustainable` count per level;
what it does not print is the pool's occupancy **after** the ramp, which is the number that decides this.

**That is one line in the harness and no change to the tool**: log `pool-stats`' own `streams`/`pinned` count at the
end of the capacity cell. If it is 224 there and falls only with the next stage, the wedge is the ramp's, and the gate
has been blaming the carrier for its own instrument.

### 4.372 The slowness is a one-percent tail, so occupancy has to come from channels nobody serves (2026-11-14)

The interactive series on the wedged arm (p47, 5 wedges):

| n | p50 | p90 | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 445 | **1.3 ms** | 288 ms | **1 007 ms** | 2 900 ms |

**A 1 % tail over 1 s.** At the probes' rates that is a couple of slow requests in flight at any moment — two or three,
not 224. And the churn's own concurrency was measured in single digits (§4.371). So **no probe is waiting on 224
channels, while both the pool (`count=4 × ceiling=56`) and the stream table (`opened_len` 56 per lane) say 224 exist**.

**That leaves one shape the record has not tested: channels opened and then never handed to a visitor.** Every one of
the 56 is in `stream_opened`, which is written only by `open()` — this end dialling — so they were all opened *by the
client*, and a client opens channels either to serve a visitor or to fill the pool ahead of one. If the pool prefills
to the ceiling and does not reuse what it prefilled, the table reads 56 forever while the probes see almost nothing.

**The next read is the pool's placement code**: whether a channel it opened is tracked as *available* and handed out,
or opened and pinned without ever being placed. That is a read of the pool, not of the carrier, and it is the first
hypothesis in this line that explains *both* counts at once while every probe says the instance is nearly idle.

**Marked as a hypothesis, not a finding** — the last nine of those went down with the next measurement.

### 4.371 Neither probe can hold 224, so the occupancy is censored *and* unattributed (2026-11-14)

§4.370 said the churn's distribution is censored and that the missing tail would explain the occupancy. The series says
how censored, and it is not enough:

| reading | value |
|---|---|
| `setup_ms` samples in the run | **8 689** |
| connections the nominal rate implies (16/s over ~900 s) | ~14 400 |
| `error` samples | **18** |

So about **5 700 connections never produced a sample** — the censoring is real and large. But a completed connection
takes ~120 ms on average (8 689 over ~1 050 s is 8.3/s, i.e. roughly one in flight per worker), so the churn's own
concurrency is **single digits**, not 224.

**Which leaves the 224 unattributed**: neither probe holds that many at once, so the streams are opened by something
else or by connections whose sample was lost. The next instrument is therefore not another distribution but **an
attribution**: tag each `Conn::open` with the caller (service name and probe kind) and print the per-caller count
beside `opened_len`. That answers "who" with one run, where the last four rounds have answered "what state" four
times without saying who.

### 4.370 §4.369's "stuck copy" is ordinary half-close, and the reader is correct (2026-11-14)

§4.369 read the twenty-six peer-fin streams as the client's copy being stuck. In the code it is not: `StripeSender::
finish` (`stripe.rs:585`) sends the local fin when the **visitor's** side ends — which is exactly right, because a
visitor that has not closed may still send more. So a stream with the peer's fin and no local fin is a **visitor that
is still open**, and holding its channel until it closes is what a correct half-close does.

**Withdrawn.** The twenty-six are normal. And the other thirty (neither fin) are the same thing one step earlier: a
visitor that has been served nothing yet and has not closed either.

**Which leaves the count itself as the finding, not any flag**: 224 visitors open at once on a pool of four lanes. For
a churn series that opens sixteen a second, that is **fourteen seconds each on average** — the arithmetic §4.362 tried
and could not support with the churn's own `setup_ms`. The two are not in contradiction: `setup_ms` measures the
connections the probe **completed**, and a connection still open at the end of the run has no sample at all. The
distribution this record has been reading is therefore **censored** — the slowest connections are exactly the ones
missing from it.

**That is the last instrument to add and it needs nothing new in the tool**: count, per second, the churn connections
opened and not yet closed. It reads the censored tail directly, and if it climbs while `setup_ms` stays at 1.5 ms, the
occupancy is made of connections that never finish rather than connections that are slow.

### 4.369 What the 26 peer-fin streams say: the client's own copy is the stuck one (2026-11-14)

§4.368's distribution, read for what it implies rather than what it counts. Twenty-six of the fifty-six carry the
**peer's** fin and none carries this end's: the server finished its side, the client has not finished its own. A
stream in that state is one where the **client's copy toward the visitor** has not ended — either it is still reading
a visitor that will never send again, or it is blocked writing to a visitor that is gone.

**That is a different suspect from every one this line has cleared**, and it is on the client, in the forwarding
loop, not in the carrier: the transport delivered the peer's fin (the flag is set), so the frames arrived; what did not
happen is the local half-close that would let the stream retire.

**The instrument for it is one number per stream**: how long ago the peer's fin arrived on the streams that still have
no local fin. A value near a round trip means the copy is draining normally; a value of seconds means the copy is
stuck, and the direction it is stuck in is the answer.

**And the prediction is testable without the pool**: on a *clean* arm this count stays near zero (§4.368 measured 2),
so anything that makes it climb is the thing to look at — the pool's exhaustion would then be the visible consequence
rather than the subject.

### 4.368 The 56 are live, unfinished, in-use channels — the stalled requests themselves (2026-11-14)

The four flag counts §4.366 asked for, on the run that wedged (twin: 5 wedges, 15.015 s) against the clean arm:

| arm | `opened_len` | `abandoned` | `local_fin` | `peer_fin` | `never_used` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| product | 5 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| twin | **56** | **0** | **1** | **26** | **0** |

**Every one of the 56 is alive in both directions**: none abandoned, only one locally finished, and twenty-six carrying
the peer's fin. The other thirty have neither fin — **open, unfinished, in use**.

**That closes the chain with nothing left unexplained.** A channel that is open and unfinished is one whose forwarder
is still copying, i.e. a **visitor connection that is waiting for an answer**. Fifty-six of them per lane, 224 across
the pool, is what "every request is slow and the pool is full" looks like from inside.

**So the pool's exhaustion, the lane ceiling and the refused dials are all downstream of §4.343's loop**: a request the
server already answered is re-sent, the visitor keeps waiting, its channel stays open, and once sixteen a second of
those accumulate the pool has nothing left to give. The ceiling is not a bug; the **waiting is**.

**Which puts the work back at the one place it started**: why a client re-sends a range the server answered. That is
now the only question left with nothing measured against it, and every other measurement in this line is consistent
with it being answered.

### 4.367 The permanent entry is the lane's own handshake stream, not a leak (2026-11-14)

§4.365 and §4.366 treated the entry whose age equals the run as a leak. Read in the code, it is the **lane's root
stream**: a lane's first stream runs the Noise KK handshake and its secret becomes `LaneRoot`, from which every later
stream's keys are derived. That stream is created when the lane is and lives as long as the lane does — so *one entry
per lane, with an age equal to the run*, is exactly what a healthy lane looks like.

**It explains every reading without a defect**: §4.365 measured 17.9 minutes on the product arm and 17.7 on the twin
in an eighteen-minute run, and §4.366's `opened_len` of 5 and 4 is one root stream plus the few live channels.

**So the permanent entry is withdrawn as a defect**, and with it the two fixes that chased it. `0b05065` (a stream both
ends have closed is retired) and `73da8ac` (a stream that never carried a byte is retired) stay, because each is
correct on its own terms and both have tests — but neither was fixing anything the record can point at, and this entry
says so rather than leaving two "fixes" implying a bug that is not there.

**What remains is the ceiling and nothing else**: on a wedged arm four lanes reach 56 live streams each; on a clean arm
they stay near the root stream. That is the whole of the defect's description now, and the next instrument is the one
§4.366 named — the flags of the streams that make up the 56, not the one that is permanent.

### 4.366 Retiring never-used streams does not remove the permanent entry (2026-11-14)

§4.365 guessed the entry whose age equals the run was a stream opened and never used. The fix (`73da8ac`: a stream
with `send.base() == 0` and nothing outstanding is retired when abandoned) is in, with its tests — and the entry is
**still there**:

| arm | `opened_len` max | `oldest_opened_ms` max | wedges |
|---|---|---|---|
| product | 5 | **1 040 694 ms** | 0 |
| twin | **56** | 982 862 ms | **2**, 15.015 s |

So it is not a never-used stream. Both arms still carry one entry whose age is the whole run, which means whatever
holds it is not `abandoned` either — the `abandoned` gate is the only path into every retirement rule this file has,
and a stream that never becomes `abandoned` never leaves.

**The fix stays** (it is correct on its own terms and covered), but the permanent entry needs the one fact not yet
printed: **which** stream it is. One line at the moment the table's oldest entry changes would name it — the id, and
whether `abandoned`, `local_fin`, `peer_fin` and `send.base()` are set — and that is the next instrument.

**Meanwhile the ceiling reproduced on the twin** (56, two wedges), so the wedge itself is unchanged and the two
questions remain separate: the permanent entry is a leak that a clean arm shows, and the ceiling is what a wedged arm
shows.

### 4.365 The oldest entry in the stream table is as old as the run, on both arms (2026-11-14)

The age instrument (`oldest_opened_ms`, `9bf88f1`) on a run where **both arms were clean** (`0 / 0`):

| arm | `opened_len` max | `oldest_opened_ms` max |
|---|---|---|
| product | 6 | **1 073 478 ms (17.9 min)** |
| twin | 4 | **1 068 469 ms (17.7 min)** |

**The oldest stream has been in the table since the run began**, on both arms — and this run lasted eighteen minutes,
so that entry is the *first* stream the lane ever opened and it has not been retired by any path: not `settle`'s
three conditions, not the abandoned reaper, not the both-fins rule added in §4.359.

**It is a real leak and a small one** — with `opened_len` at 4–6, it is one or two entries per lane, not the 56 a
wedged arm carries. So it does not explain the ceiling by itself; it is a separate defect found on the way, and one
that a clean arm proves exists without needing the wedge at all.

**The next read is why that one stream never enters `settle`**: the candidate is a stream that was opened by a first
packet and then never carried another frame — no fin, no ack of its own, no close — which is the *server-side mirror*
of §4.348's 7 500 channels that never put a first byte on the wire. If the two are the same population seen from the
two ends, that is the first time this line has joined a client-side count to a server-side one.

### 4.364 The pool agrees with the window line, and it says why: pinned at four tunnels on its ceiling (2026-11-14)

The comparison §4.363 asked for, the pool's own line on the wedged arm:

```
pool-stats: pool still at its stream ceiling pool=session:10.10.0.254:2400
            carrier="mhd" count=4 ceiling=56
```

**Two instruments, one run, the same number**: the pool charges `count=4 × ceiling=56 = 224` streams, and the window
line reads 56 on each of its four lanes. Neither is an artefact of the other.

**And the pool names the reason it cannot get out**: `count=4` is the arm's `pool_cap` (`tunnels`), a pinned
parameter — its `report_saturation` comment says so in the code, "a pinned pool cannot dial its way out". So when all
224 streams are charged, a new channel is refused, the pairing gets nothing, and the visitor's dial is refused.

**What is still unexplained is who holds 224 handles**, and this entry narrows it to that single question with both
instruments agreeing on the count. The forwarder's idle timeout (300 s) and the churn's own latency (p50 1.5 ms)
have each been shown not to produce that many on their own; what has not been measured is the **age** of the charged
streams — how long each handle has been held — which is the one distribution that says whether they are accumulating
or merely concurrent.

### 4.363 The churn series does not carry the occupancy either (2026-11-14)

§4.362's arithmetic needed the churn to average near fourteen seconds. Measured on the same run, the churn series'
own `setup_ms`:

| arm | n | p50 | p90 | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| product | 9 544 | **1.5 ms** | 401 ms | 1 050 ms | 5 003 ms |
| twin | 6 038 | **2.6 ms** | 401 ms | 1 666 ms | 5 005 ms |

**A median of 1.5 ms and a p99 of a second cannot fill 224 channels at sixteen a second** — that needs fourteen
seconds *on average*. So occupancy is not rate × latency either, and §4.362's explanation goes the way of the others.

**What is left standing is the measurement alone**: on a wedged arm, four lanes each hold **56 live streams** (224
in total, `local_fin` false), while a clean arm holds **4 per lane**. Every explanation this record has offered for
how they get there — a leak of forwarders (§4.361), a churn concurrency (§4.362) — is refuted by the next number.

**The one thing not yet asked is where those streams come from at all.** 224 live streams is far more than the
soak's churn rate implies and far more than the interactive probe holds. The pool's own `pool-stats` line reports
`streams`/`pending`/`pinned` per pool each second and has not been read against this measurement; that is the next
thing to read, and it is a comparison of two instruments on the same run rather than another hypothesis.

### 4.362 The ceiling is an amplifier, not the cause: 16 a second times a slow request (2026-11-14)

§4.361 said 224 forwarding tasks never ended. Reading the forwarder says otherwise: `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 300 s
and both the striped and unstriped paths cut a group that has seen no activity (`stripe.rs:859`), so a task that
never ends would have to be *active* for twenty minutes.

**And the arithmetic says the same**: the soak's churn series opens 16 connections a second. A pool with 224 channels
is exhausted when **16 × latency > 224**, i.e. when a request takes **more than 14 seconds**. The wedge's own
`wedge_max_s` readings are 15, 25, 55, 125 — all above that.

**So the occupancy is a consequence**: something makes a churn request slow, concurrency rises until the pool has no
channel left, and *then* new dials are refused — which is the failure the probe records. The ceiling turns a slow
request into a refused visitor; it does not cause the slowness.

**Which puts the line back where §4.343 left it**, with one thing added: the 14-second threshold is the number to
beat. Anything that keeps a churn request under fourteen seconds keeps the pool from filling, whatever it is —
and §4.343's finding (the client re-sending a range the server had already answered) is a *plausible* way to spend
fourteen seconds on a connection that should take one round trip.

**So the next thing to measure is not the pool but that loop**: the re-sent range and its waiting time, on a channel
that is slow. The pool's exhaustion then becomes an effect that stops once the loop does.

### 4.361 Every lane reaches 56 on the wedged arm, so the whole pool is out of channels (2026-11-14)

The per-lane reading §4.360 asked for, from the same run:

| arm | lane | `opened_len` max |
|---|---|---|
| product (0 wedges) | all four | **4** |
| twin (3 wedges, 125.125 s) | **all four** | **56** |

**So it is not placement** — the wedged arm's four lanes are *each* at 56, i.e. **224 concurrent live streams** and a
pool with no channel left. The clean arm's four lanes never leave 4.

**And the 224 are not half-open** (§4.360 measured at most 2), which means they all have `local_fin` **false**: this
end never finished them. A stream is finished by its forwarder when the copy ends; 224 of those forwarders never
ended and are still holding their handles.

**That is the defect's shape**: a channel's forwarding task does not terminate, so the stream stays live, so the lane
never frees a slot, so after enough churn the pool is out of channels and every new visitor's pairing gets nothing.
It explains every measurement in this line — the pool being healthy while dials are refused, the no-lane-death, the
absence of any error counter, and the fact that it takes minutes of churn to appear.
