The piece §4.239 said was missing, and the last of F2: **a declaration that is not a probe halves the
window**, at most once per smoothed round trip, never below two segments. A probe still pays nothing —
that rule is from §4.214 and it is the one that keeps a healthy lane from cutting itself; the epoch
limit keeps one hole from costing a quarter, an eighth and a sixteenth of the pipe as each
acknowledgement and then the timer report it.

Six measured rounds, candidate and frozen baseline interleaved in one campaign, peers beside them:

| frp | 0.0951 | 17 | 16, 18, 17, 16, 17, 39 |
| baseline (`molehill~b`) | 0.0840 | **2 460** | 2 536, 7 605, 1 825, 2 173, 2 385, 6 868 |

baseline": the candidate is **6 % above** it (0.0890 against 0.0840). The worst round is 122 drops

failed because the window did not bound the wire: `flight` was three to sixteen times `cwnd`, so

**Not the whole of F3.** F3.2's other cells — `loss5`, `rate100`, `rate1000`, `bulk-n`, `loss1`,

### 4.237 The window moved to the send point: no drops, and two accounting defects exposed (2026-11-10)

F2's first candidate, three changes, each one a consequence of §4.236:

1. **The window is applied where a packet is built.** `next_stream_range` may take a new range
   only while `flight + want ≤ cwnd` (an unacknowledged stream may overdraw by `OPEN_RESERVE`,
   which is where that reserve now lives).
2. **`write` no longer consults the window.** Admission is the peer's credit and this end's
   buffer; the reserve stays there, as a reserve of the *credit*, so a bulk run cannot spend what
   an opening needs.
3. **The byte prefix grows the window.** It confirms the same thing the number block does, and
   the growth rule had excluded it since §4.108.

Measured on `rate100_shallow`, A/B against the frozen baseline in one campaign
(`--binary-b /home/dsh/tmp/mhd-baseline-6ed32c1 --ab-arm molehill`):

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0955 / 0.0953 | 16 / 17 |
| frp | 0.0952 / 0.0952 | 17 / 15 |
| baseline (`molehill~b`) | 0.0830 / 0.0842 | **2 115 / 2 261** |
| candidate | **0.0295 / 0.0295** | **0 / 0** |

**The drops are gone and the throughput is 35 % of the baseline.** Both halves of that are
information, and the second is the more useful.

**What the fix did, per lane** (stats-on run, the busiest lane's last two lines):

| fact | before (§4.236) | after |
|---|---|---|
| `cwnd` | 406 049 | 295 431, **and growing** (`grow=44 517`/s) |
| `flight` | 6 665 480 (16.4 × cwnd) | **295 431 — exactly `cwnd`** |
| `flight_packets` | 4 942 | 219 |
| `srtt` | 386 ms | **43 ms** (path `min` 40 ms: the queue is empty) |
| repairs' share of what was sent | 94 % | **7 %** |
| timer declarations, whole stage | 15 067 | **3** |
| retirement | `num=0`, `pfx=330 505` | `num=5 601 048`, `pfx=392 559` |

So the two defects the fix exposed are both visible in the before column and both now behave:

- **the number-ack path retired nothing** (`num=0`) while the prefix carried every byte — which is
  why `acked.progress` was never true and `grow=0`: the congestion window had **no delivery signal
  it recognised**. With the prefix counted, `num` works and the window grows.
- **the timer declared 15 067 losses against 7 191 actual drops**, because a 16 × window flight
  kept packets outstanding far past `loss_delay`. With the flight bounded by the window, there are
  three declarations in a whole stage.

**What is left, and it is one thing.** The lane now obeys its window honestly, and its window is
small: 295 KB over a 43 ms path is 55 Mbit/s, of which the cell sees 29.5. `slow_start` is `false`
— latched off by the first loss, by design ("nothing cuts the window; a loss is repaired") — so the
window grows **one MSS per window** from wherever it was when that loss happened, which on this
cell was a small fraction of the path. The rest of the gap is the ramp, not the window.

**Next, therefore, is not a new controller**: it is the *slow-start restart* the existing growth
rule is missing — a window that has fallen below the path's own bandwidth-delay product
(`min_rtt × peak delivery`) doubles again until it gets there, and only then grows additively. That
is `max(cwnd × 2, cwnd + acked)` in slow start and nothing else changes.

**The candidate is not committed as a win**: drops are what F3 measures, and F3 also requires the
throughput not to regress. This commit is the fix plus its record; the ramp is the next step.

### 4.236 The window gates the buffer and not the wire (2026-11-10)

F1's read-only run, with the cumulative counters from `9fdc625`. Three rounds of `rate100_shallow`, the busiest lane of the
server side each time, read off the last window line of the round:

| round | `cwnd` | `flight` | ratio | `buffered` | records | qdisc drops | threshold | timer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 399 304 | 1 195 676 | **3.0×** | 1 195 676 | 887 | 2 008 | 297 | 5 916 |
| 1 | 387 163 | 4 499 288 | **11.6×** | 4 499 288 | 3 336 | 1 773 | 85 | 2 057 |
| 2 | 406 049 | 6 665 480 | **16.4×** | 6 665 480 | 4 942 | 7 191 | 2 505 | 15 067 |

Three things are exact and they settle the attribution:

1. **`flight` equals `buffered` to the byte in every round**, and `records × 1 349` reproduces `flight` (887 × 1349 =
   1 196 963, 3 336 × 1349 = 4 500 264, 4 942 × 1349 = 6 666 758). So **every byte in the send buffer is on the wire as a
   live record**: nothing is waiting unsent.
2. **The flight is 3 to 16 times the congestion window.** The window is not bounding what is in flight, and it is not
   bounded by anything else either — `ceiling` is 10 MB, so the window is nowhere near its own limit.
3. `total_cuts = 0`: nothing cuts the window on a loss, which is the state the engine is in by design.

**The mechanism.** `Conn::write` admits bytes against `cwnd - flight_bytes()`, and `next_stream_range` then sends whatever
`has_unsent()` holds **without re-checking the window**. So the window gates *enqueue*, not *transmit*: bytes admitted when
the flight was momentarily small stay in the buffer and are emitted later, when the flight is large. The two numbers agree
exactly because the pump always drains the buffer to the wire.

That explains, in one line, why every window-side controller in §4.212–§4.227 "barely engaged": **the window was never the
constraint on the wire.** It explains the drops too — the wire carries `buffered` bytes over a path whose queue is 100
packets deep, with no rate limit anywhere between them.

**And it is the difference from TCP that matters.** TCP applies the congestion window where a segment leaves, so
`flight ≤ cwnd` is an invariant of the wire. Here it holds only for the buffer.

**Which row of F1.3's table this is:** "判损存在，但 `cwnd` 或实际 flight 没有相应下降" in its general form — the control is
applied at the wrong boundary. The fix is not a controller: it is to apply the existing window at the existing send point
(`MHD-FINALIZATION-PLAN.md` F2).

**Also measured, and worth recording:** the timer declares 5 916 / 2 057 / 15 067 losses against 2 008 / 1 773 / 7 191
actual qdisc drops — 3×, 1.2×, 2.1×. The timer over-declares when the queue is deep, which is the positive feedback
§4.203 described, now counted cumulatively rather than inferred from a one-second sample.

### 4.234 Three of the third plan's conclusions are withdrawn, and why (2026-11-10)

Before the fourth plan starts, three readings it was built on do not say what they were taken to say. The measurements
stand; the conclusions do not.

**1. The `SendLedger` is a per-second interval, not a lifetime total.** `pump.rs`'s once-a-second window line calls
`Conn::take_ledger()`, which is `std::mem::take`: every field in it is cleared as it is read. So `cuts=1`, `held=19` and
`paced≈2100` are counts **within that second**, and "the loss response fired once in a lane's whole life" (§4.214) and
"the BDP cap engaged 19 times" (§4.215) are misreadings of a one-second sample. **Withdrawn with them:** the conclusions
"this carrier has no clock" (§4.218) and "the loss signal is too sparse to steer anything" (§4.214). Re-summing the
per-second lines of the same runs gives 2 486 / 2 352 for `cuts` over three rounds of the shallow cell and 74 for `held`
on one lane of one round — orders of magnitude away from the numbers those conclusions rested on.

**2. `molehill~aa` is not an unmodified baseline.** It is a *second instance of the same binary* on another port: an
A/A noise control, which is exactly what it is good for and all it is good for. Several verdicts used it as the
"does not regress" guard (§4.226, §4.227, §4.231–§4.233), which compares a candidate with itself and cannot detect a
regression at all. **Those verdicts are void** and the cells have to be re-measured against a real baseline build
(`--binary-b`).

**3. The experiments that failed carried implementation defects of their own.** The peak estimator had no growth and sat
on the 256 KiB/s floor (§4.232); the ramp and the cut shared one timestamp so the cut never fired (§4.232); a probe was
charged as a loss, stalling a Noise round trip at 11 (§4.214); a bucket refilled at its own measured output locked at
the floor (§4.217); the harness clock ran 22 seconds ahead of the test's `now` (§4.224); `next_a` pushed the clock past
the retransmission deadline it was measuring (§4.231). **What those rounds refute is those implementations.** They are
not evidence that the mechanism families are unusable, and the third plan read them that way.

**What survives as evidence:** the path facts measured with the read-only instrument (§4.230: `min_us ≈ 40 100` against
`srr_us 204 718–311 698`, `cwnd` 376–407 KB, `rate100_shallow`'s qdisc limit of 100 packets), the attributed drop
location (§4.228: `mhbsrv/v-srv2` qdisc, i.e. the tunnel leg's egress), and every number whose method was sound.

**The fourth plan's response** is not another candidate: it is to stop guessing, add **cumulative** counters beside the
interval ones, and let one read-only attribution run choose the place to fix (`MHD-FINALIZATION-PLAN.md`, F1).

### 4.233 The probe cycle buys back the throughput and not one drop (2026-11-10)

A¹³: A¹²'s peak estimator, inflight cap and multiplicative cut, plus the one piece not yet tried — a **probe cycle**.
Every eight round trips the inflight allowance rises to `3 × BDP` for one round trip; if the delivery peak rose by more
than 2 % the higher peak is kept, and if it did not the ceiling falls 2 % and the allowance returns to `2 × BDP`.

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0953 / 0.0955 | 17 / 17 |
| frp | 0.0951 / 0.0955 | 16 / 17 |
| molehill (A¹³) | **0.0821 / 0.0833** | **1 546 / 2 310** |
| molehill twin | 0.0828 / 0.0817 | 7 583 / 1 234 |

**The throughput is back to the twin's level** — the probe cycle did its job — and **the drops are unchanged**, still two
orders above the peers' 16. The controller engages (`cut2=10…11`). Reverted whole.

**Fourteen mechanisms, and the pattern is now quantitative rather than suggestive.** On this cell the carrier does one of
two things: send at about 0.082 Gbit/s and take 1 500–2 900 drops, or send at about 0.023 Gbit/s and take none. Every
control tried lands on that line, and the line is the shaper's: at 100 Mbit/s a 2 MB buffer holds 160 ms, and the
carrier's own round trip on this path is five to eight times its minimum (§4.230).

**So the defect cannot be closed by a control law inside this architecture**, and the honest recommendation is to record
it as known and bounded: the throughput cost against TCP is 8–11 % (§4.228), the drops do not storm (§4.211), and
`transport`, `loss1`, `bulk-n`, the integrations and the striped cell all hold. The alternative is a different data path
(a per-lane kernel pacing facility, or a TCP fallback that engages on loss-heavy paths), which is a project of its own and
outside this stage's boundaries.

**Reverted whole**: the tree is `4f0d8d2`'s state, 107 tests green.

### 4.232 The peak-rate controller runs and lands at minus thirty percent drops for minus three percent throughput (2026-11-10)

A¹² again, with the harness fixed (§4.231) and with the two defects its first run exposed corrected:

1. **The peak had no growth**, so the lane sat on the 256 KiB/s floor: measured `pk262144k`, throughput 0.0028 —
   the same lock as every earlier pacer, and for the same reason (the peak can only rise when a sample exceeds it, and
   the samples come from what the schedule released).
2. **The ramp and the cut shared one timestamp**, so the ramp consumed the round trip the cut needed: `cut2=0` on every
   lane while the peak ran away to 512 GB/s. Once separated, the cut fires (`cut2=10…11`).

With both fixed:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0955 / 0.0954 | 16 / 16 |
| frp | 0.0950 / 0.0952 | 17 / 16 |
| molehill (A¹²) | **0.0808 / 0.0811** | **1 532 / 2 138** |
| molehill twin | 0.0832 / 0.0832 | 1 635 / 2 110 |

**Drops down by about thirty percent, throughput down by about three** — the best trade any of the thirteen mechanisms
has produced, and still two orders of magnitude above the peers' 16. The primary is missed, so it is reverted whole.

**What thirteen mechanisms establish.** The drops scale with how far the send rate exceeds what the shaper can carry
(§4.216's arithmetic), and every control that keeps the rate near that figure pays throughput; the ones that do not keep
the rate there keep the drops. The peers escape the trade because their rate control is TCP's, which reacts to loss and
delay together with a tuned multiplicative decrease and runs in the kernel.

**The defect is therefore characterised, not fixed**, and the honest options are unchanged: build a controller with its
own measurement programme (the shape here is close — the peak estimator, the inflight cap and the cut are right; what is
missing is a probe cycle that raises the rate deliberately rather than by doubling), or record the cell as known and
bounded.

**Reverted whole**: the tree is `1de5729`'s state, 107 tests green.

### 4.231 The peak-rate controller passes 106 of 107 tests and stops on one, by the rule (2026-11-10)

A¹² as the last entry proposed it: pace at the **windowed peak** delivery rate (ten round trips, expiring), bound new
data in flight at `2 × BDP` (`min_rtt × peak`), and cut the rate 15 % on a loss or a queueing delay, once a round trip.
Repairs and probes exempt. That maximum is the estimator none of the eleven earlier mechanisms had — an average of what
the lane was sending settles where it started, a peak of what arrived does not.

**It compiles, and 106 of 107 tests pass.** The one that does not is
`a_lost_opening_packet_is_re_sent_within_the_cheap_timer`, and it fails for a reason that is about the *harness*, not the
controller: that test asserts `poll_timeout()` equals the retransmission floor, and `poll_timeout()` has, since §4.221,
been `min(timer, credit refill)`. Reading `recovery.poll_timeout()` directly — the timer itself — returned a deadline at
the current instant rather than 20 ms ahead, so the assertion still fails, and I do not yet know why: the timer should
have been re-armed on the last send.

**Four attempts on that one test, so by the standing rule this stops rather than becoming a fifth.** What is established:
the controller's shape is right (peak rate, inflight cap, multiplicative cut); what is not is how a padded sender and the
retransmission floor interact in the fake-clock harness — the same class of problem that took four rounds over the
`pump` harness (§4.219–§4.223).

**Nothing landed**: the tree is `83b33c1`'s state, 107 tests green, no controller in the engine. The next round should
first give the recovery timer its own accessor for tests (`Retries::deadline()`), which makes that assertion independent
of the schedule, and then re-run A¹² unchanged.

### 4.230 The path is not shallow: 40 ms of path, 2 MB of buffer, and a relative target still misses (2026-11-10)

The instrument the last entry asked for, on the shallow cell with the send schedule in place and no controller:

```
cwnd=376371  ceiling=10485760  srtt_us=311698  min_us=40101
cwnd=407398  ceiling=10485760  srtt_us=204718  min_us=40101
```

**Three facts, and they overturn the premises of nine attempts.**

1. **`min_rtt` is 40 ms and it is stable** — the path's own length is measurable, so a queueing-delay
   signal is available. The estimate was never the problem in the way §4.229 supposed.
2. **The queueing delay is 165–272 ms**, i.e. `srtt` is five to eight times `min`. At the delivery rate
   (§4.228: 0.083 Gbit/s ≈ 10.4 MB/s) that is **a 2–3 MB standing queue**, which is exactly what the
   first controller measured (`q3122136`) and read as a broken estimate.
3. **The benchmark's shallow path is not shallow.** A 2 MB buffer at 100 Mbit/s is 160 ms of buffering:
   it is a *bufferbloated* shaper. The "queue of tens of kilobytes" that §4.218 assumed — and against
   which a 32 KiB target looked reasonable — does not exist on this cell.

**So the target became dimensionless**: the round trip may not exceed twice the path's own length. That is
A¹¹, and it still misses:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0953 / 0.0955 | 16 / 17 |
| frp | 0.0951 / 0.0950 | 63 / 16 |
| molehill (A¹¹) | **0.0668 / 0.0660** | **2 667 / 5 055** |
| molehill twin | 0.0734 / 0.0740 | 3 451 / 1 865 |

The controller engages (`trim=6…8`, queue peaks 71–150 ms over the path), the throughput falls 10 % below
its own twin, and **the drops do not move into the peers' range**. Reverted whole.

**Eleven mechanisms, and the same trade every time**: keep the drops, or keep the throughput. The peers do
not face this trade because their rate control is TCP's, which reacts to *both* loss and delay with a
multiplicative decrease that has been tuned for thirty years, and which runs in the kernel for free.

**What that means for the defect is a decision, not another rule**: either the carrier gets a real
controller (bounded inflight at `BDP × gain` with a multiplicative decrease on delay *and* loss, which is a
design with its own measurement plan), or this cell's behaviour is recorded as known and bounded — a
throughput cost of 8–11 % against TCP, with drops that do not storm (§4.211: no repair storm, 107 tests
green, `transport` unchanged).

**Reverted whole**: the tree is `ae049e8`'s state, 107 tests green, no controller in it.

### 4.229 The queue target stops the drops by stopping the traffic, and its estimate is the flaw (2026-11-10)

A⁹ pre-registered a queue-target controller: `queue = (smoothed_rtt − min_rtt) × delivery rate`, trimmed proportional
toward 32 KiB and grown 2 % a round trip below it, with the rate — not the window — as the controlled variable. It passes
its suite, and on the shallow cell:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0954 / 0.0955 | 16 / 16 |
| frp | 0.0951 / 0.0952 | 17 / 16 |
| molehill (A⁹) | **0.0233 / 0.0245** | **0 / 0** |
| molehill twin | 0.0235 / 0.0004 | 0 / 86 |

**The drops are gone and so is the throughput** — 0.023 against a 0.095 path and against today's 0.083. Its own guard
(the same-run twin) passes, but a three-and-a-half-fold throughput regression is a new defect, not a fix, so it is not
landed.

**The doubling start makes it worse in the right direction and still not enough.** With `×2` while no trim has happened:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| molehill | **0.0358 / 0.0331** | **404 / 465** |
| molehill twin | 0.0462 / 0.0481 | 113 / 126 |

Drops fall from 2 153 to 404 and throughput rises from 0.023 to 0.036 — still 2.6 times below the path.

**Both runs print the diagnosis.** The ledger's `trim=NqPEAK` field reads `trim=3 q3122136` on one lane: **the queue
estimate reached 3.1 MB against a 32 KiB target.** An estimate two orders of magnitude out means the controller is
steering by the wrong number, and the arithmetic says why: if `min_rtt` is sampled small on this path, then
`smoothed_rtt − min_rtt ≈ smoothed_rtt`, so the "queue" becomes the **whole bandwidth-delay product** (2.5 MB, §4.225)
rather than the queue on top of it. A queue estimate built from a minimum that small cannot distinguish "the path is
empty" from "the path is full".

**That is the next thing to fix, and it is a measurement problem inside the controller**: `min_rtt` needs to be the
minimum over a window long enough to be a path property (and floored), or the estimate needs a second anchor — the
delivery rate is already there, the missing piece is a trustworthy `min_rtt`. Until that is right, every queue-driven
trim is steering by a number that is the BDP in disguise.

**Reverted whole** — the tree is `ae049e8`'s state with no controller in it, 107 tests green.

### 4.227 A⁸ judged against the same-run twin fails too, and `loss5` fails harder (2026-11-10)

A⁸ changes the threshold, not the mechanism, so A⁷'s binary answers it on both cells. Shallow cell, against the criteria as
written:

| criterion | reading | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `dropped_packets ≤ 3 439` (half the unpaced baseline) | **2 576 / 2 471** | **pass** |
| throughput not below the same-run twin | **0.0751 / 0.0754** vs twin **0.0799 / 0.0813** | **miss** (6 %) |

And the heavy-loss cell, which the carrier currently passes, with the same binary:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | guard |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0484 / 0.0171 | — |
| frp | 0.1798 / 0.2532 | — |
| molehill | **0.2537 / 0.0649** | **0.3628** |
| molehill twin | 0.1240 / 0.2107 | — |

**The ramp costs the cell the carrier already wins.** Halving the drops on a cell it loses, at the price of the cell it
wins, is not a trade this stage can accept — the boundaries put throughput above everything except latency — so it is
reverted whole again (`84037cd`).

**Ten mechanisms have now been measured against this defect**, five of them in the last three rounds: window gate, repair
budget, loss halving, BDP ceiling, burst budget, measured-rate pacer, `cwnd/srtt` pacer, schedule with run-sized credit,
`cwnd/min_rtt`, and the rate-led ramp. The best of them (the ramp) halves the drops and costs 6 % on the shallow cell and
two thirds on `loss5`. **The shallow cell's drops and the heavy cell's throughput are coupled through the same mechanism,
and no single-knob variant moved one without the other.**

That is the finding to hand over. The next step is not another knob: it is a decision about what the shallow cell is
*for*. If `rate100_shallow`'s peer parity is a requirement, the carrier needs a queue estimate the peers get from TCP's
own control loop, which is a design of its own; if it is a diagnostic cell, then the current carrier's behaviour there
should be recorded as known and bounded rather than fixed at the cost of `loss5`.

**Reverted whole.** The tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green, no schedule and no ramp in the engine.

### 4.226 The rate-led ramp is the best-balanced variant yet and still misses both thresholds (2026-11-10)

A⁷ as pre-registered: the rate becomes the controlled variable (`paced_rate`), starting at
`INITIAL_CWND / min_rtt`, doubling once per smoothed round trip while the path answers and neither a loss nor a
queueing delay has been seen, then 2 % per round trip, and trimmed 15 % on a loss or when
`smoothed_rtt > min_rtt × 1.25`. The window still grows on acknowledgements; it no longer decides the pace. All 107 tests
pass with it unchanged.

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0954 / 0.0955 | 17 / 17 |
| frp | 0.0951 / 0.0950 | 244 / 15 |
| molehill | **0.0751 / 0.0754** | **2 576 / 2 471** |
| molehill twin | 0.0799 / 0.0813 | 4 618 / 5 869 |

**Both thresholds miss** — 0.075 against the 0.090 guard, 2 471 against the ≤ 100 primary — so it is reverted whole, as
pre-registered. But the shape is different from every previous attempt: **the drops fall by nearly two-thirds from the
unpaced carrier (6 878 → 2 500) and the throughput stays within 10 % of it (0.083 → 0.075)**. Every other mechanism
either kept the drops or kept nothing else.

**And the guard was mis-set, which the record should say.** 0.090 is 95 % of the *peers'* 0.0954, and the unpaced
carrier does 0.083 — **the guard is above what mhd does today**, so no variant that does not beat today's carrier can pass
it. The honest no-regression criterion for this cell is the same-run twin's throughput (0.0799/0.0813 here) and the
same-run baseline's drops, not an absolute that the baseline itself fails.

**So the next pre-registration changes the guard, not the mechanism**: A⁷ again, judged by "throughput not below the
twin" and "drops at most half the unpaced baseline", with the absolute 0.090 recorded as the target it is not yet
meeting.

**Reverted whole** (`7cc0ed7`, after `c11989b` re-applied the schedule for the trial): the tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107
tests green, no schedule and no ramp in the engine.

### 4.225 The schedule reduces the drops twenty-five-fold and cannot keep the throughput (2026-11-10)

The clock was built, made to pass the whole suite (`6957cf0`; the harness clock running twenty-two seconds ahead of the
test's was the last blocker — §4.224's `flight = 2000` reading), and measured. It engages: `paced ≈ 2100` per lane.

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0955 / 0.0955 | 16 / 17 |
| frp | 0.0951 / 0.0951 | 15 / 246 |
| molehill (`cwnd / srtt`) | **0.0006 / 0.0241** | **0 / 87** |
| molehill twin | 0.0233 / 0.0227 | 271 / 279 |

**The drops fall thirty-fold and the throughput falls fourfold.** Primary met in one round, guard missed by four times →
**reverted whole**, as pre-registered.

The cause was identifiable before the second run: `smoothed_rtt` **contains the queue the schedule exists to avoid**, so
pacing by it lowers the rate that keeps the queue empty. The obvious correction — `cwnd / min_rtt`, the path without its
queue, which is what `window_ceiling()` has always used — was pre-registered and measured:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| molehill (`cwnd / min_rtt`) | **0.0010 / 0.0012** | 0 / 0 |
| molehill twin | 0.0006 / 0.0252 | 0 / 89 |

**Worse, and now the reason is not a parameter.** A rate of a megabit against a path of ninety is the floor rate, which
means `cwnd` never grew — and it cannot: **`cwnd` grows only on acknowledgements, and the schedule decides how much data
there is to acknowledge.** Every one of the nine mechanisms tried since B has come back to that loop.

**So the loop is the design flaw, and it has a name in this stage's record.** The window is a *consequence* of the
acknowledgements; a schedule driven by the window is a schedule driven by its own output. The version that can break it
is a **rate-based ramp**: hold the *rate* as the controlled variable, start it at a measured-safe value and double it
each round trip until a delay or loss signal says stop — the window then follows the rate instead of the other way
round. That is not a parameter, it is the other half of the redesign the human authorised, and it is where this stops
for a decision rather than for another attempt.

**Reverted whole** (`e3675e0`): the tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green, no schedule in the engine.

### 4.224 The three remaining failures say `live == 0` with two packets on the wire (2026-11-10)

Probed `a_prefix_over_a_declared_loss_counts_those_bytes_as_late` directly with the schedule in. Two thousand bytes
written, twelve datagrams built, **two carrying stream data**, no acknowledgement — and then:

```
declared=0  expiry=Loss  sent=2000 pkt=2 ack=0
```

`Expiry::Loss` with an empty set is precisely the `self.live == 0` early return in `Recovery::on_timeout`. **Two stream
packets left the wire and no record is in flight.** That is not a pacing question and not a test-timing question: it says
the send path built data frames that `Recovery` never recorded.

Three candidate readings, none yet excluded:

1. `reap(now)` with `now` two seconds ahead drops them before the stale test runs;
2. the pick came back with `range: None` for some other reason and the frame went out unrecorded;
3. `pkt` in `SendLedger` counts something other than recorded stream sends, and the probe is misreading it.

**This is the third attempt on the same three tests**, so per the standing rule it stops here rather than becoming a
fourth. What the next round should do first is not touch the tests at all: it should print `recovery`'s in-flight count
*before* the timeout and after each `poll_transmit`, which separates reading 1 from reading 2 in one run.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green; `/tmp/schedule-credit.patch` holds the schedule
with the run-sized credit and the first-window exemption (8 failures → 3).

### 4.223 Two changes cut the failures 8 → 3, and the last three are declarations, not pacing (2026-11-10)

Rather than rewrite the harness's four send loops, two changes to the schedule itself:

1. **The credit is a run-sized burst allowance** (44 segments, not 2). The *rate* is the deadline's job: the pump wakes
   at `pace_due` and then empties a run. A two-segment credit made a wake build two packets and park the rest, which is
   a rate limiter with a two-packet burst — and against a harness that pumps once, that is indistinguishable from a
   stall.
2. **A lane paces only after its window has grown past its opening size.** The first window is how a lane discovers the
   path; it has no rate to pace against, and holding it back slows the discovery it depends on.

**The failing count went 8 → 3**, and the remaining three are not about pacing at all:

```
a_loss_re_sends_the_hole_and_not_what_follows_it:
  the first frame re-sent is the hole itself: left: None
a_prefix_over_a_declared_loss_counts_those_bytes_as_late:
  both records are stale: left: 0 right: 2
a_two_dropped_datagrams_in_one_window_are_both_recovered
```

All three drive declaration by hand — they send a few records, then call `on_timeout` or poll for a repair at a fixed
instant — and under the schedule **the records they expect to be in flight were never built**: `declared == 0` means the
table was empty, not that the timer was early. That is now a question about *when* those tests send, per test.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green; the improved patch (297 lines, the two changes
above included) is `/tmp/schedule-credit.patch`. The remaining work is three tests, each deciding what it is for.

### 4.222 The credit works and the harness has four send loops that each give up (2026-11-10)

Applied the saved patch and probed it before touching any test. One `pump` on an 8 KB transfer, with the schedule in:

```
moved=14  sent=8000 rep=0(0%) pkt=6 ack=8000 num=8000 paced=8  accept=true
```

**The schedule works**: the whole transfer completes in one pump, the credit engaged eight times, and the stream is
named. So the rule is not the problem — and that probe is the reason the rest of this round is a harness story.

The failure is that **the harness sends from four different loops** and every one of them gives up on the first `None`:

| loop | what it does when the credit says "not yet" |
|---|---|
| `pump_spaced` | waits for a pending arrival, else advances 1 ms — the only one that recovers |
| `next_a` / `next_b` | was `poll_transmit` once and return `None`; a wait loop was added, and the count moved 8 → 10 |
| `pump_dropping_one` (send side) | same, then routed through `next_a` |
| `pump_dropping_one` (ack side) | was `poll_transmit` once; routing it through `next_b` made it *worse* (10 failures) |

**Two rounds of whack-a-mole moved the count 8 → 10 → 8**, which is the signal to stop: the fix is not four patches, it
is **one** send helper (`Link::send_until(id, want)`) that every loop calls, and rewriting the eight tests on top of
it. That is a harness refactor, and bundling it with the rule is how the last four rounds of this stage went wrong.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green. The schedule remains `/tmp/schedule-credit.patch`
and the next round starts with the harness refactor, not with the rule.

### 4.221 The schedule is a credit bucket now, the suite terminates, six tests assert the old contract (2026-11-10)

The slot arithmetic from §4.220 was the wrong shape: a slot that advances per *packet* still lets a pass overdraw it into
the future, and the suite hung on that (killed three times). The right shape is the one the seven failures had already
argued for — **credit that accrues with time** — but with the rate the maximum of the two that used to lock:

- `schedule_rate()` = `max(cwnd / smoothed_rtt, measured delivery rate, 256 KiB/s)`, divided into segments per second;
- `take_credit(now)` accrues `rate × elapsed`, capped at two segments, and answers whether new data may leave;
- repairs and probes are exempt (they exist to unblock the peer and the clock);
- `pace_due()` puts the refill instant into the pump's deadline, so a paced lane wakes for its packet;
- the ledger gained `paced=` so a run can prove it engaged.

**The suite terminates with it** — no hangs — and the implementation is saved as `/tmp/schedule-credit.patch` (282 lines)
so the next round starts from it rather than from scratch.

**Six connection tests fail, and every one of them asserts the timing contract this replaces.** Two examples, quoted:

```
a_finished_exchange_leaves_nothing_counted:
  internal error: entered unreachable code: the stream is named on arrival
a_loss_re_sends_the_hole_and_not_what_follows_it:
  the first frame re-sent is the hole itself: left: None
```

The first pumps once and expects the stream to have been opened by that pass; under pacing the open is one slot and the
data another. The second expects three later packets to arrive in the same instant the hole was dropped, because that is
how the three-behind threshold used to fire. **Both are true statements about unpaced sending and false ones about
paced sending**, and rewriting them means deciding what each test is actually for — which is the work left.

**Committed: nothing in the engine.** The tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green; the harness step is in, the rule
is a patch on disk, and the six tests are the gap between them.

### 4.220 The schedule is authorised, its arithmetic is fixed, and five tests are left (2026-11-10)

The human authorised option ① — the schedule — so this round did the two halves the last one named.

**The harness half is landed** (`a02df07`): `pump` advances virtual time a millisecond at a time when nothing was built
and nothing is in flight, bounded, so a sender that answers "not yet" is waited for rather than declared quiet. All 107
tests pass with it and the engine unchanged.

**The rule half is written and its arithmetic is fixed.** The first version put the slot *ahead* by one spacing on
every call — `sent_at + spacing` — which wedges: a pass asks, is refused, asks again, and the slot never comes back.
**A hang, not a failure**, which is why the suite had to be killed twice. The correct rule is that the slot is *virtual
send time*: it starts at the first send and advances **exactly one spacing per packet actually sent**, never ahead of
the work. A pass then emits the number of segments the elapsed time has earned and stops, which is what a paced sender
is.

**With that fixed, five connection tests fail and nothing hangs**, and they fail for one reason that is now precise:
they poll `poll_transmit` themselves, in a loop with a single `now`, so the schedule gives them two packets where they
expect nine. They need a harness helper that keeps polling with an advancing clock (`drain_a(now, want)`), not a
different schedule.

**Not committed in the engine**: the schedule, with the five tests still red, would put an unverified rule in the tree.
The tree is `a02df07`'s state, 107 tests green, and the remaining work is one helper and five tests.

### 4.219 The send schedule compiles and cannot be tested yet, which is the honest stopping point (2026-11-10)

The step the seven failures point at — a **schedule** rather than a budget: `Conn` keeps `sent_at`, computes `next_due` as one
segment per `schedule_rate()` (the larger of `cwnd/srtt` and the measured delivery rate, floor 256 KiB/s), the picker
releases new data only when `now >= next_due`, and `poll_timeout` puts that instant into the pump's deadline so a paced
lane wakes for its next packet instead of sleeping to the retransmission timer.

**It compiles, it is coherent, and ten of the fake-clock connection tests fail with it** — all of them the same way: a
`pump` call now emits one or two packets where it used to emit the whole run, so a test that pumps eight times for six
packets no longer finishes its transfer. That is not a bug in the schedule; it is the schedule *working*, against a
harness whose tests were written when a pass could send as much as it liked.

**So the schedule needs the same treatment the delayed link got in §4.205**: land the harness that can express paced
sending first, with the rule inert, and only then the rule. Concretely: `pump` must advance its clock by the schedule's
spacing (or the tests must pump for enough virtual time), and the ten tests' loop counts become functions of the transfer
size rather than constants. That is a change to the test link, and it is the fourth time this stage has hit the same
class of blocker — the measuring apparatus, not the mechanism.

**Not pursued further here.** The schedule is the redesign the human has been asked to authorise, and its first
deliverable turns out to be another harness change; landing both in one round would put an unverified rule on top of an
unverified harness, which is the mistake this stage has already paid for twice.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.218 The window-rate pacer fails the same way, and seven mechanisms now agree (2026-11-10)

A⁵ — refill the bucket at `cwnd / smoothed_rtt` instead of at the measured rate — was implemented, with the bucket
starting full, an idle lane exempt, and the pump's timer taught to wake for a refill. Two unit-test lessons came first
(a bucket starting empty can never send its first packet; an idle lane must never be paced), and then the cell:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0954 / 0.0955 | 16 / 17 |
| frp | 0.0953 / 0.0952 | 16 / 220 |
| molehill | **0.0008 / 0.0008** | **0 / 0** |
| molehill twin | 0.0006 / 0.0008 | 0 / 0 |

**The drops are zero again because the traffic is nearly zero** — a hundred times below the guard. Reverted whole.

**Seven mechanisms have now been measured on this cell and none of them moved the drops into the peers' range**:

| # | mechanism | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | repairs inside the window | falsified at the unit level (waits for room only the repair can make) |
| 2 | repair budget `cwnd/2`, never blocking | drops halved, throughput fell |
| 3 | halve `cwnd` on a declared loss | fires **once** per lane |
| 4 | BDP ceiling (`Rtt::min × rate`) | engages **19** times per lane |
| 5 | per-pass burst budget | no change: bounds a burst, not a rate |
| 6 | pacer at the measured rate | locks at its floor (input is its own output) |
| 7 | pacer at `cwnd/srtt` | near-zero throughput, zero drops |

**What that pattern says, and it is not "try an eighth".** Every controller this carrier has — or could have without a
redesign — derives its rate from its own window; pacing by that rate throttles the acks that would grow the window, and
the lane settles a hundred times below the path. Meanwhile the *unpaced* carrier sends **135 Mbit/s into a 100 Mbit/s
pipe** (§4.216), because nothing in it is a function of time. The two facts are the same fact: **this carrier has no
clock. It sends whenever the pump runs, and it grows its window only on acknowledgements.** A controller bolted onto
that either never engages (the window ones) or locks at zero (the rate ones).

**Conclusion handed over, per the plan's own rule.** The shallow-queue defect is not a missing knob: it needs the send
path rebuilt around a clock — a schedule the pump reads (when the next packet is due) rather than a budget it checks —
which is a redesign of the pump and the window together, not another rule on top of them. That is beyond what this
stage's pre-registrations allow, and the seven measurements above are the case for it.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.217 A pacer at the measured rate zeroes the drops by zeroing the traffic (2026-11-10)

A⁗ — a token bucket at the **measured** delivery rate, gating new data only, repairs and probes exempt — was
implemented with a `paced` counter, and it took two runs to learn what it says:

| run | arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` | `paced` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first | molehill + twin | **no result: every round failed** ("iperf3 … Connection reset by peer") | — | ~990 |
| second (with a 256 KiB/s floor) | molehill | **0.0004 / 0.0006** | **0 / 0** | — |
| | rathole | 0.0956 / 0.0954 | 17 / 17 | — |
| | frp | 0.0952 / 0.0950 | 15 / 16 | — |

**The first run's failure was a bug, not a verdict**: a rate measured over a window in which nothing was confirmed is
zero, and pacing to zero parks the lane — every product round died on iperf3's control connection. A floor of 256 KiB/s
fixed the stall, and then the second run said the real thing.

**The drops are zero because almost nothing is sent.** Throughput is 0.0006 Gbit/s — a hundred and fifty times below the
guard — against the peers' 0.095. The primary metric is met in the most useless way possible, which is why the guard
exists.

**And the reason is structural, not a tuning issue**: the bucket refills at the rate the acknowledgements *measured*,
and those acknowledgements measured the rate the bucket allowed. **A pacer whose input is its own output locks in
whatever it started with** — here, the floor. It can never ramp up, because ramping up requires sending faster than the
measurement, and the measurement is the limit.

**So the input has to be a target, not a reading.** The window already is one: `cwnd / smoothed_rtt` is the rate a lane's
own window implies, it grows when the window grows, and pacing at it splits a window over its round trip instead of
firing it in one burst. That is the next pre-registration (A⁵), and it is a genuinely different rule from A⁗ even though
both are token buckets.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.216 The burst budget fails too, and the arithmetic says why: the carrier sends 135 Mbit/s into a 100 Mbit/s pipe (2026-11-10)

A‴ — cap each pass at `min(44, max(4, cwnd/(4·MSS)))` datagrams — was implemented and measured on the shallow cell:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0957 / 0.0954 | 16 / 16 |
| frp | 0.0951 / 0.0950 | 17 / 16 |
| molehill | 0.0840 / 0.0785 | **3 111 / 4 417** |
| molehill twin | 0.0821 / 0.0836 | 1 973 / 2 621 |

Primary misses (needs ≤ 100) and the throughput guard misses too. **Reverted whole.**

**And the ledger from the same cell says exactly what is wrong** (§4.211's run, per lane, per second):

```
sent=16926295 rep=635379(3%) pkt=12551 ack=9305795
```

**16.9 MB posted in one second is 135 Mbit/s through a 100 Mbit/s shaper.** The carrier is not merely a little over; it is
a third over, all second, and the difference is dropped and then re-sent — which is a loop that never converges because
nothing in it ever asks the sender to slow down.

**Why the per-pass cap did not fix it**: a budget per pass bounds a *burst*, not a *rate*. The pump runs pass after pass
with no gap, so four datagrams per pass at pump speed is the same throughput as forty-four. **Pacing is a function of
time, and nothing in this carrier is a function of time.**

**And why the BDP ceiling did not fix it either** (§4.215): on a 200 ms path at 100 Mbit/s the bandwidth-delay product is
**2.5 MB**, and the shaper's queue is a few dozen kilobytes. A window of one BDP is therefore a window a hundred times
the queue — correct for a path with a deep buffer, ruinous on a shallow one. `Rtt::min` times the rate is the *path's*
capacity, not the *queue's*, and the two are not the same number here.

**The mechanism that is missing is a pacer**: a token bucket at the measured delivery rate, so the sender's rate is a
function of time and of the path, not of how fast the pump happens to loop. That is a different mechanism from all five
tried so far (window gate, repair budget, loss halving, BDP cap, per-pass burst), and it is the one the arithmetic above
points at directly.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.215 The delay ceiling barely binds either, so the window is not what fills the queue (2026-11-10)

A″ — cap `cwnd` at the bandwidth-delay product (`Rtt::min × measured delivery rate`, gain 1.0), with a `held` counter
so the same run could say whether it engaged — was implemented and measured on the shallow cell:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` | `held` (max per lane) |
|---|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0955 / 0.0956 | 16 / 16 | — |
| frp | 0.0952 / 0.0953 | 16 / 16 | — |
| molehill | 0.0852 / 0.0828 | **7 294 / 2 298** | **19** |
| molehill twin | 0.0820 / 0.0824 | 1 737 / 6 868 | — |

Primary misses by two orders, guard (≥ 0.090) misses. **Reverted whole.**

**Three instruments now agree, and that is the result.** The loss halving fired **once** per lane (§4.214); the BDP cap
held the window back on **19** acknowledgements in a whole lane (§4.215); the repair budget moved the drops half the
distance and no further (§4.213). A `cwnd` that no controller can move is a `cwnd` that was never the binding
constraint on this cell — the sender is not window-limited there, so shrinking the window neither helps nor is even
felt.

**What that leaves, stated as a hypothesis with a test.** If the sender is not limited by bytes in flight, it is limited
by *how it posts*: the pump emits up to `SEND_RUN` (44) datagrams back to back in one pass, a ~59 KB burst, and a
shallow shaper queue has to absorb all of it or drop the tail. TCP, which both peers use, paces by the acknowledgement
clock and never hands a queue that shape. That is a different mechanism from every attempt so far — burst shaping, not
window regulation — and it is testable in one cell in two minutes.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.214 The loss response is right and barely fires, which is the finding (2026-11-10)

A′ — halve `cwnd` on a declared loss, at most once per smoothed round trip, floor two segments, slow start latched off
— was implemented, with a `cuts` counter in the lane ledger so the same run could prove it engaged. Two design
decisions came out of the unit suite before any bench time:

- **A probe is not a loss.** The first version cut on every `on_timeout` that returned records, including the
  probe branch, and `a_noise_stream_carries_a_hundred_round_trips` stalled at round 11: on a silent-but-healthy path
  the timer probes, and charging the window for that collapses it. The cut now fires only when the expiry is
  `Expiry::Loss`.
- **One hole declared by two mechanisms is one cut**, which is what the per-round-trip limit is for.

Measured on the cell the defect lives in (`rate100_shallow`, `bulk-1`, two measured rounds, stats on so the ledger
exists):

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` | `cuts` (max per lane, cumulative) |
|---|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0954 / 0.0955 | 17 / 16 | — |
| frp | 0.0952 / 0.0952 | 17 / 16 | — |
| molehill | **0.0827 / 0.0824** | **6 878 / 7 078** | **1** |
| molehill twin | 0.0838 / 0.0825 | 1 867 / 7 030 | 1 |

The primary misses by two orders of magnitude and the throughput guard (≥ 0.090) misses. **Reverted whole.**

**But the `cuts` column is the result.** A lane runs for sixty seconds at ~1 700 packets per window and the rule fires
**once in its whole life**. So the miss is not "the rule is wrong" — it is that **the loss signal arrives too rarely to
steer the window at all** on this cell. The shaper overflows, the carrier does not notice, the window keeps whatever it
had, and the next second overflows again. Every previous candidate on the declaration side (§4.186–§4.213) was trying to
tune a signal that this cell barely generates.

**What that points at.** A window that must be right *before* the first loss needs a signal that does not wait for one:
either a delay-based bound (keep `cwnd` at the bandwidth-delay product the acknowledgements measure, and treat a growing
queue as the brake), or an explicit ceiling from the path's own queue estimate. mhd has the RTT estimate already
(`Rtt::min` is there for the window ceiling) and no delay-based control at all.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.213 The repair budget halves the drops and misses, and the reason points somewhere else (2026-11-10)

The budget from §4.212 — repairs may have at most `cwnd/2` outstanding, counted apart from `flight`, never blocked —
was implemented and measured on the cell the defect lives in:

| arm | `throughput_gbps` | `dropped_packets` |
|---|---|---|
| rathole | 0.0955 / 0.0952 | 60 / 16 |
| frp | 0.0952 / 0.0951 | 16 / 16 |
| molehill (with the budget) | **0.0800 / 0.0627** | **1 373 / 1 068** |
| molehill twin | 0.0725 / 0.0843 | 1 228 / 7 078 |

Before the budget the same cell read 0.0829 / 0.0838 with **2 261 / 2 465** drops. So the primary moved **in the right
direction and by half**, and that is not enough: the criterion is *the same order as the peers' 16–17*, and 1 068–1 373
is still two orders away; the throughput guard (≥ 95 % of a peer = 0.090) misses as well. **Reverted whole**, and the
unit suite never even noticed — the five-percent-loss transfer still delivered, so the budget does not deadlock the way
the window gate did.

**What the number says instead.** A repair budget bounds one of the two streams that fill the queue, and the other one
is the one nobody has touched: **new data**. The window on this cell is around **2.3 MB** — roughly 1 700 packets — on a
path whose queue is a hundred-odd packets deep. Nothing in this carrier reduces that window when packets are lost: it
grows on acknowledgements and it is cut by nothing. On a deep path that is merely optimistic; on a shallow one it
*guarantees* overflow, and every drop this cell records is that guarantee being kept.

**So the missing mechanism is a loss response, not a repair budget.** mhd has never had one — the summary in the plan
says it plainly ("nothing cuts cwnd on loss"), and four rounds of work on the *recovery* side were changes to what
happens after a declaration while the declaration's *cause* sat untouched on the sending side. The textbook rule is a
halving per round trip on a declared loss, and it is the next candidate; it is a different mechanism from every attempt
so far, so it gets its own pre-registration.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.

### 4.212 A's first part dies in the unit test, which is cheaper than the bench (2026-11-10)

A's pre-registration says repairs must be inside the congestion window. Implemented literally — the range picker
refuses a repair when `cwnd − flight == 0` — the suite answered in twelve seconds:

```
five_percent_loss_on_a_fake_link_delivers_without_storming:
  every byte arrives even when one in twenty is dropped:
  sent=128155 rep=29678(23%) pkt=95 ack=98477 num=121410 pfx=6745 late=29678 loss=2t/20m
  left: 98477  right: 131072
```

**Three quarters of the transfer arrives and then it stops.** The reason is structural, and it is the same one §4.188
measured from the other side: `flight_bytes` **includes the repair records**, so gating a repair on
`flight < cwnd` waits for room that only the repair itself could make. A repair is not new data competing for the
window — it is the *same* bytes, already counted, being sent again. Blocking it asks the window to open while forbidding
the only thing that can open it.

So part 1 as written is **falsified at the unit level, in one test, before any bench time**: cheaper and more decisive
than §4.188's four-arm run, and it says why that run failed too.

**What the shallow-queue defect needs instead.** The exemption is not the problem in itself — a repair has to be allowed
to overtake — the problem is that nothing bounds how *much* repair traffic a lane puts on a shallow queue. Two levers
that do not close the loop:

1. **A repair budget proportional to `cwnd`**, counted separately from `flight` (e.g. at most `cwnd/2` bytes of repair
   in flight at once), so repairs are bounded but never blocked by the window they are trying to open;
2. **Pacing the repairs** — the picker already runs once per pass, so a byte-per-pass budget per lane sets the rate
   directly, and the shallow queue's depth is what decides whether that is enough.

Both are written here rather than tried in the same round: the first was falsified by a unit test in one minute, and the
second is a different mechanism that deserves its own pre-registration.

**Committed: nothing.** The tree is §4.211's state, 107 tests green.
