> no send loop waiting on a read** — and §4.421 established that none is parked in `write` either.
>
> **Which leaves one shape**: they are streams with **no forwarding group at all** — channels opened, never used, never closed.
> And that is §4.348's measurement arriving from the other side: **7 500 of 15 485 channels in a soak never put a first byte
> on the wire.** Those opens hold a lease, the lease holds a pool slot, and nothing ever releases it because no group exists
> to end.
>
> **So the defect is the abandoned open**: `open_stream` succeeds, the channel is written into the pool's lease, and if the
> visitor goes before the forwarder ever starts, nothing closes the stream.

> **§4.433 (the tick arithmetic; superseded by the per-lane count below) Converting the two-second read ticks
> back into streams (≈600 ticks per stream per twenty-minute run): the **clean** arm's 14 557 is about **24** streams, which
> is exactly `rr-16`'s 16 persistent sockets plus the bulk stage's handful. The **wedged** arm's 36 765 is about **61** — the
> same 24 plus roughly **32 that the harness did not open and does not hold**.
>
> **So the extra thirty-odd idle visitors are the tool's own**, and they are churn's: the probe closed its side and the tool
> kept a socket open. That is not a stream-table question at all — the table is a consequence — it is **the client's local
> listener not closing an accepted connection when its forwarder ends**.
>
> **The next measurement is the visitor socket's own lifetime on the client**: `accept` → the moment the fd is dropped, per
> connection, one line each. If those 32 show an accept without a drop until minutes later, the defect is found and it is in
> the listener, not in `Conn`.

> **§4.432: the send loop is waiting on a silent-but-open visitor, tens of thousands of times.** The send loop already has a
> two-second read deadline (`stripe.rs:502`) with its own line: a soak logged **14 557** of them on the clean arm and
> **36 765** on the wedged one. So `src.read_buf` returns nothing for two seconds, repeatedly — the visitor is **open and
> silent**, which is exactly what an idle persistent connection looks like (`rr-16` between requests, a bulk stream between
> bursts).
>
> **And the counts scale with the number of idle streams** (about 600 two-second ticks per stream over a twenty-minute run:
> 56 streams ≈ 33 600, close to the 36 765 measured; 24 ≈ 14 400, close to 14 557). So this line is proportional to the
> population and does not by itself discriminate the arms — but it does settle one thing: **`local_fin` is false because
> the visitor really is still open**, not because the send loop is stuck somewhere unseen.
>
> **Which returns the question to where it started and narrows it to one word**: why does the arm that wedges keep ~56
> visitors open while the other keeps ~24? Both run the same scenarios, so the difference is in what the tool does with a
> visitor once its request is answered — and the measurement that answers it is the *count of open visitor sockets* per
> arm, which the bench's own `service_sockets` already samples.

> **§4.431 (the diagnostic never fired either, and that is the answer to the clause question): no *live* stream has both
> fins.** With `4291601` in, a soak whose arms wedged (5 and 3, up to 145 s) logged **zero** `kept by the periodic pass`
> lines on either arm. So at no point did the table hold a stream with `local_fin && peer_fin` — the 56 live streams have
> **at most one** fin, and §4.368 measured exactly that (26 with the peer's, 30 with neither, **none with both**).
>
> **Which moves the missing half to `local_fin`**: the client's send loop never finished for those streams. It is not parked
> in `write` (§4.421: zero), it is not waiting on a fin (there is none), so it is **waiting for the visitor's EOF that it
> never sees** — or not being polled at all.
>
> **And the earlier measurement now makes sense**: §4.429's "1 267 of 1 674 closed with `peer_fin = true`" was measured **at
> close**, long after the group finally ended — not while the stream was live. The live population is the other shape.

> **§4.430 (the periodic-retire fix is in and it never fired — reverted).** With `72ebe5b` in (retire a stream that is
> `local_fin && peer_fin && unacked == 0 && recv.is_drained()` in the periodic pass), a soak whose **both** arms wedged
> (2 and 4 wedges, 61 and 76 ceiling lines, 60 and 75 expiries) logged **zero** `retired by the periodic pass` lines on
> either arm, and `opened_len` / `live_gt_10s` stayed at **56**. Reverted (`d5a9b7c`), both clippy builds green.
>
> **So at least one of the four clauses is false for exactly the streams that matter** — and `abandoned` is known false, so
> it is `local_fin`, `peer_fin`, `unacked == 0` or `recv.is_drained()`. §4.429 measured `peer_fin` true for 1 267 of them,
> which leaves **the unacknowledged fin or undrained bytes** as the clause that holds the entry.
>
> **The next instrument is one line, not a run**: in the periodic pass, for a stream that has `local_fin && peer_fin` but is
> skipped, log which clause refused it (`unacked`, `recv`). That names the last unknown in this chain, and it costs one
> debug line.

> **§4.429 (the mechanism): the long-lived streams are mostly **finished**, and nothing re-settles them.** Joining the
> retirement ages against the fin flags on the same run: of the **1 674** streams that retired after 60 s, **1 267 closed with
> `peer_fin=true`** and 407 without.
>
> **So two thirds of the tail had both directions finished and still sat in the table for over a minute.** That is not a
> forwarding-group problem at all — it is the **table entry**: `Conn::settle` is what removes a stream from
> `stream_opened`/`streams`, it runs only on **events** (a close, an acknowledgement), and a stream whose last event was the
> peer's fin has no further event to trigger it. The periodic reaper does not cover this case either: `reap_abandoned`
> requires `send.held() > 0`, and a finished stream holds nothing.
>
> **Which names the fix exactly**: the periodic pass must also settle a stream that is **finished and unacknowledged-free**
> — `local_fin && peer_fin && send.unacked() == 0`, the same predicate `settle` already uses for `closed_both` (§4.359).
> One clause in `reap_abandoned`, no new state, and it retires the finished-but-unvisited entries within one tick instead of
> leaving them for `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT`'s five minutes.
>
> **That is the defect this whole line has been chasing**: not a leak in the forwarder, not a missing fin, not the grace —
> **a table entry whose only removal path is an event that never comes again.**

> **§4.428 (the retirement ages): the occupancy is a heavy tail, not a leak.** `mhd stream retired age_ms`
> on the wedged arm over **13 983** streams:
>
> | p50 | p90 | p99 | max |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **21 ms** | **6 835 ms** | **140 201 ms** | 183 974 ms |
>
> **Half the streams retire in 21 ms — the product is fast.** But the tail is enormous: 10 % live past **6.8 s** and 1 % past
> **140 s**. At 13.5 openings a second that tail alone fills the pool:
>
> ```
> 1 % × 140 s × 13.5/s  ≈ 19 slots
> 9 % × 6.8 s × 13.5/s  ≈  8 slots
> persistent rr-16 + bulk ≈ 24 slots
>                         ≈ 51 — against a measured 56 per lane
> ```
>
> **So `every tunnel is at its stream ceiling` is produced by one stream in a hundred living two to three minutes**, plus a
> tenth living several seconds, plus the harness's own persistent connections. The number fits without any leak, any
> missing fin and any grace.
>
> **And the tail is bounded by `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (300 s)** — which is why nothing lives past ~184 s: those streams are
> not stuck forever, they are **held far too long for a millisecond exchange**.
>
> **The next question is the only one left and it is narrow**: what makes one churn channel in a hundred live two minutes?
> The candidates that survive are the ones with no fin (23 of 13 983) and the ones whose group waited on the grace.

> **§4.427: the returning fin arrives 99.8 % of the time, so §4.426's race is a tail, not the cause.** On the wedged arm the
> client closed **13 983** streams: **13 960 with `peer_fin=true`, 23 with `peer_fin=false`**. The fin comes back.
>
> **Which kills the missing-fin theory as the explanation** and re-opens the reading of §4.368: the 30 of 56 that "carried
> neither fin" were a **snapshot of live streams**, not of closed ones — young channels caught mid-flight, exactly what a
> 56-deep standing population looks like.
>
> **So the stands are: 56 live, >10 s old, no grace, no parked writer, fins delivered in 99.8 % of closures.** Every
> component behaves, and the lane still holds 56. What has not been measured is **how long a churn channel's group lives
> from the visitor's close to the lease's release** — one interval, at one stream, and it is the only number in this whole
> line that has never been taken.

> **§4.426 (the returning fin; superseded by the count below), so the missing one is on the way back.** The wedged arm's server
> log carries 78 800 fin/EOF lines and, for its streams, `mhd stream closed … peer_fin=true local_fin=true`: **the server side
> of every channel completes**. Yet the client measured **30 of 56 with no peer fin** (§4.368). So the fin is produced and
> not seen — which is the shape this record met at the very beginning: **`mhd stream retired  age_ms=1`** on the client, a
> stream retired within a millisecond while its peer was still sending to it (§4.343).
>
> **So the four-hop chain has one hop that is not a filter but a race**: the server sends the fin into a stream the client has
> already retired, and a retired stream's frames are dropped (`is_retired_stream`). The client's `stream_opened` entry is
> gone, the group still holds the lease, and nothing will ever close it.
>
> **That makes the next check small and specific**: on the client, does `mhd stream closed` (or retirement) for a churn
> channel ever happen **before** the group's recv direction ends? One line at both events with the stream id answers it.

> **§4.425: the server has no `copy_bidirectional`; both ends forward through `spawn_group`, and the fin has four hops to make.**
> `src/core/server.rs` never copies with `copy_bidirectional` (the only `shutdown` calls are session handles), so the server's
> channel forwarding is the same stripe forwarder the client uses. The churn's close is therefore a **four-hop chain**:
>
> ```
> probe closes → client forwarder sees EOF → sender.finish() → fin on the stream
>              → server recv_loop sees fin → closes toward the echo
>              → echo sees EOF → closes → server send_loop sees EOF → sender.finish()
>              → fin back on the stream → client recv_loop ends → group ends → lease drops
> ```
>
> **A hang at any hop leaves the stream open exactly as measured** (§4.368: of 56 live, 26 had the peer's fin and 30 had
> neither — the 30 stopped somewhere before the second fin). And each hop has an instrumentable moment.
>
> **The next step is to instrument the chain once, on one churn channel, with the stream id**: `fin sent`, `fin received`,
> `echo EOF`, `fin sent back`. Four lines, one stream, and the hop that never prints names the defect.

> **§4.424: the echo closes when its peer closes, so the backend is not holding anything.** `workloads.py`'s `serve` runs
> `read_direction` as `while True: data = conn.recv(65536); if not data: return` — it returns on EOF, so when the probe's
> connection goes the echo's side goes with it. **The harness backend keeps nothing open** (§4.423 is refuted), and the
> missing fin must therefore be the **tool's server-side copy** not finishing — not the peer's silence.
>
> **So both ends of the missing fin are inside the tool**: the server's forwarder never sends it, so the client's stream waits
> for it forever. That is a different suspect from every one examined in this goal: not the grace, not the client's write, not
> the backend — **the server-side copy's own end**.
>
> **The next read is `src/core/server.rs`'s channel forwarding**: which condition ends the copy toward the visitor, and what
> keeps it from doing so when the visitor's request is answered but the connection stays open in the tool's own view.

> **§4.423 (the lead that fits every remaining fact): the server side never sends its fin.** §4.368 measured, on the same lanes,
> that of the 56 live streams **26 carried the peer's fin and 30 carried neither** — the client's streams are waiting for a
> fin that never arrives. A stream whose peer never finished cannot end, cannot be reaped by the grace (which starts only
> when one direction ends), and does not park a writer: it simply sits. **That is exactly the state that survived every
> check of the last three rounds.**
>
> **And the shape of it points at the benchmark's own backend**: the churn probe talks through the tool to the echo service
> the harness starts inside the client namespace (`workloads.py`, `ECHO_PORT = 2401`). If that echo keeps each connection
> open after replying — a keep-alive backend — then the tool's server-side copy never ends, no fin travels back, and **every
> churn channel stays open on the client for as long as the backend holds it**. The pool then fills with channels whose
> requests finished long ago, which is the 56.
>
> **The check is one read, not one run**: does the harness's echo close the connection after echoing, or does it loop on the
> same socket? If it loops, the defect is the harness's, and the product's only fault is holding a channel open for a peer
> that never closes — which is what `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` is for, at five minutes.

> **§4.422 (a contradiction that reopens it): the clean arm holds 5–6, and it runs the same rr and bulk.** §4.421 blamed the
> occupancy on the benchmark's own concurrent connections — but `rr-16` and the bulk stage run on **both** arms, so if they
> were the occupants the clean arm would sit at the same 56. It sits at **4–6**. **The extra fifty are the churn's**, and
> that is the A/A argument of §4.410 again, which has not been refuted.
>
> **So the leak is real and it is churn-specific, while three separate checks came back zero** — no grace, no parked writer,
> no growth. That combination has one natural shape left: **the churn group's tasks are alive and not blocked**, waiting on a
> future that nothing will complete — most likely the receive direction waiting for frames that were never delivered because
> the *client* stopped reading that stream (the pool refused its channel? no — the channel existed), or the visitor-side
> copy waiting on a socket the probe already closed.
>
> **The next instrument, and it is one line in the churn's own path**: log, for a group older than 10 s, which of its two
> directions is still alive and which `await` it is parked at. That is a `select!` instrument, not a counter.

> **§4.421 (the last measurement, and it closes the leak question): nothing is parked.** `mhd stream writer parked for the
> first time` — **zero on both arms**, the wedged one included. So no send loop is blocked in `Conn::write`, and the standing
> 56 are not blocked writers either.
>
> **Put that beside the rest and the leak hypothesis is gone**: no grace ever ran (0 lines), no writer ever parked (0
> lines), and the population is **steady at 56** rather than climbing. What is left is the ordinary case — **56 connections
> that are open because their visitors are open** — and the arithmetic supports it: `rr-16` holds 16 sockets for its whole
> stage (`rr.py:_connect` keeps them), bulk holds its `-n` for its stage, and churn's own in-flight set sits on top.
>
> **So the answer to "who occupies the 224 slots" is: the benchmark's own concurrent connections, and a pool of 4 × 56 that
> the soak's mix reaches.** The refusal is then a capacity wall, not a defect — `every tunnel is at its stream ceiling`
> is exactly what that line is for, and the wedge is the visitor's 10 s wait for a channel the pool will not open.
>
> **This is the characterisation the objective allowed for, and the decision belongs to the user**: widen `tunnels`, lower
> the churn rate in the soak profile, or accept the ceiling as the documented capacity of the default configuration.

> **§4.420 (the shape is a standing population, not a rising one.** `opened_len` sits at 56 while churn retires ~13 streams a
> second, so the lane is not accumulating a leak that grows — it holds a **steady** 56, which is the signature of groups
> that **stay** open rather than of a counter that never decrements. Combined with §4.419 (the grace never ran, so neither
> direction ended on those groups), the remaining explanation for a churn channel is that its **send direction is parked in
> `Conn::write`** and therefore never reads the visitor's EOF.
>
> **Where to look, precisely**: `stripe.rs`'s `send_loop` → `StripeSender::write` → the lane's `Conn::write` admission
> (credit / window / buffered). A park there with no wake-up would hold the slot exactly like this, and the bench already
> has a line for it — **`mhd stream writer parked for the first time`** (`lane.rs`), which fires once per stream and can be
> counted on the wedged arm to confirm parked writers in bulk.

> **§4.419 (decisive, from the log alone): the grace never ran on the wedged arm.** Counting `half-close grace expired` in the
> wedged run: **0 on the twin that wedged (56 live streams, 145 ceiling lines)** and 1 on the clean product arm.
>
> **So the ten seconds are not the grace's at all** — the grace never even started, which means for those channels **neither
> direction ended**. The visitor did close (the probe uses a context manager, §4.417), so the **send direction never got to
> its EOF**: it is blocked writing into the tunnel and never returns to read the visitor's socket again.
>
> **That is the last link and it points at `Conn::write`'s admission** — the credit/buffer gate this record studied from the
> other side long ago. A churn channel whose reply is written while the lane is at its ceiling has nowhere to put the bytes,
> so its send loop parks, the visitor's EOF is never read, the group never ends, and the slot is held until something else
> kills it.
>
> **The next measurement is exact and needs one line**: on the send loop, log when it parks in `write` (stream, bytes,
> which bound refused: credit, window or buffered) and when it leaves. That distinguishes "blocked on space" from "blocked
> on the peer".

> **§4.418 (the characterisation the objective asked for): the pool is too narrow, and the reason is the hold time.**
> Counting the workload's own occupancy:
>
> | population | streams held | for how long |
> |---|---|---|
> | `rr-16` | 16 | the whole stage — its sockets are kept, not closed per request (`rr.py:_connect`) |
> | bulk (`-n`) | ~8 | the whole stage |
> | churn, 13.5 a second | **~135 at a 10 s hold** | 1.3 ms of work, then the slot waits |
>
> **135 + 24 ≈ 159 of 224 slots (71 %)**, before any burst, and the per-lane limit of 56 is reached sooner than the pool
> total when placement is uneven — which is exactly what the logs show (all four lanes at 56, 145 ceiling lines).
>
> **So both statements are true and they are the same statement**: the pool is too narrow **because** a millisecond
> exchange costs a slot for about ten seconds. Halve the hold and the occupancy halves; double `tunnels` and the ceiling
> doubles. **Which of the two to change is a product decision, and it is the user's** — the objective says not to change
> product configuration unilaterally.
>
> **What the code cannot do on its own**: two fixes aimed at the release path (the early-cut grace, `3c0f98c`) changed
> nothing measurable, so the ten seconds are not a stray wait in `spawn_grace` that a condition can remove. They are the
> time this workload's channels genuinely spend open in the forwarder.

> **§4.417: the probe does close, and the ten seconds do look like the grace.** `run_churn`'s `ping` uses
> `with socket.create_connection(...) as sock`, so the visitor's socket gets its FIN when the block exits. The client's send
> loop should see that EOF, `sender.finish()`, end that direction — and **start the grace**, which cuts the other one ten
> seconds later. `live_gt_10s = 56` with `live_gt_60s = 4` is exactly the shape of "held just over ten seconds".
>
> **So the grace is very likely the holder after all, and §4.416's dismissal was too quick**: the early-exit condition
> `delivered >= highest` was compared on `Frames`, which counts **data frames** and keeps advancing while a reply is in
> flight, so it may have been false at every 250 ms poll for exactly the groups that matter.
>
> **The condition to use instead**: cut when **both directions are finished** — the send loop has ended (visitor EOF seen)
> **and** the receive direction has delivered everything **and** the stream has carried its fin. That is a state, not a
> race, and it needs the receive loop to publish "no more frames will arrive" rather than "delivered == highest so far".
>
> **§4.416 (the grace fix is in and the wedge survives — reverted).** With `3c0f98c` in, the twin still read
> `opened_len 56`, `live_gt_10s 56`, **145 ceiling lines, 140 expiries, 3 wedges (75.075 s)** while the product arm stayed
> clean. So ending the grace early changes nothing here, and it was **reverted** (`a3ea939`).
>
> **And the reason is now obvious in the code**: `wait_until_idle` only runs **when one direction has already ended**
> (`spawn_grace` is spawned on that event). The streams that occupy the slots are the ones where **neither direction
> ends** — the group is alive in both directions, so no grace ever starts and nothing cuts it.
>
> **So the 10–60 s holds are not the grace's**: they are groups that stay open because **the visitor's connection stays
> open** (or a copy blocks). That is §4.368's shape, and the next question is exact: for a churn channel that should be
> finished, which side is still open sixty seconds later.

> **§4.415 (incorrect as a root cause; kept for the record): the half-close grace waits ten seconds of idle.**
> `stripe.rs:1075`–`1101`: when one direction of a forwarding group ends, `spawn_grace` calls `wait_until_idle`, whose own
> doc says it *"wait[s] until a group has made **no progress** for ten seconds"*, and only then aborts the other direction.
>
> **Ten seconds is the whole defect**, and the arithmetic closes on it:
>
> ```
> churn openings          13.5 a second   (§4.377)
> × grace                 10 s            (this function)
> = streams held          ≈135            — against a pool of 4 × 56 = 224
> measured live            live_gt_10s = 56, live_gt_60s = 4   (§4.414)
> ```
>
> **A millisecond exchange occupies a slot for ten seconds**, so the churn's own rate is multiplied by the grace and the
> pool fills; the ceiling then refuses the next channel, the pairing gathers nothing, and the visitor waits out two
> five-second budgets. **Every number this record has collected is a consequence of that one constant.**
>
> **The fix is to cut a direction that has nothing left to drain instead of waiting ten seconds for it**: the grace already
> computes `missing = highest - delivered` before it fires — when that is zero the receive direction has delivered
> everything and can be cut at once. A short idle bound (a few hundred milliseconds) covers the genuine tail. **That is
> the next change, and it is the last one this defect needs.**

> **§4.414 (the occupants are 10–60 seconds old).** On the arm that wedged (4 wedges, 10.01 s, 67 ceiling
> lines), the live histogram reads:
>
> ```
> opened_len max = 56   live_gt_1s = 56   live_gt_10s = 56   live_gt_60s = 4
> ```
>
> **Fifty-six live streams, every one older than 10 s, only four older than 60 s.** So the occupants are streams **ten to
> sixty seconds old** — while the requests they serve take milliseconds (§4.377: median 1.3 ms). The clean arm never passed
> 6, with the same 4 old ones (its root stream and a few long-lived channels).
>
> **That is a leak of ten to sixty seconds, not of minutes**, and it explains every earlier censored reading: `held_*`
> never saw them because they had not ended, and the completed-lease mean was diluted by thousands of short streams that
> did end. `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 300 s, so a group that never finishes is only cut at five minutes — far beyond the
> 10–60 s this measures.
>
> **So the defect is the forwarding group's end condition** (§4.407's next instrument is now the right one: which direction
> ends last, and by what). Fix that and the ceiling stops being reached for reasons the workload does not explain.

> **§4.413 (first reading of the live histogram): on a clean arm, most live streams are already old.** A run whose both arms
> were clean (`0 / 0`) read `opened_len` max **4–5** and `live_gt_60s` max **3–4** — so **three or four of the four or five
> live entries are older than a minute**, on an arm with no wedge at all.
>
> **Two readings of that, and the second is the interesting one**: either the lane's root stream plus a couple of long-lived
> channels is the whole population (the root is as old as the lane, §4.367), or `stream_opened` **keeps entries whose
> streams are already closed** — the §4.365 thread, which was withdrawn when the root stream explained *one* entry, not
> four. **Four per lane is not a leak that fills 56**, but the question is now exact: does that number grow on the arm that
> wedges?
>
> **So the next run must be one that wedges**, and the reading to take is the `opened_len` / `live_gt_*` pair **on the
> ceiling lines**, not the run's maximum.

> **The live age histogram is BUILT (`64a7e30`) and its reading is the first thing the next stretch must take.**
> `mhd window` now carries `live_gt_1s`, `live_gt_10s`, `live_gt_60s`, counted from the lane's own `stream_opened` map — the
> first aggregate in this record that counts **live** streams instead of completed ones. Read it against `opened_len`:
> **`live_gt_60s == 1` is the lane's root stream and is normal; `> 1` is the occupant this record could not see.**
>
> **A plan that was made before the map was read**, kept for the record: `Conn::stream_opened` is already a map of live
> stream id → creation `Instant`, and `queue_sizes()`/`oldest_opened_ms()` already read it. So the live age histogram is
> three filters over that map, printed beside `opened_len` on the mhd window line:
>
> ```rust
> pub(crate) fn live_ages(&self, now: Instant) -> (usize, usize, usize) {
>     let mut one = 0; let mut ten = 0; let mut sixty = 0;
>     for at in self.stream_opened.values() {
>         let age = now.duration_since(*at);
>         if age >= Duration::from_secs(60) { sixty += 1; }
>         else if age >= Duration::from_secs(10) { ten += 1; }
>         else if age >= Duration::from_secs(1) { one += 1; }
>     }
>     (one, ten, sixty)
> }
> ```
>
> and `live_gt_1s/live_gt_10s/live_gt_60s` on the window line. **Note the lane's root stream is one of them** (§4.367) —
> expect at least one entry in whichever bucket covers the lane's age, and subtract it mentally.
>
> **An earlier plan, kept for the record**: it needs a data structure, not a line: a histogram of **live** lease ages — count the
> currently charged streams older than 1 s, 10 s and 60 s. `StreamLease` already carries `charged_at`; the pool keeps only
> a counter, so this needs a small registry of charge times (push on charge, remove on drop) or an age histogram updated
> at both ends. **That is the first task of the next stretch, and nothing else should be attempted before it.**
>
> **Two traps paid for in full, do not repeat them**: `cargo clippy --all-targets` passing does **not** mean the build is
> green — the minimal `server,client` build must be run too (it caught 19 errors once and 3 another time); and a
> statistic measured on `Drop` says nothing about what is still alive.

### The account that was here before


> **A trap for whoever adds that counter.** `run_mux_data_channel` is compiled in the **minimal** `server,client` build too,
> with its multiplex pieces `cfg`-stripped (`stripe` becomes `()`, `open_stripe_stream`/`tunnel.open_stream`/
> `write_tunnel_prologue`/`PROLOGUE_BUDGET` vanish). Adding a call or a constant there compiles in the default build and
> **fails the minimal one with ~19 errors** — which is exactly what happened this round: the edits were discarded with
> `git reset HEAD -- src/ && git checkout -- src/` and the tree verified green at `6df43cc`. **Run
> `cargo clippy --all-targets --no-default-features --features server,client -- -D warnings` before staging anything in
> that function.**

> **§4.412: the capacity is 4 × 56 = 224, and the churn needs about fourteen.** `ceiling()` is
> `tunnel_ceiling(self.inner.shared.stream_cap)` — **per tunnel** (`multiplex.rs:2204`), and the refusal message says so
> ("every tunnel is at its stream ceiling; this pool is at its configured tunnel …"). So the pool really can carry 224
> concurrent streams, and §4.377's opening rate times any plausible churn hold time is an order of magnitude below that.
>
> **Which means the occupants are not the churn's concurrency at all.** Something else is charged to those lanes in
> hundreds — the `rr-16` and bulk stages are the only other producers, and the A/A contrast (§4.410) says the difference
> between the arms is not theirs. The one population that fits both statements is **churn streams that never ended**, and
> §4.411 explains why the completed-lease average could not show them.
>
> **So the one measurement that settles it is the live age histogram** (§4.411), and it is the only thing left to build.

> **§4.411: the held-time line counts *completed* leases, so it cannot describe the ones that are stuck.** `note_held` runs
> on `Drop` — it records the hold time of streams that **ended**. A stream that is still holding a slot when the pool
> refuses is **not** in that average at all, so `held_mean_ms=1044` describes the population that *did* end and says
> nothing about the occupant.
>
> **And the arithmetic says the same**: 13.5 openings a second (§4.377) times a 1 044 ms mean is **≈ 14 concurrent
> streams**, nowhere near the 224 the ceiling implies. The lines agree with each other and disagree with the ceiling, which
> is what a censored statistic does.
>
> **So the ceiling's occupant is the tail that never drops** — and the only way to see it is a **live** count by hold age,
> not a completed-lease average. That is the next instrument: on the ceiling line, report how many *currently charged*
> streams are older than 1 s, 10 s and 60 s. `StreamLease` already carries `charged_at`; the pool needs to walk its live
> leases (or keep an age histogram updated on charge).

> **§4.410: the bulk cannot be the occupant, because it runs on both arms.** The soak's timeline runs the same bulk stage
> in the same conditions on the product arm and the twin, so whatever the bulk holds is held on **both** — while the
> ceiling was reached **133 times on one arm and once on the other** (§4.406). The occupancy that differs between them is
> therefore **not the bulk's**: it is the population that also differs, which is the churn's thousands of short streams.
>
> **So §4.406's reading stands after all, with a better argument than the mean**: a stream that should have been released
> at the end of a millisecond exchange is still charged to a lane, and on one arm that happens often enough to fill all
> four. §4.409's caveat is answered by the A/A contrast rather than by the aggregate.
>
> **The next measurement is still the split one** — the churn population's own hold time — but it is now a confirmation
> rather than a fork: if it reads milliseconds the ceiling is a rate problem and the 133-vs-1 contrast has another cause,
> and that would be worth knowing before any fix.

> **§4.409 (a caveat that must be settled before the next conclusion): the 1 s mean may be the bulk stages, not a leak.**
> The soak's timeline runs a bulk (iperf3) stage in every condition, and a bulk stream **legitimately** lives for its
> stage. The **187 s maximum sits right against the 180 s stage length**, and a mean of ~1 s over 13 730 leases is exactly
> what a mix of thousands of millisecond churn streams and a handful of 180-second bulk streams produces.
>
> **So §4.406's sentence — "a stream is held a thousand times longer than its request" — compares a churn request with an
> aggregate that includes the bulk streams, and that comparison is not sound.** The measurement is right; the *reading* is
> unproven.
>
> **The next measurement must separate them**: `held_mean_ms` per call site, or simply the same line restricted to streams
> whose request took under 100 ms (the churn), which is exactly the population the ceiling is starving. If the churn's own
> holds are milliseconds, the ceiling is a rate problem and the pool is simply too narrow for 16 connections a second.

> **§4.408: the carrier has no one-second hold timer either.** The only one-second constants in `src/transport/mhd/` are a
> log throttle (`conn.rs:422`, "one log a second, however many writes the gate refuses") and the pump's starve check
> (`pump.rs:878`). Neither defers a release. So the 1 044 ms mean is **not a timer anywhere** in the carrier, the
> forwarder or the pool: it is how long the forwarding groups of this workload actually live.
>
> **That makes the group-exit instrument of §4.407 the only remaining measurement**, and its question narrower: of the
> groups that live a second, which direction ended last and how.

> **§4.407: the second is not a timer.** The only one-second sleeps near the data-channel path are a statistics reporter
> loop (`client.rs:1542`) and the pool's own tick (`multiplex.rs:179`), neither of which holds a lease. So the 1 044 ms mean
> is **the distribution of forwarding-group lifetimes**, not a fixed grace — which fits a distribution whose maximum is
> 187 s: some groups take a second to finish and one took three minutes.
>
> **The next instrument is on the group's end**: log, per group, which direction finished first, when the second one ended,
> and whether it ended by EOF, by the half-close grace, or by `FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (300 s). One line at the group's exit
> (`stripe.rs`, where `spawn_inner`'s select finishes) names the shape of the 1 s and of the 187 s, and those two are the
> whole of this defect.

> **§4.406 (THE MEASUREMENT): a stream is held for a second on average and 187 seconds at worst.**
> ```
> pool-stats: pool still at its stream ceiling count=4 ceiling=56
>             held_count=13730  held_mean_ms=1044  held_max_ms=187401
> ```
> On the arm that wedged (3 wedges, 90.09 s; 133 ceiling lines) against 1 ceiling line on the clean one.
>
> **A churn request lives milliseconds (§4.377: median 1.3 ms) and its stream is held 1 044 ms on average — a thousand
> times longer — with a worst case of 187 seconds.** That is the ceiling's cause: 4 lanes × 56 slots are occupied by
> streams that have already served their request, so the pool refuses the next channel and the visitor waits out two
> pairing budgets.
>
> **The defect is therefore the stream's release, not the pool's size** — and the next question is exactly one: what keeps
> a `StreamLease` alive for a second (and sometimes three minutes) after its visitor's exchange is over. The candidates
> are the forwarding group's two directions (a copy that never sees EOF) and the half-close grace
> (`FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 300 s, which brackets the 187 s maximum).

> **§4.405: the exact path, read and ready (one edit, no guessing left).** `PoolState` is
> `{ entries: Vec<PoolEntry>, next_cursor, count, handover }` (`multiplex.rs:620`), and each `PoolEntry` carries the
> tunnel's `counters: Arc<TunnelCounters>`. So the one line to add at the ceiling site is:
>
> ```rust
> let (held_count, held_mean_ms, held_max_ms) = {
>     let state = self.inner.state.lock();
>     let mut count = 0u64;
>     let (mut nanos, mut max_nanos) = (0u64, 0u64);
>     for entry in &state.entries {
>         let (c, _, _) = entry.counters.held_peek();
>         count += c;
>         nanos += entry.counters.held_nanos_value();
>         max_nanos = max_nanos.max(entry.counters.held_max_value());
>     }
>     (count, if count == 0 { 0.0 } else { nanos as f64 / count as f64 / 1e6 }, max_nanos as f64 / 1e6)
> };
> debug!(… count, ceiling, held_count, held_mean_ms, held_max_ms, "pool-stats: pool still at its stream ceiling");
> ```
>
> **Or, simpler and equally decisive**: put `held_peek()` on `TunnelCounters` as a three-value reader (the `take_held`
> at `multiplex.rs:409` already computes exactly those three, only clearing them), call it per entry, and print the sum.
> **The first version of that needs a non-clearing reader; that is the only new code.**

> **§4.404: where the counters live, so the next edit is a read-first one.** `TunnelPool` is
> `{ inner: Arc<TunnelPoolInner> }` (`multiplex.rs:1004`), and `TunnelPoolInner` holds `shared: Arc<PoolShared>`,
> `state: Mutex<PoolState>`, `dial`, `preferred` and `pins`. The per-tunnel `TunnelCounters` are therefore reached
> **through `state`** (or through whatever `PoolState`'s entries carry), **not** as a method on the pool — which is why
> the two attempts at `self.held_peek()` failed to compile.
>
> **The next edit is one read followed by one line**: find the field of `PoolState`'s tunnel entry that holds
> `Arc<TunnelCounters>`, sum `held_peek()` across the entries, and print `(count, mean_ms, max_ms)` on the ceiling line.
> Two attempts have already died on guessing that path instead of reading it.

> **§4.403: the leases are genuinely held, and their hold time is already measured but not printed there.** `StreamLease`'s
> `Drop` (`multiplex.rs:495`) decrements the tunnel's stream count unconditionally, so the ceiling is not a counter leak: 224
> leases really are alive when the pool refuses. And `TunnelCounters::note_held` already accumulates **count, mean ms and
> max ms** of hold time (`multiplex.rs:400`), but the line that fires at the ceiling —
> `pool-stats: pool still at its stream ceiling … count=4 ceiling=56` — does not print them.
>
> **The next instrument is one line: put `held_count/held_mean_ms/held_max_ms` on that ceiling line.** If the mean hold time
> is milliseconds, the leases turn over and the ceiling is a *rate* problem; if it is seconds, something is holding streams
> far past their request and that holder is the defect.

> **§4.402 (THE ANSWER, and it was already in the log).** The caller of `run_mux_data_channel` has always logged the error —
> `debug!("{:#}", e)` at `client.rs:3004` — and a soak's client log contains, in order of count:
>
> ```
> 165  Failed to run the data channel: Failed to open a multiplexed data channel:
>      every tunnel is at its stream ceiling; this pool is at its stream ceiling
> 164  the pool refused a data channel: every tunnel is at its stream ceiling; …
> 37   Failed to run the data channel: Failed to read data cmd: early eof
> ```
>
> **165 — exactly the gap of unfinished opens measured in the same run (12 528 started, 12 363 finished).** No new instrument
> was needed; every one of the sixty-six, the forty-five and the 165 were **the pool refusing the channel because every
> tunnel is at its stream ceiling**.
>
> **So the whole chain is closed, and it ends where §4.322 first pointed**: the client opens a channel, the pool refuses it
> because all four lanes are at 56 streams, the open returns that error, the server's pairing gathers nothing and expires,
> and the visitor is refused 5–10 s later. **The defect is the ceiling being reached at all** — streams that are not
> released — not anything in the pairing, the delivery or the open path.
>
> **The next question is therefore the one holding the ceiling**: why a lane holds 56 live streams when the probes' own
> concurrency is single digits (§4.376) and every channel is retired within 5 ms (§4.397). That is the last link, and it is
> inside the pool's accounting.

> **§4.401 (measured): the unfinished opens are not stalled at all — they fail.** With all three bounds and counters in, a
> run whose twin wedged ten times (45.067 s) read **`prologue_stalled` 0, `open_stripe_stalled` 0, `open_plain_stalled` 0**,
> while the gap persisted: **12 528 opens started, 12 363 finished** (165 unfinished) and 195 pairing expiries.
>
> **So those opens do not wait — they return an error**, and the only paths left that do so are the two propagated ones
> (`open_stripe_stream(...)?` and `tunnel.open_stream()?`) and the prologue write (whose failure counter is also 0). **The
> error is swallowed by the caller and nothing counts it.**
>
> **The next instrument is the last one this chain needs**: count and log the **error** returned by those two opens — not a
> stall, an error — with its text. That text names the cause directly, and the two candidates the record already has are a
> pool that will not place (no lane below the ceiling) or a group released under the open.

> **§4.400 (measured): the correspondence is exact and neither guard fires.** On a run whose twin wedged four times: the
> client **started 19 039 opens and finished 18 994** — a gap of **45** — and the server logged **45 pairing expiries**.
> Both guards read **0**: `prologue_stalled` (the write) and `open_budget_expired` (the placement).
>
> **So the gap is real, reproducible, and equal to the expiries in every run measured** (66 = 66, then 45 = 45), and it is
> **not** in either of the two awaits that now carry a bound. The open is stranded somewhere else in that task — the only
> remaining candidate is inside `open_stripe_stream` itself, below the bound the reverted build had and this one does not.
>
> **The next instrument therefore wraps the two calls separately and counts each**: a bound and a counter on
> `open_stripe_stream` and on `tunnel.open_stream` individually. With the prologue ruled out by measurement, the answer is
> one of those two, and the counters will say which without another hypothesis.

> **§4.399 (measured, and it named the wrong await).** No panic in the client log, so the task is not dying that way: **it is parked.**
> And the one await between `channel open started` and `channel open finished` that has **no bound and no guard** is the
> write itself — `write_tunnel_prologue` → `conn.write_all(...).await`. `prologue_failed` counts `Err`, not a **hang**, and
> `OPEN_BUDGET` (in the run that had it) wrapped `open_stream`, not this write.
>
> **So the sixty-six are opens parked in `Conn::write` waiting for room in a stream's send buffer** — the admission this
> record has studied from the other side all along (`MAX_BUFFERED`, the opening/small-flight reserves), reached through the
> one call that writes **before** any pump has had a chance to drain.
>
> **The next instrument is two lines and it is the last one needed**: a `tokio::time::timeout` around the prologue write
> with a short budget, logging `group` and the elapsed time when it expires. If it fires for exactly those sixty-six, the
> hang is proven and the fix is in the admission — a stream's first prologue write must not wait behind a full buffer.

> **§4.398 (measured, and it is the whole of the gap).** The sixty-six are exactly the opens that never finished: of the 66
> groups whose pairing expired without a delivery, **66 started and 0 finished**, and over the whole run **13 937 opens
> started against 13 871 finished — a difference of exactly 66**.
>
> **And neither guard fired**: `open_budget_expired` is 0 (the placement never returned late) and `prologue_failed` is 0
> (the write never failed). An open that neither completed, nor failed, nor timed out, in a task that was scheduled within
> 6 µs — is an **open whose task was dropped mid-flight**. That is the cancellation this record first suspected in
> §4.384 and could not confirm; it is now the only shape left.
>
> **The next instrument is on the drop**: a guard on the open task that logs when it is dropped before it reaches either
> end (`group`, and the stage it had reached). A `Drop` on a small state struct in `spawn_data_channel`'s future does it,
> and the stage names which await it was parked in.

> **§4.397 (measured): the transport delivers what the client sends, and the missing ones were never sent.** On the wedging
> arm: the client logged `first byte of a stream sent` for **7 267 distinct stream ids**, the server logged a first packet
> for **7 266 distinct ids** — a difference of **one**. So every stream whose first byte left the client arrived at the
> server.
>
> **And 6 744 of those streams were retired within 5 ms of being created** (`mhd stream retired  age_ms<5`), which is what
> a churn series looks like from inside: open, one request, retire.
>
> **So the sixty-six are channels the client opened and whose first byte was never sent at all** — the open finished, the
> task ran, and the pump never put the selector on the wire for them. That is the last link, and it is on the client's
> send path rather than in the carrier.

> **§4.396 (measured, and it closes the server side completely).** On the arm that wedged: the server created **13 874**
> streams (`first packet for an unknown stream`), **13 873** reached delivery, and **13 895** selectors were read. So the
> server saw essentially every channel it delivered — **and the sixty-six opened by the client never became streams
> there at all**. Their first packet never arrived.
>
> **Which leaves exactly one link and it is the carrier's**: a channel the client opens, whose packets the server never

> age_ms=…` for it says which.

> **§4.392 (measured, and thought to be the root cause).** The new line shows the expired groups **do** reach delivery with the
> right group — groups 7472, 7473 and 7581 each logged one `reached delivery` beside their one `pairing budget expired`.
> So `deliver(group, ch)` ran, with the number the client sent, and the pairing that had asked for that number still
> expired.
>
> **Which means `deliver` found no waiter for the group** and the channel fell through to the shared queue. And that is
> a race in the code this record has been reading all along:
>
> 1. `pair_striped_group` **sends** the requests (`data_ch_req_tx.send(...)`, `server.rs:4575`);
> 2. then its `select!` polls `data_ch_rx.take_for(group)` — and `take_for` is what **registers the group's slot**
>    (`groups.insert(group, tx)`, `server.rs:3877`).
>
> A channel that arrives between (1) and (2) finds no slot, is delivered to the shared queue instead, and the pairing
> waits for a slot that was registered a microsecond too late. The comment in `take_for` — *"Registered before the first
> look, so a delivery landing between the look and the wait is not lost"* — protects the wrong interval: between the
> **look and the wait**, not between the **ask and the look**.
>
> **Correction before implementing (this round's read of `deliver`).** `deliver` logs `mhd channel delivered` **only on a
successful `try_send`**, and the expired groups never log it. So the slot was **not absent** — `try_send` returned
`Full` or `Closed`, and both of those fall through to the shared queue (`server.rs:3812`). `Closed` means the receiver
was already gone, i.e. the pairing had **`unclaim`ed** its slot — on an earlier iteration, or when an attempt ended.

**So the race is not "ask before register" but "unclaim before arrival"**: the pairing gives up its slot at the end of an
attempt, asks again for the next one, and a channel that was in flight for the old slot arrives when that slot is closed,
is pushed to the shared queue, and the pairing — now waiting on a *new* slot — does not look at the shared queue for
that group again in the same attempt.

**And the group id itself is allocated inside the retry loop** (`server.rs:4572`–`4573`: `'gather: loop { let group =
GROUP_IDS.fetch_add(1, …) }`), so **every attempt is a new group** and the previous one is `unclaim`ed on the way out
(`4683`). A channel in flight for the old group therefore arrives at a closed slot, is pushed to the shared queue, and
is never seen by the pairing — which by then is asking under a different number. **That is the whole defect**: a pairing
that needs a second attempt cannot receive the channel the first attempt had already caused the client to open.

**The fix is two lines, and it is the smallest in this record:**

1. move `let group = GROUP_IDS.fetch_add(…)` and `let group_bytes`/`cmds` **out of** `'gather: loop` — one group per
   visitor, not per attempt;
2. **do not `unclaim` on the retry path** (`4683`): the slot must outlive the attempt that failed, so a late channel
   lands in it and the next `take_for(group)` returns immediately.

**Earlier note on the fix (superseded):**

1. **keep the slot alive across attempts** — register once per group and hold the receiver across the retry loop instead
   of unclaiming it at each attempt's end;
2. only then the ask-before-register ordering, which this entry still recommends but as a second step.

**The fix that was specified before this correction (kept for the record):**

1. **`ServerChannels::register(&self, group: u32) -> Option<mpsc::Receiver<C>>`** — the registration half of
   `take_for` (`server.rs:3870`–`3885`): allocate `mpsc::channel(1)`, `groups.insert(group, tx)`, return `rx`; `None` for
   `group == 0`.
2. **`take_for` becomes `take_registered(&self, group: u32, claim: Option<&mut Receiver<C>>)`** — its loop unchanged
   except that it no longer registers (the `claim` is already in the map), and `unclaim` still runs on every exit.
3. **`pair_striped_group`**: `let mut claim = data_ch_rx.register(group);` **before** the `for index in 0..stripes` send
   loop (`server.rs:4575`), and the `select!` arm becomes `take_registered(group, claim.as_mut())`.

Then the window between the ask and the slot's registration is gone: a channel that arrives a microsecond after the
request finds its slot, `deliver` sends into it, and the pairing takes it.

**The judgement, on the same soak**: `pairing budget expired` zero, `wedge_count` zero, and `reached delivery` equal to
`mhd channel taken` for every group.

> into `groups` before the send loop, then have `take_for` use the already-registered receiver.

> **Earlier (end of the 80 rounds):** `data_ch_rx.take_for(group)` **does** filter by group (`server.rs:3868`

>
> After the take the loop does one thing before counting it:
>

> if write_and_flush(&mut ch, &cmds[gathered.len()]).await.is_ok() {

>     let _ = data_ch_req_tx.send(DataChannelRequest::ReleaseGroup(group_bytes));

> **Status at the end of this stretch: the defect is OPEN and the finalisation is NOT written.** Twenty-two rounds of
> the goal above went into it. What follows is the state, the seventeen explanations that are dead, and the one
> measurement that is ready and not yet read.

**Measured, and it moves the defect out of the client's open entirely**: joining the 48 groups whose pairing expired
against the client's own open lines — **all 48 started and 34 finished**. So for thirty-four pairings the client opened
the channel, wrote its prologue and logged the finish, and the server's pairing still gathered **nothing**.

**That is the last link and it is a routing one**: the channel is fully introduced — 14 547 channels accepted, every
selector read (§4.378) — and it does not land on the pairing waiting for its group. The group travels in the prologue;
what has not been compared is **the bytes the client writes there against what the server parses** — width, order, or
which side of the pairing the value is stamped from.

**Next, and it is one comparison**: `write_tunnel_prologue`'s group field against the server's read of it, and against
`pair_striped_group`'s `group_bytes`. If they differ in width or order, every channel lands on the wrong pairing or on
none, which is exactly `gathered=0` with a channel that opened and finished.

**Earlier this round, and still true**: with `1fc7323` built and a run where both arms wedged (1 and 3,
max 10.01 s), `started_us` reads **p50 6 µs, p99 17–19 µs, max 141 µs** over 17 073 and 19 513 channels. The spawned
tasks are **scheduled immediately**; there is no runtime starvation.

**So the channel that never finishes is not waiting for the scheduler, not waiting in the placement (§4.383's bound never
fired) and not failing its prologue (§4.384's counter is zero).** The remaining shape is that the task is **cancelled
mid-open** — dropped by whatever owns it when the visitor goes — which is why no finish line and no error line exist.

**The next instrument therefore measures cancellation**: a line when the task is dropped before it logs a finish, joined
by group. If those groups are the ones whose pairing expired, the chain closes: the visitor gives up, the task is
cancelled, the channel never arrives, the pairing gathers nothing.

**Superseded note** (kept because it cost a run): `1fc7323` prints `started_us` (spawn → first poll) on the `channel open finished`
line, which is the field that says whether a spawned data-channel task is *scheduled*. `spawn_data_channel`'s own
comment is the reason it matters: *a spawned task not scheduled for a second is a saturated runtime, and the wait is
otherwise attributed to the carrier*. **Build release first** — the last attempt ran the previous binary and read zero
of them.

**Seventeen explanations are dead**, each with a reading against it: the pairing budget, the listener, the backlog, pool
saturation, the lane's stream ceiling, lane death, the build, the transmit queue, the write wake, the sealed refusal,
out-of-order initiation, the second arm, the arm's position, the pinned acknowledgement frontier, id reuse, the shared
topology, the host's load/CPU/IO/memory, "born bad", the forwarder leak, churn concurrency, the permanent stream-table
entry, the capacity ramp, the stale-claim refusal (§4.381), the placement bound (§4.383 — **reverted**, it made wedges
longer), and the prologue failure (§4.384 — the counter stays at zero).

**Three fixes remain in the tree** from this stretch, each correct on its own terms and test-covered, none of them this
defect: the buffer-ceiling reserve for openings (half the dropped visitors gone), the both-fins retirement, and the
registered-claim re-registration.

**What is measured and stands**: the wedge needs a campaign that starts the tool more than once (§4.337); the pool sits
at `count=4 ceiling=56` while every probe's own concurrency is single digits (§4.364, §4.376); the control-plane hop is
**122 µs** and the client starts the open **19 µs** later (§4.385 below); 43 pairings expire with `gathered=0` on an arm
that accepted 14 547 channels (§4.379); and the two `channel open` log lines live in **different functions** —
`open_data_channel` (3850) and `run_mux_data_channel` (1577) — so an open that starts and never finishes never reached
the second (§4.384).



**One defect is open and it blocks the finalisation.** It is: on a soak, a fresh dial is refused for 10–25 s
(`wedge_count` 6–9). Everything this line has established, and the fourteen explanations it has refuted, are in
§4.335–§4.382.

**The mechanism is now measured, and the next change is a bound.** For a group whose pairing expires, the client logs
`channel request read` (122 µs after the ask) and then `mhd channel open started` **19 µs later**, and **never** logs
`mhd channel open finished` — where a healthy channel logs both with `open_us=42`. So the open begins immediately and
hangs: placement waits for a lane below a ceiling that four lanes at 56 have already reached (§4.372), while the
server's two five-second budgets run out.

**§4.383 (this round): the bound did not fire and made it worse.** Measured with `d88ce7a` in:
product 6 wedges / **45.044 s**, twin 2 / **85.085 s**, 174 and 134 expired pairings, and `open_budget_expired` **0**
on both arms. So the open that never finishes is *not* waiting in the placement the bound wrapped, and the change
correlated with longer wedges — it is **reverted** (`git revert d88ce7a`, 410 tests green).

**§4.384 (measured): the prologue never fails either.** With `99dcf0f` in and the product arm wedging seven times
(max **160.16 s**), `prologue_failed` reads **0** and the error line never appears. So the missing `open finished` is
**not** a prologue failure.

**And the two log sites are in different functions** — `channel open started` is written by the control-command handler
(`client.rs:3857`) and `channel open finished` by the data-channel handler (`client.rs:1629`). A channel that logs the
first and never the second never reached the second: the open was *started* by the command handler and the data path
for it never ran.

**Which leaves the hand-off between those two functions**, and it is now read: `open_data_channel` (3850) logs
`started` and ends with

```rust
spawn_data_channel(active.args.clone(), tunnel, stripe, queued_at);
```

— the channel is **handed to a spawned task**, and `channel open finished` is written by `run_mux_data_channel` (1577),
which that task must reach. So `started` without `finished` means **the spawned task never got as far as the finish**,
and both things measured so far — the placement bound and the prologue — are inside that task and never fired.

**And the task's first-poll stamp already exists**: `spawn_data_channel` records `let spawned = Instant::now()`, and
its own comment says why — *"a spawned task that is not scheduled for a second is a runtime that is saturated, and the
wait is otherwise attributed to the carrier"*. Inside the task, `started_us = spawned.elapsed()` (`client.rs:2944`) is
taken at the **first poll** and handed to `run_mux_data_channel` (`:2956`), which prints it on the finish line.

**So a channel that is spawned and never runs would show a huge `started_us` on the channels that do finish** — the
distribution of that field is the measurement, and `grep -c started_us` over a whole run's client log returned **0**,
which means the field is not reaching the log in this build. Printing it is the next instrument, and it is one line.

**The instrument that was planned, kept for the record**: a line at its entry and a line after `open_stream` returns, so the three
possibilities separate — never scheduled, scheduled and blocked before the open, or open returned and the handler never
ran.

**What an earlier round located**, kept for the record: the only statement between `channel open started` and `channel open finished`
that can end the function is

```rust
write_tunnel_prologue(&mut stream, args.service_id, tunnel, group).await?;
```

Tracing shows a **healthy** channel logs both lines. A **failed** prologue write returns through that `?` and logs
**neither a finish nor an error** — the caller's error is swallowed. So the channel *was* placed (`open_stream`
returned a stream, which is why the bound never fired) and **the write that introduces it to the server failed**.

**And the previous paragraph's "bound never fires" is exactly consistent with that.**

**What an earlier paragraph said**, kept for the record: an open that starts 19 µs after the request and never logs
`open finished`, and a bound around `open_stream` that never fires. The two are only compatible if the open ends by a path that does not log a finish and
does not wait in that call — a cancellation, or an early error the handler swallows. **That is the next thing to
find**, and it is a code read of the handler, not a measurement.

**The fix that was attempted, and is now withdrawn:**


1. **bound the placement** — `open_stream` fails after a short budget instead of waiting indefinitely;
2. **answer the request** — on failure the client tells the server, so the pairing re-asks or the visitor fails fast
   instead of 10 s later;
3. **count the refusal** — one counter for "placement had no lane below the ceiling", which is the number that says
   whether lanes are still filling after the fix.

Then one `--aa` soak: `pairing budget expired` should fall to zero and `wedge_max_s` should stop being 10 s.

**The three timestamps exist** — the server's ask (`595b684`), the client's receipt (`client.rs:4096`, logging the
group it was asked for), and the open (`open_tagged("open")`). The one measurement nobody has joined is the *join*:
run one soak and pair the three by `group`.

**The join, on the logs already on disk**: all 28 groups whose pairing expired were groups the client had *seen*
(18 962 groups reached it in that run, and `comm -23` between the two sets is **empty**). So the request always
arrives; what is missing is the answer.

**Measured on a run that wedged** (product 3 wedges / 10.01 s, twin 1 / **175.175 s**; 41 and 142 pairing expiries):

```
server asked for group=14058   18:54:19.650326
client read the request        18:54:19.650448   ← 122 µs later
client read it again (retry)   18:54:24.651162   ← 5 s later, also instant
```

**The control-plane hop is 122 microseconds.** The request arrives instantly, twice, and the client still delivers no channel
for ten seconds. So the failure is entirely on the client's side of that hop: it is asked, it knows, and it does not
place a channel.

**That is placement**, and placement is where §4.372 left the count: the pool's four lanes hold 56 streams each and a
placement that cannot find a lane below the ceiling has nowhere to go.

**And the client's open never finishes.** Everything the client logged for that group:

```
18:54:19.650448  channel request read          group=14058  at_us=…
18:54:19.650467  mhd channel open started      group=14058  queued_us=1     ← 19 µs later
18:54:24.651162  channel request read (retry)  group=14058
18:54:24.651179  mhd channel open started      group=14058                  ← again
```

**No `channel open finished` for 14058 at all** (count: zero), while a healthy group logs both lines with `open_us=42`.
So the client begins the open, 19 µs after being asked, and **the open hangs** — which is why no channel ever reaches the
pairing and why the server's budget expires twice.

**That is the mechanism, and it is one line's worth of new information**: `open started` without `open finished` is a
placement that waits for a lane below the ceiling, on a pool whose four lanes are at 56 (§4.372). It waits while the
server's budget runs out twice.

**The question is now the answer.** The server's pairing asks the client for a data channel, waits
`PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` (5 s), retries, waits five more, and expires with `gathered=0` — twice, while the same server
accepted 14 547 channels from that client in the same run (§4.379, §4.382). Three timestamps per pairing decide it:

1. **server asks** — `pair_striped_group` (`src/core/server.rs:4539`), at its `data_ch_req_tx` send;
2. **client receives** — the control-channel command branch that handles the data-channel request;
3. **client answers** — `open_tagged("open")` (`src/transport/mhd/conn.rs`), already tagged per call site (§4.377).

Log all three with the `group` number, run one `--aa` soak, and join on `group`: if (1) has no (2) the request never
arrives; if (2) exists and (3) comes seconds later the answer is late. That is the whole of what remains.

**Do not repeat these** (each has a reading against it): pairing budget, listener, backlog, pool saturation, the lane's
stream ceiling, lane death, the build, the transmit queue, the write wake, the sealed refusal, out-of-order initiation,
the second arm, the arm's position, the pinned acknowledgement frontier, id reuse, the shared topology, the host's
load/CPU/IO/memory, "born bad", the forwarder leak, churn concurrency, the permanent stream-table entry, the capacity
ramp, and the stale-claim refusal (§4.381 — a real bug, fixed, not this one).
